phases.title: 1 RAR with the US 173rd Airborne Brigade
Establishing the Task Force at Nui Dat
Long Tan and taking hold of the province
The barrier minefield and a new rotation
Tet and the first battles beyond the province
Across the region: Bien Hoa and Long Khanh

notable.summary: 1 RAR's advance guard arrived at Bien Hoa, and the battalion built up to full strength over the following weeks, first patrolling with the US 2/503 Battalion and then on its own, at first without finding anything. The Prince of Wales Light Horse, with ten armoured personnel carriers, came under its command in mid-June. The battalion's first shots were fired by its mortars at a suspected enemy village on 25 June, and it first saw the enemy on 26 June, when two Viet Cong camps were found and five Viet Cong escaped. That day an accidental grenade explosion killed two Australians, fatally wounded a third and wounded seven, and killed one American and wounded two; the first casualty from enemy action was an officer of the Light Horse, wounded on 28 June.

A hand grenade went off accidentally in 1 RAR, killing two Australians outright and wounding eight, one of whom died of his wounds three days later in Saigon; one American was killed and two wounded. A court of inquiry was convened under the battalion's second-in-command, and a memorial service for those killed was held at Tan Son Nhut airport on 2 July.

On Operation 3/65, 6 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, clearing a track, saw a Viet Cong section of seven to ten men and opened fire. Two Australians were wounded. One Viet Cong was killed and three possibly wounded, and the Viet Cong withdrew west.

On Operation 3/65, 12 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, silently cleared a camp and then ambushed five Viet Cong coming back to it along a track, killing one and possibly wounding two. The others escaped towards a nearby village; the platoon withdrew for artillery and air strikes on the village, which fell wide, and a later search found nothing.
Two soldiers of 12 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, were wounded by shrapnel when a booby trap exploded, and were evacuated.

On Operation 3/65, 10 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, destroying two ox carts, was fired on by about two Viet Cong. One Australian was wounded in the face and evacuated. The Viet Cong disappeared while the platoon secured the area for the medical helicopter; one may have been wounded.

On Operation 3/65, B Company, 1 RAR, found and destroyed a camp for about 100 men, with huts including one set up as a lecture theatre, surrounded by an extensive trench and bunker system. It had not been occupied for four to six months.
On Operation 3/65, B Company, 1 RAR, found an ambush position for 200 to 300 men, with weapon pits unoccupied for six to nine months. It was too large to destroy.

On Operation 6/65, 6 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, at a halt, met two Viet Cong coming from the north. When challenged they tried to escape and threw a grenade, and both were killed; one was a woman. One Australian was wounded by the grenade and evacuated.
On Operation 6/65, 2 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, had a contact with a section of Viet Cong, who fled after the first exchange of fire. Two Australians were wounded and evacuated.
On Operation 6/65, A Company, 1 RAR, saw an armed Viet Cong, who fled north at once.
C Company, 1 RAR, moved out by armoured personnel carrier to join 7 Platoon in searching the area of a reported tunnel, but found nothing and returned to base, leaving 7 Platoon in the area.
On Operation 6/65, 4 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, found a camp and fired on three Viet Cong in it, who escaped north leaving two blood trails. The camp and a cache of two tons of rice were destroyed.

On Operation 6/65, 4 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, had a contact with three Viet Cong in a large camp, shooting one in the chest, as pools of blood later confirmed. All three vanished, presumably into well-hidden tunnels. The camp of 18 huts with weapon pits, bunkers and tunnels was destroyed and later hit by an air strike; Claymore mines and grenades were found.

2 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, found a camp of three huts, and while destroying it a grenade hidden in a hut roof exploded. One Australian and two New Zealand members of the artillery forward observer party received minor shrapnel wounds.

3 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, was fired on by a sniper, and one Australian was killed. The sniper fired again later; contact drills failed to find him, but a section sent to circle back onto the track caught him running away at about 100 metres. The next day another sniper, seen wearing a camouflage suit, fired on the platoon at a creek crossing and escaped a cordon and sweep. The platoon commander recommended trying to block a sniper's line of withdrawal once it was known, and found the grenade launcher extremely useful.
B Company, 1 RAR, had a contact with a Viet Cong, who was wounded but escaped, leaving a blood trail. A French bolt-action rifle was captured.

The forward scout of 22 Section, 8 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, on a search-and-destroy patrol, came upon three local-force Viet Cong standing in a clearing. Shots were exchanged, and one Viet Cong fell; the other two ran off, one apparently hit. When the two tried to come back for the body, fire from the section commander, scout and grenade launcher drove them off, and the body, a home-made rifle and ammunition were recovered.
B Company, 1 RAR, detained a Viet Cong suspect, who was handed over to the South Vietnamese Army.
C Company, 1 RAR, came upon a local-force Viet Cong, who escaped north.

On Operation Iron Triangle, men of 8 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, riding in armoured personnel carriers, hit an anti-tank mine made from a 105mm shell. Nine Australians were injured, with shrapnel wounds, a broken ankle, bruising and shock, and the American driver of the carrier was killed.

On Operation Iron Triangle, 8 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, leading the company along an unused track, set off a grenade booby trap with a trip wire tied to a branch; the forward section had passed it safely, but a member of platoon headquarters triggered it. Four Australians were wounded, including the platoon commander. Carriers with the medical officer and the commanding officer arrived within ten minutes. The lesson drawn was that troops must be well spaced at all times.

On Operation 13/65, 9 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, crossing a clearing, saw enemy moving on a track, and the commander of 3 Section laid an ambush, killing two Viet Cong and wounding four. The enemy counter-attacked and recovered one body, but the platoon captured two Chinese carbines, a home-made grenade, webbing, documents, food and equipment such as hammocks.
On Operation Iron Triangle, two booby traps went off near A Company, 1 RAR, injuring two Australian soldiers, a New Zealand gunner and a Vietnamese policeman.

On Operation Iron Triangle, the machine-gun group of 7 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, standing to in the company harbour, saw three Viet Cong creeping up to probe the perimeter, perhaps for a grenade attack. It waited until they were near the forward pits, then opened fire, killing two and wounding the third as he tried to escape; his body was found the next day. An M1 carbine and nine grenades were captured.

On Operation 13/65, 8 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, saw 18 Viet Cong crossing a creek north of its own crossing point and opened fire. The enemy fired back, fatally wounding one Australian in the throat. The platoon's return fire scattered them, and artillery and mortar fire was quickly brought down on the area.

On Operation New Life, 1 RAR moved into Vo Xu village with little trouble; 52 Viet Cong were captured and several rallied. Clearing the rest of the village that afternoon, 4 Platoon, B Company, part of the cordon, came under machine-gun and rifle fire from across the La Nga river from a force of just under a platoon, apparently covering other Viet Cong escaping by boat. The platoon returned fire, and mortars, artillery and helicopters engaged the enemy; the platoon commander estimated four enemy were killed, though no bodies were recovered. Two Australians were wounded, one of whom later died of his wounds.

On Operation New Life, after securing the road from Vo Dat to Chanh Duc, 1 RAR attacked Vo Xu village. C Company, mounted in 1 APC Troop's carriers, made a frontal assault down the road, with A Company in support and B and D Companies giving diversionary fire. It met light fire entering the village but quickly secured its objective; two Viet Cong were thought to have escaped through tunnels. Four Viet Cong were recorded killed.
On Operation New Life, 1 RAR assaulted the Brass Monkey feature after air and artillery bombardment, with B Company leading. The feature was deserted, with no sign the Viet Cong had ever occupied it.

On Operation New Life, after Vo Xu village had been cleared and handed to a South Vietnamese Army unit, 1 RAR returned to Chanh Duc. The next morning the northern part of Chanh Duc, known as Duc Hanh, was cleared of Viet Cong using helicopter Eagle Flights and an advance down the road through the village. Thirty-nine Vietnamese were detained, 20 of them confirmed Viet Cong and six ralliers, and clearing patrols found a workshop making sharpened bamboo stakes and two tons of rice.

On Operation New Life, D Company, 1 RAR, attacked Chanh Duc village. 12 Platoon, crossing the moat to seize a foothold, was fired on from the front and flank; it fought off 14 to 20 enemy near the church and pinned down an enemy section crossing a road, on which artillery was brought down, and detained seven suspects. With C Company in support and mortar and artillery fire on enemy positions, the company cleared down the line of the road, using tear gas on tunnels, and the Viet Cong fled north. Seven Viet Cong were killed. The platoon commander noted that ammunition carried was barely enough, and that the road made it easy to adjust artillery fire. The battalion, joined by the armoured personnel carrier troop, harboured in the village, where there was light enemy fire and sniping over the next nights.

On Operation Hump, 1 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, leading the company up a hill, came under fire from at least three machine-guns dug in at the top, and was pinned down. 3 Platoon tried to outflank to the left under heavy fire, easing the pressure but losing a man killed whose body could not be recovered. With the section commanders hit, darkness approaching and the Viet Cong outflanking them, both platoons withdrew under fire after a two-hour battle, unable to recover two of their men, listed missing believed killed, or equipment left on the hill, including two machine-guns. Four Australians were wounded, and enemy casualties are not known. The platoon sergeant recorded that the men worked magnificently; an inquiry was later held into the circumstances and the location of the two missing men.
On Operation Smash, 12 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, made contact with seven Viet Cong and called artillery onto them. Two Viet Cong were killed and two weapons captured.
On Operation New Life, B Company, 1 RAR, saw three suspected Viet Cong but could not catch them.

On Operation New Life, a Viet Cong rallied to C Company, 1 RAR, handing over a shotgun. The next day US military intelligence staff, with the battalion intelligence officer and an interpreter, took him to higher headquarters.
On Operation New Life, A Company, 1 RAR, found a Viet Cong hut and a cache of 100 cubic feet of rice nearby.
On Operation New Life, D Company, 1 RAR, found a sharpened-stake booby trap, and rice was recovered from a cache found earlier.
On Operation Smash, A Company, 1 RAR, found a cache of unhusked rice about 800 metres from the battalion harbour. 12 Platoon, D Company, relocated it, and the rice was destroyed.

12 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, clearing ground for a battalion harbour, walked into open country covered by a Viet Cong ambush of about four to seven men firing grenades and automatic weapons from well-built bunkers. Several soldiers were wounded, including the platoon commander, and two medics going forward to help the wounded were killed. A flanking attack by the company support section met no opposition, and the contact ended after 80 minutes; in all two Australians were killed and six wounded. Engineers later recovered clothing, rice, four Russian bolt-action rifles, ammunition and grenades from the bunkers, and the lessons drawn were to avoid open areas and keep medics back until it was safe to send them forward.

B Company headquarters, 1 RAR, was moving forward to meet a C Company patrol when a command-detonated mine exploded beside the main track, killing an officer and wounding a lance corporal. The company fired into a bamboo clump thought to hide the Viet Cong, and a second mine was set off. A radio operator taking over the wounded man's radio was then shot in the chest by a sniper from the same clump, and later a 4 Platoon machine-gunner passing the area was shot dead from there too.

Engineers used a Mighty Mite air blower to force smoke and tear gas into tunnels found by B Company, 1 RAR, to reveal other entrances and deny the tunnels to the enemy. An engineer corporal inspecting a shaft between tunnel levels lost his respirator and was asphyxiated by the gas and lack of oxygen, and was dead when rescuers reached him; two others were badly affected trying to reach him and were evacuated by helicopter. Important documents, including a well-produced propaganda photograph book, were found in the tunnels, and other caches of food, documents and medical stores were found inside the company perimeter. One cache had a hinged trapdoor wired to two grenade booby traps, which had failed because the grenade pins had been left splayed.

10 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, was moving to block for a sweep by 12 Platoon when the platoon commander and a section commander were fired on while investigating voices in some scrub. The area proved to be heavily fortified with trenches and was slowly cleared; during the sweep a sniper in another trench system hit a lance corporal and was himself shot, though his body was not found. The three or four enemy, armed with a sub-machine-gun and a French rifle, withdrew through the trenches into a tunnel. Two more Australians were wounded in the incident, and one Australian was recorded killed.

12 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, in ambush, saw about ten Viet Cong (two seen, others heard) coming to collect information from women in huts in the ambush area. The platoon let them come as close as possible before the stop group opened fire, killing two, whose bodies were later dragged away by the others; a search next morning found blood stains and drag marks. The lesson drawn was that safety catches must be off when a platoon is in ambush.

12 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, sweeping towards a blocking force, came into an area of widespread booby traps. The forward section accidentally set off a grenade booby trap, lightly wounding two men, while two or three enemy riflemen sniped at the platoon, which fired back. The lesson drawn was to beware of vines, cord and wires, as they are often connected to grenades.

On Operation Rolling Stone, later that night the same 1 Section, 4 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, ambush opened fire on about 15 enemy approaching the track, and the leading group went down. Ordered to withdraw, the patrol fired on another group of about ten as it pulled back, and then shot dead a Viet Cong who walked out of the rubber trees and tried to join them, even speaking to them, thinking they were his comrades. In all four Viet Cong were killed and two wounded and captured, and an AK-47, seven Chinese rifles, 15 grenades, a flare pistol, documents and equipment were taken. The company commander called it a highly commendable display of good soldiering: the patrol engaged 28 Viet Cong and inflicted considerable casualties without receiving fire in return.

On Operation Rolling Stone, a standing patrol from C Company headquarters, 1 RAR, opposite the company water point, saw a Viet Cong moving across its front, and every weapon opened fire at once. He was seen to drop and was heard going into the bush. A sweep next morning found nothing, but engineers found three bodies two days later.
On Operation 4/66, A Company, 1 RAR, made contact with two Viet Cong, killing one. Grenades and shovels were captured.

On Operation Roundhouse, E Troop, 17th Cavalry, a US unit, made contact with about a platoon of Viet Cong. One trooper was wounded, and one Viet Cong was killed or wounded. By evening 60,000 pounds of rice, two trucks, nine truck tyres and a jeep had been found and sent back to brigade.
On Operation 4/66, A Company, 1 RAR, fired on five Viet Cong, apparently wounding one, as a hat and sandal were later found. Later two more Viet Cong were contacted in the area.

On Operation 4/66, a machine-gunner of 9 Section, 9 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, on picket duty, heard movement on the track he covered and waited until a group of Viet Cong stopped and squatted behind a bush about 20 metres away before opening fire; the rest of the platoon fired at where his tracer showed. A clearing patrol next morning found two bodies, which were buried, from a group of at least four. A Chinese carbine, an AK-47, an SKS carbine, four sets of webbing, food, documents and ammunition were captured.
On Operation Silver City, the US armoured unit attached to 1 RAR made contact with about a squad of Viet Cong. An air strike on the place was estimated to have killed six and wounded six more.

On Operation Silver City, B Company, 1 RAR, reported that three men, two Australian engineers of 3 Field Troop and a US soldier, were wounded when a Claymore mine went off in front of a Mule, a light transport vehicle, carrying rice out of a captured cache.

On Operation Silver City, 2 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, was guarding engineers clearing booby traps from a cache of about 420 bags of rice before blowing it up. 6 Section, with two machine-guns, saw enemy approaching in open formation and held fire until they were eight to ten metres away; the enemy fired back at once, pinning down the section and platoon headquarters, until 1 Platoon's machine-gun fire across the front relieved the pressure. The five-minute fight was with about 25 Viet Cong of the mobile force. A sweep found two bodies and signs of a third being dragged away, and three Viet Cong were recorded killed; a Chinese light machine-gun, an AK-47, ammunition, equipment and documents were captured. One Australian was wounded and later flown out.

On Operation Silver City, 2 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, was setting a night ambush on a well-used track when 20 to 25 enemy arrived just before last light. The first group spotted the machine-gunner of the stop group, which opened fire before the enemy reached the main killing group, and for seven or eight minutes held them off as they tried a counter-ambush drill. The stop group then withdrew into the main position, and the patrol moved 40 metres back across the track, settled for the night and called artillery onto the enemy's escape route. At least three Viet Cong were killed, their bodies dragged away by their comrades.

On Operation Silver City, a patrol of the US armoured unit attached to 1 RAR made contact with a squad-sized group of Viet Cong. One American was killed; two Viet Cong were believed killed and two wounded.

On Operation Silver City, a 13-man patrol of 7 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, acting as a cut-off party, stopped to check its location when its lead machine-gunner saw two Viet Cong and fired. A tremendous volume of fire came back from right across the front, pinning the patrol down for five minutes until the Viet Cong suddenly broke contact. One Australian was killed. The enemy, estimated at more than 25 and well armed with automatic weapons, had been in an L-shaped ambush position, and mortar fire was called onto their line of withdrawal.

On Operation Abilene, a ten-man ambush from 11 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, was sprung by its machine-gun when five Viet Cong walked into the killing ground. Four fell and one escaped; grenades were thrown at two who seemed to be crawling away, and meanwhile another apparently crawled off. The patrol withdrew 100 metres for the night and searched at first light. Three Viet Cong were killed, one of them a woman, one was possibly killed and one escaped wounded; two weapons were recovered.

On Operation Abilene, the deputy commander of the US 1st Division, landing at the Binh Ba airstrip, reported Viet Cong moving away south-west. B Company, 1 RAR, and 1 APC Troop gave chase, and with company headquarters mounted in carriers caught about 12 Viet Cong fleeing into the jungle east of the rubber plantation. Two were killed by fire from the carriers and a third was hit and dropped his rifle, later found bloodstained; the Viet Cong did not fire back, and an air strike was put on their escape route. Grenades, a grenade launcher, two Garand rifles, documents, equipment and ammunition were captured. Lessons drawn were the value of quick follow-up and the need for better communication between carrier commanders and the infantry riding with them.
On Operation Abilene, two soldiers of A Company, 1 RAR, were wounded when they accidentally set off a booby trap.

On Operation Denver, as B Company, 1 RAR, moved into a harbour position, the leading section of 5 Platoon saw three Viet Cong coming up the ridge towards it. At about 60 metres they realised they were walking into an Australian patrol and turned to escape, and the platoon opened fire. One was killed at once, one was wounded and died within three minutes, and the third escaped wounded. A Garand rifle and an M1 carbine were captured.

On Operation Abilene, C Company, 1 RAR, made contact with three Viet Cong; one was wounded and captured and another wounded but escaped. Sweeps around the Binh Ba airstrip continued, with C Company capturing three suspects and B Company detaining 28, who were sent to the prisoner cage for questioning.

On Operation Abilene, 1 Section, 8 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, in a three-group ambush sited 15 metres off a moonlit track, opened fire as five Viet Cong hurried through the killing ground, followed closely by four more. Two were seen to fall before dust obscured the area; the Viet Cong did not fire back, and a quick search found no bodies, so the patrol moved to its alternative position. Next morning four heavy blood trails were found, and a wounded Viet Cong found along them was shot dead at about ten metres. A pack, hats, webbing, a magazine and trousers were captured; the section commander recommended siting all pits to fire into the killing ground and considering Claymore mines for ambushes.

A patrol from A Company, 5 RAR, met an enemy soldier who opened fire on them with an automatic weapon. 6 Platoon, B Company, which was collecting water nearby, was drawn into the contact. One Australian soldier died of his wounds; he had been shot by his own side during what may have been a contact with the enemy.
A platoon of B Company, 5 RAR, made contact with five enemy soldiers, killing one and wounding another. A rifle was found.

1 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, surrounded a hut where three enemy were searching for food, killing one and wounding and capturing another, who died during the night. The record notes they were probably civilians.

A B Company patrol, 5 RAR, saw four heavily armed enemy in green. Shortly afterwards an A Company patrol fired on a separate party of four in black carrying a mortar tube, who slipped away without firing back and were seen again later that morning. An enemy body found later may have come from this clash.

B Company, 5 RAR, clashed with four enemy near a bunker system, throwing grenades at them. Automatic weapons were captured behind a hut, a blood trail was found, and a wounded enemy officer was captured nearby soon afterwards.
3 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, made contact with three enemy near a cache of 12 tons of rice, opening fire on the first, who was dressed in black, and killing one.

A patrol of 10 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, was hit by enemy 120 mm and 82 mm mortar fire, killing two Australians and wounding four. Artillery fired on the 82 mm mortar positions, and an air strike hit the 120 mm mortar's.

D Company, 5 RAR, sweeping the north-east of Hoa Long for enemy mortar positions, came under light mortar fire, and one Australian was killed and three wounded, from D and E Platoon, 1 APC Squadron and 1 Field Squadron. Radar placed the mortars at Long Phuoc village, and artillery fired on them with unknown results.
A platoon of D Company, 5 RAR, made contact with eight enemy soldiers, killing three and recovering two rifles and an automatic weapon.
9 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, made contact with four Viet Cong, killing two. One grenade was thrown at the Australians, and there were no Australian casualties.
7 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, set off an enemy grenade booby trap, and two Australians were wounded and evacuated by helicopter.

The leading section of 3 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, was examining a recently used track when about six armed enemy approached. They spotted the section's boot marks and its leader, who opened fire, and the riflemen joined in before the machine-gun could be set up. One enemy was killed and carried away, another was wounded, and a rifle was captured; the section leader was critical of his Owen gun, whose rounds would not go through the bush.

B Company, 6 RAR, was manning a cut-off line on a track in a battalion cordon when its sentries opened fire on two groups of Viet Cong, probably most of a company. 6 Platoon brought artillery down on the enemy, but when it rose to clear the area it was hit by rifle and mortar fire, and one Australian shell fell short into the company's position, killing two and wounding several. By the time the enemy withdrew the company had two killed and twelve wounded; at least six enemy were killed and about fifteen wounded. The commanders afterwards debated whether the troops' strict fire discipline had let the enemy's fire go unanswered for too long.

C Company, 6 RAR, was part of a two-company cordon, with two other companies driving the enemy towards it, when it met an estimated Viet Cong company. As the enemy withdrew, covered by a rearguard of about 15, C Company called in artillery; two Australians were wounded, which the battalion's commander put down to a platoon mistaking its own position rather than to the artillery. The company then came under mortar fire and fought several small-arms clashes, hitting about four enemy, and found a large bunker system nearby. Four enemy bodies killed by artillery were recovered over the following days.
B Company, 6 RAR, saw an unknown number of Viet Cong, and artillery fired on them. An intelligence summary says six bodies were found and numerous blood trails seen.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's ambush beyond the patrol commander's name; six enemy were recorded killed and one wounded.

A half-platoon ambush of 7 Platoon, C Company, 6 RAR, about a kilometre outside Nui Dat, stopped an old man in an ox cart sent ahead by the Viet Cong, but its position was given away. In a heavy attack before dawn one Australian was shot and killed and two others seriously wounded, and were evacuated by a US helicopter guided in by lit stoves. One enemy body was found the next morning, with signs of more wounded, and a rifle was captured.

1 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, preparing a company harbour, found six or seven Viet Cong, with more behind, gathered unawares 30 metres away. A section leader, thinking he had been seen, opened fire and dropped one, and a fierce firefight followed as the enemy, heavily armed and setting up a Claymore to fire into company headquarters, attacked. A flanking move led by the platoon commander drove them off; one Viet Cong was killed and one wounded, and three Australians were wounded, the commander among them.

The Battle of Long Tan. D Company, 6 RAR, 108 strong, was following fresh tracks east of Nui Dat when 11 Platoon met a few Viet Cong and then a much larger force. From about 5.30 pm the company was attacked by at least a company, later found to be far more, under heavy machine-gun and mortar fire in heavy rain, and held on until A Company arrived in armoured personnel carriers after 7 pm. Close artillery fire broke up many of the attacks; low cloud ruled out air strikes, and helicopters flew in ammunition and took out the wounded. Seventeen Australians were killed and nineteen wounded; 245 enemy were recorded killed. The company commander afterwards reported that the M60 machine-guns jammed in the mud and that the men needed to carry more ammunition.

During the Battle of Long Tan, A Company, 6 RAR, rode out from Nui Dat in the armoured personnel carriers of 3 Troop, 1 APC Squadron, to relieve D Company. On the way it clashed with the support company of the D445 Battalion, causing about 15 casualties, and then with two companies of the 275th Regiment, causing about 45 more, before joining D Company as the enemy withdrew. Four Australians were wounded.

The Viet Cong shelled the Task Force's artillery lines at Nui Dat with about 66 rounds from 82 mm mortars and what was thought to be a 70 mm howitzer, killing one Australian and wounding 24. The artillery returned fire within seven minutes. A patrol from B Company, 6 RAR, later found the firing positions, with signs of a hurried departure, blood trails and carts used to take bodies away. This was the night before the Battle of Long Tan.

An SAS patrol covering the open ground north-east of the Nui Dinh Hills watched enemy parties gather at a hut across the Song Sa. In heavy rain, nine enemy were seen going into the house, and the patrol opened fire, killing five at once; the enemy fired only two shots back. A search the next day found that most of them had been killed.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's contact beyond the patrol commander's name; three enemy were recorded wounded.

B Company, 5 RAR, had gone into harbour when a machine-gun group saw two enemy watching from behind palm fronds and opened fire as they withdrew. The enemy fired only one or two shots, but one killed an Australian in the platoon latrine, 15 metres from the enemy through dense bush.

2 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR, pursuing the enemy fired on by 1 Platoon, found and killed the wounded man, who threw several grenades, then attacked the two others, who had opened fire, and killed them. The party, about 15 local Viet Cong, had been carrying medical supplies, probably to a hospital; weapons, medical supplies and clothing were recovered, and the company needed more ammunition.

1 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR, was astride a track near a company-sized camp when three local Viet Cong walked towards it. The sentry held his fire until they were 22 metres away and killed the first two, and the machine-gunner wounded the third; two weapons were captured. The company commander noted that despite days of air, artillery and mortar fire the Viet Cong still used the tracks in daylight.

A standing patrol of 9 Platoon, C Company, 6 RAR, was probed four times by five local Viet Cong under covering fire, and engaged them several times until they gave up, wounding two. One Australian was wounded.

A section of 11 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, in ambush on a track near its company base, opened fire early on five enemy, wounding one before the machine-gun jammed; the ambush leader shot dead the leading man, and the enemy fired back and withdrew. The company commander said the ambush should have done better: the machine-gun could not cover the whole killing ground, and the section all fired at the first enemy.
A Company, 6 RAR, made contact with two armed Viet Cong in black, killing one and possibly wounding the other. A Chinese rifle and a pack of documents were recovered.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's contact beyond the patrol commander's name; one enemy was recorded killed and one wounded.

10 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, found two well-hidden huts, surrounded them and opened fire on a group of 18. Five escaped downhill, and ten, nine men and a woman, were killed; six rifles and two other weapons were captured.

8 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, advancing north-west, was fired on by six to eight Viet Cong from four places; sweeping the area, a soldier tripped a booby trap, wounding six or seven Australians. The area was thick with booby traps, and an air strike and artillery hit it, with no known result.
A platoon of C Company, 5 RAR, set off another booby trap, wounding five Australians. Booby traps had been tied to vines to channel the platoon up a track.

5 RAR's Assault Pioneer Platoon was investigating inhabited, booby-trapped caves when a lone sniper shot a sentry in the back. One Australian was killed and two wounded, the two by ricochets of their own fire off the rocks. An enemy was wounded and retreated into a cave, which was attacked with a flamethrower, and he was believed killed.
South Vietnamese troops passing B Company, 6 RAR, set off a two-grenade booby trap, wounding two of their own and four Australians of A Company; three stayed on duty and one was evacuated.
A soldier of 1 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, tripped a booby trap, wounding four. A Chinese grenade and an 81 mm mortar-round booby trap were found nearby and destroyed.

10 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, guarding the company's rear, smelt Viet Cong near a mangrove swamp and followed tracks to a small camp. The commander set one section as a fire base and led two in from the side; a woman was killed, and three men who tried to swim the creek were shot and swept away. Four enemy were recorded killed, and three packs captured.

Five enemy approached 6 RAR's Assault Pioneer Platoon in harbour at night and opened fire when a sentry challenged them. One Australian was killed and two wounded; the record notes the dangers of the rules of engagement.

5 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, in an observation post above a village D Company was searching, saw ten men run into the mangroves and a creek, and after clearance opened fire with two machine-guns. Artillery was brought down, and when a sampan came to pick up a swimmer the guns and artillery fired again, stopping because the village was only 750 metres away; an aircraft then strafed the area. One enemy was killed and four possibly wounded.
In the afternoon the enemy fired more command-detonated mines at 2 Troop, 1 APC Squadron's carriers, wounding three infantrymen inside and slightly damaging a carrier.

A section of 4 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, checking a track junction, was setting up its machine-gun when an enemy rifle fired, killing the gunner's number two, who had gone to help the gunner unwrap his ammunition. A sweep found nothing; an old woman had seen ten Viet Cong leave the area.

A reconnaissance patrol of 9 Platoon, C Company, 6 RAR, was fired on with a machine-gun and grenades by local Viet Cong in ambush pits along a track. It flanked them, and its fire set off an enemy Claymore; a sweep found a camp with booby-trapped tunnels and a dead section commander of the D445 Battalion, with blood trails from others.

A command-detonated mine exploded against D Company, 6 RAR, killing one Australian and wounding ten, with three civilians also wounded. About half the casualties, including the man killed, were caused by an Australian Claymore mine carried by an NCO, which went off in the blast. The record also notes evidence that a Vietnamese woman who ran to the scene was wounded or killed by soldiers who mistook her for an enemy.

8 Platoon, C Company, 6 RAR, moving to a night ambush, heard talking and found twelve heavily armed Viet Cong eating dinner. The platoon opened fire, killing five and wounding four, and captured twelve weapons and much ammunition.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's contact beyond the patrol commander's name; four enemy were recorded killed.

An SAS patrol heard voices and saw people approaching from the west, and opened fire as the second man began to follow the leader onto an old timber track. The first two men were hit in the back and the third was also hit; one enemy fired back with an automatic weapon before the firing stopped amid groaning and crying. More groups of enemy were heard nearby on both sides, so the patrol could not search further and broke contact to the south. It found two blood trails and saw a third man hit and fall, and estimated there were eight enemy in the ambush area.

4 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, was in a linear ambush when sentries at its southern end heard two Viet Cong approaching. The first sentry moved forward to look up the track, the enemy saw the movement and fired, killing him and wounding the second sentry in the foot. The fire was returned but the enemy had gone, and a sweep found nothing. The company commander thought the sentry's reaction had shown a lack of discipline and endangered his mates.

6 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, on alert in ambush after 4 Platoon's contact, opened machine-gun fire when two enemy stepped out of thick young bamboo in front of it. Movement was heard in the bamboo, so grenades and grenade-launcher rounds were fired, killing one enemy. Of four regional force Viet Cong contacted, two were killed and two wounded, and a Thompson submachine-gun and a large number of documents were captured. Artillery was fired on the enemy's escape route.

1 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, and about 15 Viet Cong coming down a jungle track saw each other at the same time, and two machine-guns opened fire; by the tracer and a full moon the enemy were seen in green uniforms and bush hats with weapons slung. Two enemy were killed, or one by body count, and an M1 carbine was captured; blood trails suggested others were wounded, but following them found nothing more. Artillery was fired after the contact and again on movement beyond the perimeter later that night.

2 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, part of a company ambush system covering an enemy track complex, had been in place since the previous afternoon when it heard 1 Platoon's contact. Shortly afterwards nine enemy came running down the track, talking animatedly, and the machine-gun opened the ambush, followed by heavy fire and grenades. The enemy dropped to the ground and fired back with rifles, grenade launchers and grenades. Two enemy were killed and two wounded; they were from the well-trained Chau Duc C20 Company.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's contact beyond the patrol commander's name; one Australian was wounded, and one enemy was recorded killed and one wounded.

A Company, 5 RAR, made contact with about 25 local Viet Cong crossing a creek, coming from the same area as the previous night's fight. A 1 Platoon sentry opened fire and was joined by the machine-gun and five riflemen; the leading two enemy fell and the rest scattered and tried to work around the company's flanks, but 1 Platoon met this with fire and a hooking move of its own, and helicopter gunships strafed the enemy. One enemy was killed and one wounded.
A visual reconnaissance aircraft spotted two Viet Cong hiding in a tree, and artillery fired on them, possibly killing both.

12 Platoon, D Company, 6 RAR, heard two sections of enemy to its west and called in artillery to drive them towards its position. About an hour later it made contact with an enemy force of about platoon strength, and artillery was brought down again. Two blood trails were found in a nearby camp the next day.

After A Company, 6 RAR, ran into a dug-in enemy position, B Company was ordered to assault it with A Company's support. Following artillery fire, B Company attacked and was pinned down by fire from all sides, including heavy machine-guns, Claymore mines and light mortars, revealing a heavy weapons company supporting well-hidden positions of D445 Battalion. With casualties mounting, four air strikes were made, and 2 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, came in to recover casualties; one carrier was disabled by three recoilless rifle rounds, killing its driver and wounding its commander and the wounded inside. After a four-hour battle the companies withdrew into a night position 200 metres away, and the enemy withdrew overnight; eight Australians were killed and 21 wounded, with 50 enemy recorded killed. The commanding officer said he had not launched a full battalion attack because he was ordered to finish at last light, and that the action showed the need for tanks.

B Company, 5 RAR, was being carried by 3 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, into position for a Task Force attack on the Viet Cong stronghold of the Long Hai Hills when the leading carrier hit a powerful mine on a dirt track. Two cavalrymen and two infantrymen were killed, the rest aboard were badly wounded, and the carrier was thrown on its side. When no ambush followed, soldiers ran from their carriers to help the medics and set off more anti-personnel mines, killing or wounding most of the medics and the company headquarters; normal mine drills had been ignored. Engineers ordered everyone to keep still while they cleared the mines, medical help came by helicopter, and Operation Renmark was cancelled. In all nine Australians were killed and 26 wounded.

6 RAR was flown in by helicopter to cut off enemy forces withdrawing from an attack on Phuoc Hai. As 2 Platoon, A Company, pushed into the jungle to secure the landing zone, its sergeant shot a sniper in a tree, and enemy automatic weapons opened up; the right-hand section swept to within 20 metres of one gun when another opened fire, wounding five men. The platoon had run into a dug-in company of D445 Battalion, with its heavy weapons company, in bunkers with overhead cover. Six Australians were wounded and three to six enemy killed, and the platoon withdrew 150 metres, at a time when it had no mortar support and artillery fire had been interrupted.

During a battalion cordon and search, C Company headquarters, 5 RAR, set off a booby trap while holding an orders meeting. Three Australians were killed and five wounded. The record says the mine was probably a booby trap laid by friendly forces.

A Company, 6 RAR, moving in support of B Company's attack on the main enemy position, came under sniper fire, and two enemy were killed. A Company supported B Company and guided the armoured personnel carriers in to recover its casualties; one of the guides was wounded doing so.

11 Platoon, D Company, 6 RAR, was eating before moving to its night ambush position when the platoon sergeant saw two local Viet Cong in the open 20 metres away; he shot and killed one and probably wounded the other. A section swept the area and found and killed the second man, and a carbine was captured. One Australian was wounded in the shoulder.

6 RAR was set to intercept enemy forces withdrawing from the attack on Lo Gom. As 2 Platoon, A Company, left its lunch position, the forward scout heard a rifle being cocked, and the platoon engaged a well dug-in enemy platoon, then pulled back 50 metres while artillery and mortars hit the position. The enemy replied with 60mm mortars, lightly wounding two Australians. A Company then attacked behind heavy artillery and mortar fire and took the position as the enemy withdrew; one enemy body, 20 to 30 fighting pits and an AK-47 were found. The enemy were the rear of 2 Battalion, 275 Regiment, covering the battalion's withdrawal across the Song Rai.

B Company, 6 RAR, with 2 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, was sent to ambush boats supplying the enemy, and at dawn engaged five motorised sampans 250 metres offshore. Three were sunk and two badly damaged, mostly by the armoured vehicles' .50 calibre machine-guns. Six enemy were recorded killed.

Half of 6 Platoon, B Company, 6 RAR, was sent to check a sandhill covered in dense 2-metre scrub where movement was suspected. After 120 metres, fire from a hidden pit 5 metres away hit the machine-gun's number two, and the gunner was hit from another hidden pit after one burst. The half platoon withdrew; the full platoon then attacked with armoured personnel carrier support and rescued the two wounded, and 5 Platoon swept the area as the enemy withdrew. Six to eight enemy of 2 Battalion, 275 Regiment, had been in three bunkers and five other positions, and were hit by a large airstrike and heavy artillery fire. Three Australians were wounded, two of whom died; there were no known enemy casualties, and an SLR rifle was captured.

The Reconnaissance Platoon, Support Company, 5 RAR, in ambush, made contact with four enemy, killing two and wounding two. One Australian was wounded in the leg by a burst of automatic fire. Claymore mines had not been used because the paddy field gave little cover and they would have been too close to the platoon. Artillery supported, and a search next morning found blood trails, sandal marks, field dressings, drag marks and scattered rice.

An ambush by 3 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, in the Task Force's area, caught five enemy coming up a track. The leading man was shot dead with an Armalite and a Claymore mine was fired, and the others ran into a nearby creek, where they were hit by grenades. Artillery was fired into the area, and the enemy came back later that night, probably to look for bodies. Two enemy were killed and three wounded; the bodies and three blood trails were found the next day, and the dead were buried where they lay.
C Company, 6 RAR, found a cache of 80 tons of rice. It was booby-trapped, and three Australians of 8 Platoon were wounded.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's ambush beyond the patrol commander's name; five enemy were recorded killed and one wounded.

A soldier of 4 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, set off a US M16 mine north of Phuoc Loi, killing one Australian and wounding two. The mine had been set beside the road in line with a fence; the local sub-sector said it had laid no mines there, engineers found no others, and it could not be told how long it had been there.

A soldier of 4 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, set off an anti-personnel mine after the engineers had swept for mines up to a line of pickets; the platoon commander, following the mine detector, had stepped outside the line. One Australian was killed, the platoon commander was very seriously wounded in both legs and later died, and another soldier suffered severe shock. The mine, not an M16, blew a hole a metre wide and half a metre deep.

An SAS patrol was setting an ambush when 12 enemy came walking along the track. Three patrol members fired at 2 to 5 metres, killing three enemy, and a fourth was hit twice in the back and fell behind bushes. The patrol then came under fire from several AK-47s, an M1 rifle and a carbine, withdrew, and was lifted out.

2 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR, was returning from night activity astride Route 23 south of Xuyen Moc when a soldier crossing the road set off an anti-vehicle mine. He died of his wounds, and one other Australian was wounded.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's ambush beyond the patrol commander's name; two enemy were recorded killed and one wounded.
An engineer of 1 Troop, 1 Field Squadron, set off an M16 mine while laying it in the barrier minefield. Six soldiers were wounded, two of whom later died.

An ambush by 9 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, made contact with four or five Viet Cong, killing three and wounding one. Four weapons were captured, an M16, an M1 Garand, an M2 rifle and a Thompson submachine-gun, along with equipment. Artillery was fired on escape routes and helicopter gunships were called in, and the platoon was resupplied with ammunition.

While mines were being laid in the barrier minefield, a member of a mine-arming party from 7 RAR's Assault Pioneers set off an M16 mine, killing a sapper of 1 Field Squadron and wounding two others. It is recorded as a friendly-fire incident.
Two engineers of 1 Field Squadron were killed when an anti-lift device exploded while they were laying M16 mines in the barrier minefield.

9 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, found enemy tracks in a creek bed near a partly destroyed bunker system and was deploying when three enemy were seen. Two were shot dead immediately and the third escaped. One Australian was slightly wounded by shrapnel from a grenade launcher.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's ambush beyond the patrol commander's name; three enemy were recorded killed.

After its earlier contact, an SAS patrol realised it was being followed, went to ground and opened fire at 15 metres as 15 to 20 enemy attacked in extended line. After a long firefight in which three enemy were killed by SLR fire, the patrol broke contact and moved to another lying-up position. The enemy mortared the area on and off all night and searched for the patrol, at times coming quite close.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's ambush beyond the patrol commander's name; three enemy were recorded killed.

US 175 mm guns directed by an aerial observer of 1/83 US Artillery fired on bunkers; three men in black ran out, and the area was fired on again, possibly killing all three. Gardens in the area were destroyed.

D Company, 7 RAR, was moving with 12 Platoon in the lead when the rear section's machine-gun opened fire on four enemy kneeling in thick scrub; the gun jammed, its belt twisted in webbing, and the gunner was hit in the legs. The enemy moved up the column and began sniping at company headquarters, and a sniper zeroing in on the company commander was 7 metres away and aiming when the commander shot him dead with his Armalite. The commander then swept the area under covering fire and the rest of the enemy withdrew. A Garand rifle, ammunition, packs and sleeping gear were recovered.
An SAS patrol, in ambush, made contact with three Viet Cong, killing two and wounding one. Two carbines were captured.

12 Platoon, D Company, 7 RAR, in ambush, was approached by four to six enemy in single file from a direction the ambush did not cover, moving very cautiously through thick jungle. The sentry covering the south did not see the enemy scout until he was 5 metres away and coming straight at him, and shot him in the chest. The rest of the enemy returned fire and recovered the scout. One enemy was possibly killed and two possibly wounded.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's ambush beyond the patrol commander's name; five enemy were recorded killed and one wounded.

3 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment's position at Duc Thanh was shelled by 60mm mortars, and four men were slightly wounded. Artillery at Nui Dat fired back and silenced the mortars. No carriers were damaged.

Two Viet Cong approached 11 Platoon, D Company, 7 RAR, from the east and were engaged; one was killed. A sentry was surprised by an enemy coming up behind him, turned in time to deflect the rifle, and was shot in the hand, suffering broken bones, and was evacuated. Artillery engaged likely escape routes.
9 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR, engaged 12 Viet Cong and killed one.

An SAS patrol trying to capture an enemy for interrogation fired a Claymore mine, killing one of two armed enemy. The man they wanted to capture escaped, injured, while firing back. Artillery engaged the area.

An SAS patrol, inserted only minutes before, saw an enemy at 50 metres who disappeared. While it radioed for the helicopter to return, the patrol leader saw an enemy 10 metres ahead and shot him in the chest with his SLR, and another who appeared beside him was hit by three M16 bursts; one enemy was killed and one wounded. The patrol fired into a bush that moved nearby as it reached the landing zone, and was lifted out; artillery engaged the area.

After its ambush, A Company, 7 RAR, sent 2 Platoon along the track towards a suspected enemy squad; about 100 metres on it ran into heavy automatic fire from a defensive position, and 1 Platoon's right flanking attack was stopped by an enemy platoon, with seven enemy machine-guns firing at 30 metres. The rest of the company was committed with air strikes and artillery, and the enemy replied with rockets, grenades, machine-guns and rifles before withdrawing north under intense artillery and air attack after several hours. The enemy, C12 (2nd Company) of 3 Battalion, 274 Regiment, and a reconnaissance platoon, had been covering the withdrawal of their battalion from a camp a kilometre away. Six Australians were killed and 17 to 20 wounded, many slightly; an estimated 15 enemy were killed (five by body count) and 25 wounded, and artillery and air strikes were thought to have caused many more. AK-47s, an RPD light machine-gun, a B40 rocket launcher and ammunition were among the items captured.

12 Platoon, D Company, 2 RAR, found a company-sized enemy camp west of Hoi My, with a well dug-in command post, four or five well-built bunkers, weapon pits and crawl trenches. An M16 mine buried in the camp exploded, killing two Australians and wounding three. Searching found two more dug-in M16 mines and a cluster bomb set as a booby trap, along with black clothing, ponchos, knives and a Vietnamese notebook.
An SAS patrol, in ambush, made contact with about 10 Viet Cong, killing five. The helicopter was hit by ground fire during the extraction.

11 Platoon, D Company, 2 RAR, set off a mine in an enemy minefield north of My An, wounding six Australians. Engineers cleared ten M16 mines, some cluster bombs and a 105mm shell set as an anti-tank mine. The company thought an enemy sapper party had laid the mines during the night.

An SAS patrol set a Claymore ambush on a track, and four enemy in camouflage uniforms walked into it, the leader with his carbine ready and the others with weapons slung. The first three were knocked down by the Claymores and killed; the fourth opened fire with an automatic weapon and was engaged with rifles and another Claymore as he retreated up the track. The patrol then came under fire from two light weapons 30 metres up the track, withdrew and was lifted out.
12 Platoon, D Company, 2 RAR, was rejoining its company when one of the last three men, spaced 15 metres apart, trod on a mine. All three were wounded by shrapnel.

An enemy squad ambushed the first vehicle of a two-vehicle convoy from C Company, 2 RAR, at the Horseshoe, bound for Dat Do, with Claymore mines and automatic weapons at the eastern checkpoint. Three Australians were killed, one of them dying of his wounds, and two interpreters were wounded, one of whom later died; four weapons were lost. A sweep by C Company and South Vietnamese troops found only three AK-47 magazines and a squad-sized hiding tunnel near the fence. A woman living nearby said the Viet Cong had been there four days, and residents near the site were taken to 1 ATF for processing.

9 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR, surprised an enemy platoon in a platoon-sized camp of D445 Battalion and shot the leading man as the enemy fled, and it came under fire again as it followed up. Two enemy were killed and at least one wounded; documents identified them as C4 Company of D445, and a Mauser, an M1 Garand, a Chinese rifle and a Colt .45 pistol were captured. Artillery fired on two enemy escaping from the contact.

1 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR, was searching along a track when the forward scout saw a disused enemy camp; the section leader stepped to one side and set off an M16 mine. One New Zealander was killed and one wounded. The mine seemed to have been there a long time, other M16 mines were found, and locals moving through the area regularly appeared to know where the mines were.

3 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, heard chopping 75 metres away and thought it was near a company-sized camp, then saw movement 50 metres off. The company pulled back 800 metres so that mortars, artillery, helicopter gunships and bombers, with 500-pound bombs and napalm, could hit the target. A Company then swept through the area but found nothing.

Groups of 5 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, were protecting engineers blowing up a battalion-sized camp when three enemy slipped in and stole one of the engineers' rifles. A sentry saw movement and shot two dead, a 20-year-old woman and a 26-year-old man, both carrying Chinese assault rifles, sleeping gear and medical supplies, and wounded the third. The platoon followed the blood trail for 100 metres, and the forward scout shot the wounded man dead. Three weapons were captured, and the man's notebook held details of a meeting with another party.
A gun pit of 11 Platoon, D Company, 2 RAR, saw movement and fired two bursts, hitting two enemy at 20 metres. Both were killed; they carried an AK-47 and an M1 rifle.

2 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, ambushed a track in thick bamboo and high grass about a kilometre north of Long Tan, well inside the prohibited zone, when 16 Vietnamese came along it. The leading person saw the machine-gunner and raised a carrying stick, which the gunner took for a weapon, and he opened fire, joined by the rest of the ambush; the platoon commander stopped the firing when he heard a woman's voice. Four were killed, six wounded and captured, and three more taken prisoner. They were all unarmed civilians.

2 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, in ambush, saw four Viet Cong, believed to be Xuyen Moc guerrillas, moving cautiously with weapons ready 60 metres away, and let them come to within 15 metres before springing it. One was killed at once and at least two wounded; another was killed later, and tracker dogs found a wounded man who was shot dead. The fourth left a blood trail that was eventually lost. An M2 carbine, a Chinese rifle and four packs were captured.

The Assault Pioneer Platoon, Support Company, 7 RAR, escorting an engineer team, came face to face with four enemy. The forward scout shot the first, the machine-gun had a stoppage, but supporting fire built up and the enemy stopped firing and withdrew. One enemy was killed and one possibly wounded, and a rifle was recovered; the enemy had used a Thompson submachine-gun. Two pioneers were slightly wounded by shrapnel, in the foot and the nose, and not evacuated; artillery and mortars fired in support.

1 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, saw an enemy camp and heard noise from it, and was creeping up when it was seen by three enemy, whom it engaged. One was killed and two escaped wounded, and a follow-up found another body; records give two or three killed. A US carbine and a Chinese carbine were captured, and the camp held ten huts with bunkers beneath, pigs, fowls and a rice-husking machine.

3 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, in ambush, killed two Viet Cong tax collectors with a machine-gun burst. The commander then had three Claymore mines fired and more fire put into the area, but no more enemy were found. Two Chinese weapons were captured.

An SAS patrol investigating a track was approached by a group of armed Viet Cong who stopped 15 metres away, the leader seeming to have heard it. The patrol opened fire on four bunched enemy, killing two; the others fled, and the patrol thought there were more than four. During the extraction the gunships were fired on and fired back, killing one Viet Cong. There were no Australian casualties.

Acting on SAS information, D Company, 7 RAR, attacked an occupied enemy base camp while B Company ambushed escape routes. 10 and 12 Platoons drove the enemy from several bunkers, destroying one with a rocket launcher, and the company consolidated in the centre of the camp without loss. The enemy then circled around through communication trenches and counter-attacked from the east and north, getting between the reserve platoon and the others, and fired rocket-propelled grenades into the tree canopy to shower the Australians with shrapnel; grenade-launcher rounds failed to arm, a machine-gun jammed, and gunships and artillery could not be used so close. Fighting in heavy rain ended at nightfall. Two Australians were shot dead and about 20 wounded, mostly by shrapnel, ten of whom stayed on duty until the next day; three to four enemy were killed. The camp, prepared by the Chau Duc District Company, was probably used as a forward base by D445 Battalion.

A 12-man patrol of 2 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, was hit by a command-detonated mine, and the enemy also opened fire. One or two Australians were killed and seven or eight wounded. Fire was returned and artillery brought down.

Enemy outside the perimeter of 2 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR's base fired a command-detonated Chinese Claymore-type mine from about 45 metres, probably aimed at the noise of the radio; its narrow blast reached 75 metres. Two Australians were killed and five or six wounded, one more suffering shock. A helicopter visit an hour earlier may have given the position away, and rain had masked the enemy's noise as they set the mine. The company commander noted that the men who ran to the wounded risked the blast of a second mine and should have waited for a sweep.
While 2 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, was searching an enemy camp 8 kilometres west of Xuyen Moc, a booby trap killed two Australians and wounded one.

10 Platoon, D Company, 7 RAR, made contact with about seven people while crossing a creek. Three were killed and one wounded and captured; one escaped down a tunnel and two to the east. Although the enemy had fired on the patrol, those hit by its return fire were probably civilians: a boy and a girl were killed and an elderly couple wounded. The landing zone used for the medical evacuation was booby-trapped, but the booby trap was blown before the helicopter landed.

Several enemy got through 108 Field Battery's defences during the night and set four Claymore mines aimed at the sleeping quarters. Two were fired, killing a gunner; the other two did not go off. Casualties would have been higher had most of the battery not been on duty.

An SAS patrol, in ambush, made contact with seven Viet Cong, five men and two women in mixed dress carrying a large amount of food. All seven were killed, and a Chinese rifle, a carbine and an M1 rifle were captured.

12 Platoon, D Company, 2 RAR, in ambush, made contact with six Viet Cong, killing four and wounding one. An M1 Garand and two submachine-guns were captured, and a document showed one of the dead was the commander of the Xuyen Moc district platoon. A tracking team followed a blood trail until it was lost at a river, and artillery fired on escape routes.

A vehicle carrying seven people, including two Australian advisers, was ambushed by a Viet Cong force of unknown size, possibly dressed in South Vietnamese Army uniforms and using only small arms. Both Australians and four South Vietnamese soldiers were killed and one wounded, and two pistols and two carbines were lost. Civilians said the firefight lasted 15 minutes.

C Company headquarters, 7 RAR, was moving in three single-file columns when the first man of the support section came under accurate fire from an automatic weapon and several rifles and was pinned down. Fire was returned with a machine-gun, rocket launchers, grenade launchers and grenades, 7 Platoon swept through what proved to be an enemy cave and camp complex, and artillery hit escape routes. One Australian was wounded. Next morning two enemy bodies were found at a tunnel exit, and four rifles, magazines, a Claymore and two grenades were found in the camp.

2 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, in ambush, had three Viet Cong walk into the killing ground. The first saw a machine-gun and fired two shots before all three were killed by two machine-guns and a Claymore mine, one dying of wounds. Two M1 carbines and a Mosin Nagant rifle were captured.

1 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, in ambush, made contact with four or five Viet Cong in black with packs, killing two and wounding one. A Thompson submachine-gun, a Chinese rifle, a 1917 Remington rifle and seven packs, mostly of food, were captured.

10 Platoon, D Company, 7 RAR, unknowingly approached an enemy camp holding more than a company, and its forward section came under fire, three men being hit; the enemy then came forward and caused five more casualties as the platoon formed a perimeter. The company commander brought artillery and mortars onto the camp, and with 10 Platoon almost out of ammunition and enemy grenade launchers and mortars ranging onto it, gunships struck the enemy only 30 metres away. The rest of D Company came up, 11 and 12 Platoons assaulted on the flanks, and after an airstrike on the edges of the camp and escape routes the camp was cleared, the enemy withdrawing hurriedly and in some disorder. One Australian was killed and ten wounded, mostly by grenade-launcher and rocket-propelled grenade fire; enemy losses were heavy but uncertain, notionally five killed and five wounded. The enemy were C238 Battalion, concentrating for an attack on Long Binh, in a camp big enough for two companies.

2 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, still holding the previous day's ambush, heard a large body of enemy approaching and stood to in its shell scrapes. When the first five entered the killing ground, Claymore mines, machine-guns and rifles opened fire and four of the five were killed, but 20 or more enemy fought back aggressively with AK-47s, RPD light machine-guns and rocket-propelled grenades. Many of the Australian casualties were caused by rocket-grenade shrapnel; the radio operator was incapacitated, and the platoon medic died of his wounds. One Australian was killed and seven wounded, and eight enemy were killed.

A platoon of B Company, 2 RAR, near the site of its earlier contact, met two enemy and was soon under fire from AK-47s and a light machine-gun at 15 metres; three Australians were wounded, and a strong smell suggested it was on the edge of a camp. After artillery and mortars the enemy stopped firing, and four blood trails led into the camp. When the company assaulted, 5 Platoon was pinned down by a light machine-gun and rocket-propelled grenades and two more men were wounded; as each bunker was grenaded, enemy popped out of another. V Company was sent to help, gunships and an air strike came in, and after the casualties were evacuated B Company withdrew 300 metres from a bunker system much larger than first thought. Four enemy were killed; they had three light machine-guns and eight to ten AK-47s.

5 Platoon, B Company, 2 RAR, made heavy contact with 15 to 20 enemy inside a camp big enough for three squads, and called in artillery and mortars. One Australian was killed, one died of wounds and one was wounded. The enemy left two bodies, four blood trails and two drag marks, and an AK-47 was captured.

9 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR, assaulted an enemy camp and had just occupied its horseshoe-shaped defences when 20 or more enemy of 274 Regiment and the Trang Bom district unit counter-attacked. Over about three hours the enemy attacked seven times, with heavy machine-guns that cut trees in half, while gunships, airstrikes and artillery were called in; fighting continued on and off into the next morning. Two Australians were killed. At least two enemy were killed and blood trails suggested four wounded, and weapons, 15 packs, 500 pounds of rice and 200 pounds of other food were captured.

1 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR, in ambush, made contact with about ten Viet Cong, part of the same night's battle, supported by artillery and a Spooky gunship. Five enemy were killed at the time and later evaluation added more, for seven or eight in all; a heavy blood trail was found, and AK-47s, an M1, rifles, rocket-propelled grenade launchers and packs were captured.

During the Tet Offensive an enemy battalion seized much of Baria, a town of 15,000 with many brick and stone buildings, and 1 ATF sent A Company, 3 RAR (less a platoon), and nine carriers of 3 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, to protect key government buildings and drive the Viet Cong out. Rather than clearing their way on foot, the platoons were carried quickly in the carriers to the US compound and the administration and logistics compound, despite the threat of rocket-propelled grenades, with one section of carriers staying with Sector headquarters. Enemy infiltrators and rocket teams remained a constant threat for most of the battle, and the carriers were exposed from many directions because many houses had not been cleared. In heavy fighting one Australian was killed and 19 wounded; enemy casualties were put at 54, 42 of them killed.

Fire Support Base Anderson was attacked at night by at least a company of Viet Cong and a mortar platoon. The whole base was first hit accurately by 82mm and 60mm mortars and rocket-propelled grenades, and the enemy then assaulted from a high bund to the south-east in waves of grenadiers followed by rocket teams, breaking into the perimeter and causing casualties in the 3 RAR Mortar Platoon and the US B/2/35 Battery; a section of carriers from 1 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, with the battery's and mortars' fire, drove them back. Further fire and a probing attack from other directions were beaten off at the wire by machine-guns, and a second mortar attack covered the enemy's withdrawal; 3 RAR's mortars and 161 Battery engaged the enemy mortar positions, and gunships supported. Seven or eight Australians were killed and 22 to 27 wounded, including four engineers of 1 Field Squadron killed by a mortar bomb that hit their standing patrol; one American was killed and three wounded. Four enemy bodies were found, but blood, bandages and remains showed many more casualties.

V Company, 2 RAR, made contact with an enemy company and was attacked from the north, east and west with about 20 rockets and heavy automatic fire. Gunships and artillery supported. Ten New Zealanders were wounded; 13 enemy were killed and seven wounded, judging by drag marks and blood. Six AK-47s, two light machine-guns, 12 anti-tank grenades, 13 RPG-2 rounds, magazines and two sandbags of belted ammunition were captured.

After air and gunship strikes on the camp, 8 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, followed by 9 Platoon, made a wide flanking move to the right. The camp seemed deserted until four massive hidden bunkers opened fire at 10 metres, wounding three men and knocking out a machine-gun; rocket-launcher hits had little effect on a bunker, and the forward sections were pinned in crossfire and pulled back 15 metres. The company formed a perimeter and brought artillery and mortars in as close as 35 metres while the enemy probed its flanks with machine-guns and rockets; after a gunship strike 25 metres away the enemy fire slackened and they withdrew in good order. Three enemy were killed and five wounded, though the company commander said there were certainly more; 14 Australians were wounded, none seriously, six staying on duty overnight.

B Company, 3 RAR, made contact with an enemy platoon. Nine Viet Cong were killed; two Australians were killed and five wounded. The Viet Cong took a radio from an Australian signaller, and it was believed they may also have taken some weapons from the Australian casualties.
Australian and US artillery fired on an enemy mortar position. The next morning more than 18 enemy bodies were found, nine of them credited to the Task Force artillery.

An SAS patrol set a system of Claymore mines and beehive charges that went off under a tractor and trailer carrying ammunition, weapons and equipment. Fifteen bodies were counted, and a 75mm recoilless rifle and ammunition were captured; the tractor and trailer were destroyed. Gunships engaged the area, setting off two secondary explosions, an air observer was fired on, and an air strike followed after the patrol was lifted out. A defector from the unit that ran the tractor later said 21 died in the explosions.

After B Company, 2 RAR, seized the Dinh Co hill north-west of the Long Hai hills, an engineer set off a booby trap in the temple, killing himself and wounding 11 to 13 others. The area was infested with mines and booby traps, and the company commander believed the enemy were placing them in places likely to interest Westerners for their cultural value.

The forward scout of 7 Platoon, C Company, 3 RAR, patrolling in the south-east Long Hai hills, trod on an M16 mine that failed to jump and exploded in the ground, badly injuring him and another soldier. While the engineer team cleared the area, their protection party stepped outside the cleared area onto another M16 and was killed. 9 Platoon sent its engineer team with two escorts to help, and on the way down the ridge someone set off a third mine, killing the two sappers and seriously wounding the escorts. In all three Australians were killed and four wounded.
2 Platoon, W Company, 2 RAR, set off a second M16 mine north-west of the Long Hai hills, less than an hour after the first, wounding seven New Zealanders.

The commander of 9 Platoon, C Company, 3 RAR, following a path cleared by engineers in the south-east Long Hai hills, appears to have cut a corner and set off an M16 mine. The engineers, a soldier and the platoon commander were wounded, four in all, and the platoon commander, seriously wounded, died on the way to hospital.

The forward scout of 6 Platoon, B Company, 3 RAR, came within 5 metres of an enemy camp surrounded by barbed wire and was hit by light machine-gun and AK-47 fire; the platoon commander, trying to rescue him, was slightly wounded, and the whole platoon was pinned down. Artillery fired while tank T32 of C Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, was called; the enemy tried to encircle the platoon and one was killed. The tank fired canister and machine-guns, and the platoon was extricated with the scout, who had been killed; another man was grazed by a ricochet. The tanks returned with B Company the next day and found a large bunker system the enemy had abandoned.

A section of 1 Platoon, W Company, 2 RAR, protecting a landing craft, set off a mine, very probably an M16, laid along a recently made tank track. Seven men were wounded by shrapnel, and one Australian and one New Zealander died of their wounds. Three more mines were found afterwards. 6 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, reported three wounded at the same place, and the record assumes they were part of the same incident.

A patrol of 2 SAS Squadron was waiting in ambush when eight enemy walked in, in two groups of four. The second-in-command set off three claymores, wiping out the second group, and another claymore killed one of the first group and possibly another; the rest of the first group were killed with rifle fire and a grenade after one opened up with a light machine-gun. As the patrol withdrew, four more enemy fired on it from the left flank; about 12 others had stayed outside the ambush area. Six enemy were killed and one possibly killed. Artillery fired on the area, and the patrol was extracted.

A patrol of 3 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR, in ambush, engaged an enemy party of about 12 to 20 approaching from the east with claymore mines and rifle fire. Six Viet Cong were killed, and an RPG-2 with three rockets, three submachine-guns (including a Thompson) and a Garand rifle were captured. The rest withdrew north and south, and artillery fired on their escape routes with unknown results.

1 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR, ambushed about six Viet Cong coming down a track towards Hoa Long; those who escaped the first ambush group ran into a second, where more were hit. Four Viet Cong were killed, one man and three women, and an M1 carbine and five grenades were captured. Artillery fired on the area with unknown results.

A 19-man patrol of 2 SAS Squadron was sent to ambush the recently abandoned fire support base Dyke. After seeing three enemy it could not ambush, the commander sent five men after them and moved the rest on; 120 m later they met four enemy at 7 m and killed all four with rifle fire and grenade launcher. The other enemy party was then attacked.
Three New Zealand soldiers of 2 Platoon, W Company, 2 RAR, were wounded by an M26 grenade set up as a booby trap.

Fire support base Coral was attacked by an estimated enemy battalion with very heavy and accurate mortar fire, rocket-propelled grenades and a ground assault. The enemy overran a 105 mm howitzer position and tried to turn it on the Australians, and also overran the 1 RAR mortar platoon. The fighting ended at 8 am, supported by a Spooky gunship aircraft and helicopter gunships, with 161 Field Battery and 3 RAR's mortars firing from 1 km away. Nine Australians were killed and 28 wounded; 55 North Vietnamese were killed, one was captured, and seven rocket launchers were taken. 1 RAR's rifle companies were out ambushing 1 to 2 km away.

Fire support base Coral was attacked by an estimated enemy regiment. Heavy mortar and rocket-propelled grenade fire opened the attack, followed by a ground assault, and the base was defended by 1 RAR, the artillery and armoured personnel carriers of A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, supported by a Spooky gunship aircraft, helicopter gunships and an air strike on an enemy anti-aircraft machine-gun. Seven Australians were killed and 17 to 19 wounded, and two Americans were also wounded. Thirty-seven North Vietnamese were counted dead, ten more possibly killed, and one captured; later intelligence assessed that only 100 of the 790 attackers remained uninjured.

The North Vietnamese renewed their attack on fire support base Balmoral with mortar and rocket-propelled grenade fire followed by a ground attack by two battalions, recorded as the 2nd and 3rd Battalions of 165 Regiment (141 Regiment in another account). The attack broke up on the wire under helicopter gunship and artillery fire. One Australian was killed and six to eight wounded. Accounts give 47 to 55 enemy killed and six prisoners taken, one of whom died.

The North Vietnamese 165 Regiment attacked fire support base Balmoral, held by 3 RAR with tanks and armoured personnel carriers. Heavy mortar fire was followed by a ground attack supported by rocket-propelled grenades and light machine-guns; an enemy battalion group was thought to be present, with one company making the ground assault. Three Australians were killed and 16 wounded; six enemy were recorded killed and 30 wounded.

C Company, 1 RAR, on a reconnaissance in force, met three enemy and then came under heavy mortar, machine-gun and rocket-propelled grenade fire from a bunker system held by an estimated enemy company, and was pinned down. Helicopter gunships and artillery silenced the enemy mortars but could do little more because most of the fighting was at 10 to 15 m, and armoured personnel carriers could not push through the jungle; one carrier was hit by a rocket while evacuating wounded. When two tanks arrived from Coral an assault was made and eight bunkers destroyed, and the company then broke contact for air strikes. One Australian was killed and seven wounded; 24 enemy were killed, with more probably or possibly killed by air strikes and artillery. Returning on 2 June, the company found five more bodies and signs of many more buried by the bombing and shelling.

D Company, 1 RAR, with tanks of 1 Troop, C Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, returned to the site of B Company's contact of the day before, after an air strike, and came under rocket-propelled grenade, machine-gun and AK-47 fire from a well-built bunker system big enough for a company.
