The infantry protected the tanks while they cleared the jungle with canister and blew up or crushed bunkers, and the infantry also used flame-throwers; enemy RPG-2 rounds had no effect on the tanks. 10 and 12 Platoons destroyed 14 bunkers, probably closer to 18, and killed at least seven enemy, with an unknown number more crushed in their bunkers. The force broke off in fading light and withdrew behind accurate artillery and mortar fire, without loss.

A 15-man patrol of 1 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR/NZ (ANZAC), set up a base at the limit of mortar support, and nine men went out to reconnoitre for a night ambush. They tracked, stalked and killed three enemy heard talking and laughing, not knowing they were at the edge of an enemy camp, and were at once attacked by at least 30 enemy at 10 to 15 m; one New Zealander was mortally wounded and three more, including the patrol leader and the machine-gunner, were wounded by rifle grenades, and the machine-gun was lost. Mortar fire was brought in 15 to 20 m from the patrol, and an assault by 17 enemy backed by a heavy machine-gun and 15 more was stopped 10 to 20 m away by rifles and grenade launcher, with mortars, helicopter gunships and 155 mm artillery adding to the enemy's losses. Short of ammunition, the patrol held off a further attack with gunship support until sections of V Company were flown in to secure the area and evacuate the casualties. At least five enemy were killed and nine wounded.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's contact beyond the patrol commander's name; eight enemy were recorded killed.
A patrol of 2 SAS Squadron made contact with an estimated 15 enemy, killing six and possibly two more. There were no Australian casualties, and the patrol was extracted.

Elements of A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, tanks of C Squadron, and D Company, 3 RAR, had the last of four contacts with sampans running a shuttle service across the river. Nine sampans were destroyed, one with a large secondary explosion, and two possibly destroyed. One enemy was found dead on the west bank, with drag marks showing others had been pulled away, and a large quantity of rice was floating on the river.

A patrol of 2 SAS Squadron fired on five enemy coming down a trail at 5 to 10 m. The first two fell dead, the third was hit in the shoulder and fell into dead ground 15 m away, and the fourth, carrying a rocket launcher, was hit in the chest as he tried to get round the patrol's flank; the fifth withdrew. The wounded third man fired, wounding one Australian, and was then killed by a grenade thrown by the patrol commander. An AK-50 was captured.

12 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR, saw five armed enemy in green uniforms and a section opened fire at 250 m; the enemy went into a creek and two sections went after them. The company commander, watching from half a kilometre away, said over-eagerness led to a breakdown in fire and movement and fire control. Cornered, the enemy fought back with AK-47s, killing one Australian and wounding another; one enemy was killed and one wounded, and an AK-47, webbing, rice and bags were captured.

A six-man patrol of 2 SAS Squadron made contact with more than 25 enemy in khaki-green uniforms, armed with an RPD machine-gun, SKS and AK rifles and M1s, moving south to north. Thirteen enemy were killed and an unknown number possibly killed. There were no Australian casualties, but a grenade launcher was damaged.
A mine went off while the Anti-Tank Platoon, Support Company, 1 RAR, was clearing a landing zone. Six Australians were wounded by shrapnel, and one of them died of his wounds that day.

A section of armoured personnel carriers of 3 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, pushed into thick jungle and was ambushed with command-detonated mines, at least one thought to be an M16, and AK-47 fire. A trooper exposed on top of a carrier was killed and another wounded, and three infantrymen were wounded by blast and shrapnel.

2 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR, following tracks north through a defoliated area, saw three enemy and fired, killing two; the third jumped into a bunker. The enemy, estimated at two platoons, replied with three rocket-propelled grenades, three claymores and AK-47 fire down fire lanes cut through a fence, and 1 and 3 Platoons, which came up in support, were also fired on. The company withdrew so that artillery, helicopter gunships and two air strikes could hit the bunkers, and prepared to attack the next day. Three enemy were possibly killed.

A patrol of 2 SAS Squadron made contact with five Viet Cong and killed all five. Two M1 carbines, an M2 carbine and an SKS were captured, with a pack holding clothing, rice and documents, among them an award for the best soldier of D445 Battalion in 1966.

2 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR, sweeping near the previous day's contact, followed a track to a log-walled bunker system. The forward scout shot an enemy at 7 m and grenades were thrown into the bunkers, but the forward section then had three claymores fired at it and the platoon was pinned down by fire from rocket launchers, automatic rifles and 10 to 15 AK-47s at 7 m. Artillery called in close wounded one New Zealander with shrapnel from a tree burst, a friendly-fire incident, and did not relieve the platoon. Under helicopter gunship fire and smoke it broke contact, killing another enemy as it went; three enemy were killed in all. B and W Companies attacked the next day after artillery and air strikes, but the enemy had gone.

An estimated 100 enemy, identified from captured documents as from C1 Company of D445 Local Force Battalion, attacked Long Dien with recoilless rifles, rocket-propelled grenades, automatic weapons and rifles. B, C and D Companies of 1 RAR, with armoured personnel carriers, tanks and helicopter gunships, were sent in; C Company and the armour fought a company-sized force in black inside the town, and B Company fought another group on Route 23. Sporadic fighting went on until late afternoon, and artillery fired five missions in support. Eleven or twelve Australians were wounded, seven of them in C Company by a 60 mm mortar; 29 to 40 enemy were recorded killed.

5 Platoon, B Company, 3 RAR, was moving along the road in Long Dien to protect 4 Platoon's flank while it searched for a missing South Vietnamese battalion commander when its forward sections came under heavy fire from an enemy platoon, and returned it. Nine Viet Cong were killed. Two or three Australians were killed and four or five wounded, and the enemy took a radio from an Australian signaller and may also have taken weapons from the casualties.

The scout of 6 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, saw an enemy with an AK-47 on top of a bunker and fired; the enemy replied with rocket-propelled grenades, claymores and AK-47s and set off a command-detonated mine, wounding four Australians, and the company withdrew and brought artillery down on the bunkers. When it returned, 4 Platoon, struggling through dense scrub, drew heavy fire, believed killing two enemy, and had to pull back. After two air strikes, 5 Platoon tried again and was hit by another command-detonated mine and fire from bunkers the air strikes had missed; five more were wounded, one of whom died, and the company withdrew. The company commander admitted it had not at first realised what it had met or how strong the enemy was; it was also noted that helicopter gunships would have helped, and that the artillery observer was repeatedly cut out by the battalion radio net.

With air support restricted, the rifle companies of 1 RAR were relying on 3 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, for resupply along two trails, and the enemy had noticed. While deploying D Company, 1 RAR, an armoured personnel carrier hit a pressure mine of 75 to 100 lb of explosive laid in the previous two days, which threw it into the air. One trooper and one infantryman were killed, and others were wounded, one of whom later died; the carrier was badly damaged.

C Company, 1 RAR, made contact with an enemy squad, possibly killing one, and a sweep found a bunker system and a cache of an SKS, two 12.7 mm heavy machine-guns with seven spare barrels, three claymores, oil and personal equipment. An enemy soldier ran from a shelter and set off a claymore, wounding three Australians with shrapnel; he was killed. Tall trees delayed the helicopter evacuation of the wounded.

Following its earlier contact, 11 Platoon, D Company, 3 RAR, found an enemy camp and had cleared half of it when it was pinned down by heavy fire, with one man wounded. The right flank was on a steep slope and could not be turned, and 10 Platoon, sent round the other flank, was pinned by six bunkers and a sniper; its platoon sergeant was shot while organising the leading section and died of his wounds. The company withdrew for the night. An air strike hit the bunkers the next day, and when the camp was swept a day later the enemy had gone.

12 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, made contact with about 60 enemy in a large bunker system of 14 large and 10 small bunkers covering 200 by 250 m. The platoon pulled back for an air strike and artillery, and D Company then attacked and cleared all but three still-occupied bunkers, which were ambushed overnight, though most of the occupants got away. Five Australians were wounded. Six enemy bodies and two blood trails were found.

7 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR, searching for bunkers, found a company-sized system of 20 interlocking covered bunkers in thick jungle that seemed to be empty, and quickly attacked with two sections. The first bunkers were cleared easily, but halfway in both sections came under very disciplined AK-47 fire from enemy in green uniforms and pith helmets, and the casualties came in clearing three main bunkers: two Australians were killed, one died of wounds and six were wounded. Two enemy were killed and the rest withdrew east; an AK-47, 600 lb of rice, packs, medical kits and documents were captured. The platoon considered it should have reconnoitred the bunkers more carefully before attacking.

9 Platoon, C Company, 3 RAR, coming down a hill, met about 20 enemy in green uniforms coming up. The enemy fired AK-47s and rocket-propelled grenades into the trees, causing several minor splinter injuries; a dog handler wounded in the head and forearm and the forward scout, shot in the thigh, were evacuated. Six enemy were possibly killed, and the rest withdrew north.

1 and 2 Platoons, V Company, 4 RAR, were in ambush on a track system. Thirteen enemy, unarmed porters carrying packs guarded by three armed men, walked into 1 Platoon's heavy claymore ambush on the main track and were hit by nine claymores and rifle fire; four were killed, two blood trails led away, and four ran down the track into 2 Platoon's ambush. Across both ambushes seven enemy were killed and three wounded, and an ID card indicated the presence of the D2014 infiltration group.

Eight enemy in black carrying weapons and packs ran into a section of 12 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, holding a firm base. One Australian died of a head wound. Three enemy were killed, and one or two AK-47s were captured.

A patrol of 2 SAS Squadron in ambush saw six men at its rear and opened fire at 20 m with rifles and grenade launchers, and the contact went on for an hour and 20 minutes. They were a Popular Forces company under US command that had wandered into the SAS area of operations; seven of its men and a US adviser were wounded. This was a friendly-fire incident.

2 Platoon, A Company, 3 RAR, in ambush on a track 400 m from the company base, shot dead an enemy soldier, and ten minutes later was attacked by at least an enemy platoon with rocket-propelled grenades and at least three machine-guns; accurate rocket fire into a machine-gun position killed two Australians, and the enemy seemed to be enveloping the platoon. Under artillery fire, 1 Platoon came up to cover the right flank and withdrawal and was drawn into the fight, and with helicopter gunships firing very accurately the platoons withdrew to the company base. The enemy then tried to envelop the company; casualties were evacuated, a second gunship team was called in, and the company broke contact and withdrew. Two Australians died of wounds and six were wounded, mostly by rocket-propelled grenades; seven enemy were killed and up to nine more possibly killed.

7 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, searching for camps after its earlier contact, swept unsupported into a bunker complex and was pinned down at 20 m by intense automatic and sniper fire from an estimated enemy company. Two Australians were killed and five wounded; the fire was too heavy to recover the bodies, and the platoon was extracted under helicopter gunship fire at 50 m, the enemy being too close for artillery. The company, also under sniper fire, killed one enemy. A medical evacuation helicopter was hit and had to withdraw, and after gunships directed by the battalion commander suppressed the fire, all casualties were evacuated from another winch point. The camp was then hit by artillery, mortars and two air strikes.

12 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR, was in an area known to be full of enemy, and near where 11 Platoon had found and was destroying enemy camps. The platoon commander, thinking there was another camp nearby, led a group a few metres along a side track and was seen by enemy in a concealed camp about 35 m away. They set off a mine made from an 81 mm mortar shell, a claymore and a grenade and opened fire with AK-47s; the mines and grenade killed two Australians and wounded six. The platoon sergeant-major led the other two sections in an attack, but the enemy had quickly retreated. Mines, claymores and a Soviet anti-tank grenade were captured.

4 Platoon, B Company, 3 RAR, harboured north of the Firestone Trail, had six claymores covering 200 m of the trail, with a three-man killing party on duty. When 80 or more enemy began filing past, the party fired the claymores, one of which failed, and withdrew to the rest of the platoon, and artillery was brought down around the killing ground. A sweep next morning found two bodies and eleven drag marks, and rocket rounds, a grenade and a pack were captured.

A patrol of 2 SAS Squadron ambushed three ox-carts and eight enemy moving along a track, killing all eight. It then came under fire from six to eight enemy to the west, and helicopter gunships fired on the area; six more ox-carts were seen on the track. The patrol was extracted.
A patrol of 2 SAS Squadron made contact with seven enemy and killed all seven, capturing three AK-47s and an SKS. One Australian was wounded.

After its earlier contact, 2 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, found it was on the edge of a large camp, and the company commander sent 1 and 3 Platoons round the left flank to move in. 1 Platoon saw a claymore just before it exploded, wounding two Australians. After artillery fire it moved forward again and was pinned down by heavy fire; the platoon commander and a section commander were killed and another soldier was shot in the shoulder. 3 Platoon was ordered forward to 1 Platoon; the rest of the account is cut off. Two enemy were recorded killed and one wounded.

2 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR, moving west through sparse bush, was ambushed from dense cover 15 to 30 m away by enemy with about ten weapons, including a machine-gun, firing heavily and low. One New Zealander was killed and three wounded, two by gunshots and one slightly by shrapnel from artillery fire. The forward scout shot one enemy; artillery was brought in and a section swept the area, but the enemy had withdrawn. An enemy camp was found nearby.

2 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, following a well-worn track, surprised about 15 enemy hastily preparing an ambush and opened fire, killing one and badly wounding another. One Australian was shot in the head and later died, and another was wounded in the arm. The enemy withdrew to a bunker complex of about 30 bunkers, around two years old, which A Company then attacked; women's and children's clothing was found there.
A patrol of 2 SAS Squadron ambushed five enemy heading west, killing three and wounding one. There were no Australian casualties.

Up to five enemy approached 7 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR, along a track; two were killed and the platoon swept west down the track. Meanwhile another enemy approached the perimeter from the east and was shot by a sentry. Artillery was adjusted onto the first group's escape route. Two AK-47s, an M1 carbine, magazines, webbing and grenades were captured.

An Australian reaction force of four Centurion tanks, a recovery vehicle, four armoured personnel carriers and a platoon of 3 RAR, joined by a Regional Force platoon, responded to about 20 enemy occupying Ap Ngai Giao. They moved through the village to where the enemy had withdrawn to a treed creek line, which 105 mm artillery and the tanks fired on, and a Regional Force ambush squad was put into the creek. The returning enemy sprang the ambush, the Regional Force soldiers withdrew and artillery fired again; one Regional Force soldier died of wounds. Enemy casualties are not known.

2 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, moving parallel to a track, had its second section hit by two claymores fired by about six enemy near a bunker system, and the leading and rear sections came under rifle fire. The company quickly reinforced the platoon and brought artillery onto the bunkers, and the casualties were moved to a winch point for helicopter evacuation. One Australian was killed and nine or ten wounded, including a gunner and engineers attached to the battalion. The company secured the camp, but the enemy had left; claymores, a 105 mm shell rigged with a tripwire, rice and medical supplies were recovered.

7 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, moving to a new ambush position, was fired on by two enemy, and as it swept the area 10 to 15 Viet Cong opened fire from bunkers with AK-47s, an RPG-2 and a claymore. One Australian was killed and five wounded. The platoon withdrew to evacuate the wounded by helicopter, and C Company closed up and directed artillery onto the camp; the enemy withdrew and the company secured a camp of 12 bunkers. A fresh grave nearby held an enemy body thought to be from this contact.

A 28-man platoon of 8 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR, was sent to find 100 to 200 enemy seen from the air. Fourteen men reconnoitred along a paddy field bordering a small swamp while the other 14 stayed with three armoured personnel carriers as a reaction force. As the reconnaissance group crossed the tree line it was hit by a command-detonated Chinese claymore; one Australian was killed and five wounded. The reaction force moved down the paddy, fired on the area and brought the group out, and mortars fired on the area.

7 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, leading the company, was fired on by three or four enemy in bunkers with AK-47s, RPG-2s and a claymore. 7 Platoon formed a firm base and gave fire support while 9 Platoon attacked from the right flank. Two enemy were killed, and two AK-47s, a rocket launcher and 40 lb of rice were captured. Four Australians were wounded, three by shrapnel and one by a gunshot.

Four enemy in green uniforms armed with AK-47s and an RPG-2 approached 8 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR's position and were fired on. They fired back with the rocket launcher, and three Australians were slightly wounded by shrapnel. Three enemy were killed, and two AK-47s and the RPG-2 were captured.
2 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, helped by elements of the Defence Platoon, fired on three or four ox-carts at night. Six enemy were killed and one person was detained.

During a sweep, 3 Platoon, A Company, 9 RAR, came under fire from an unknown number of enemy in a large bunker system using heavy and light machine-guns, rocket-propelled grenades and claymore mines. The contact lasted three and a half hours and drew in 2 Platoon. It was broken off at last light after small arms, artillery, mortars, helicopter gunships and air strikes were used. Ten enemy were killed; one Australian was killed and six were wounded and evacuated.

A Company, 9 RAR, was packing up its claymores to leave its night position on a track when an unknown number of enemy fired three rocket-propelled grenades and AK-47s at it from the north. One grenade landed among a section of 2 Platoon gathered for orders, killing three Australians and wounding five. The platoon returned some fire and artillery and gunships were called in; the enemy withdrew with unknown losses. The lesson drawn was not to stand around in groups.

W Company, 4 RAR, had been led by the SAS into a major enemy infiltration area and set an ambush in a triangle on a main track; the enemy seem to have thought they were attacking an SAS patrol. The platoons detected movement and fired their claymore mines, and part of an enemy company replied with heavy automatic fire and at least ten rocket-propelled grenades, some of which burst in the trees. The company fired back at the muzzle flashes, supported by an AC-47 gunship and US and Australian artillery, and the enemy withdrew. Three New Zealanders were wounded by shrapnel, two lightly. The enemy removed their dead, but the next morning pools of blood, blood trails and drag marks showed heavy losses; one of the machine-guns had broken during the fight.

10 Platoon, D Company, 9 RAR, moving with two sections forward to clear higher ground, saw two enemy about 75 m on, and the left section fired on them. Two groups of enemy replied with automatic and rocket-propelled grenade fire from bunkers. Five Australians were wounded and evacuated; the record also lists five enemy wounded. The rest of the account is cut off.

5 Platoon, B Company, 9 RAR, investigating a track from a water point, ran into a sentry in a bunker guarding a bunker system, who fired a claymore and an AK-47. Two Australians were killed, one of them dying of wounds, and four wounded, all by the claymore. The platoon formed a fire base and fired back, but the enemy had withdrawn; artillery and helicopter gunships were used. The platoon commander thought they had been too obvious in following the track.

2 Platoon, A Company, 9 RAR, made contact with an estimated squad of about ten enemy dressed in black and green, who engaged the platoon from the rear before withdrawing north and south-west. Two enemy were killed and three wounded, and two rifles and seven packs of rice were captured. One Australian was shot in the stomach and two others had minor injuries and stayed on duty.

1 Troop, B Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, and B Company, 4 RAR, were fired on by enemy in bunkers and attacked them, meeting rocket-propelled grenades, machine-guns and claymore mines, with air strikes and helicopter gunships in support. Two Australians of B Company were killed and eight wounded, five from the tanks, mostly by rocket-propelled grenades, and three from B Company, mostly by claymores. One tank was seriously damaged by four or five rocket-propelled grenades. W Company joined B Company, both withdrew to let 155mm artillery hit the bunkers, and the force needed an ammunition resupply. Six enemy were recorded killed.

W Company, 4 RAR, was covering the approaches to Long Binh and standing to when a 1 Platoon machine-gun saw enemy movement and opened fire. Claymores were fired and the enemy made several attacks with infantry and rocket-propelled grenades, while closely coordinated artillery and mortars fired near the company and an AC-47 gunship attacked the withdrawal routes. At first light six enemy bodies were found, five in the arc of that first machine-gun, with nine drag marks, and rifles, seven rocket-propelled grenade launchers, 43 grenades and plastic explosive were captured. Five New Zealanders were lightly wounded by shrapnel.

D Company, 9 RAR, reported rockets being fired from about 600 metres away over half an hour. Artillery and the mortar platoon replied, and afterwards yelling and people running about were heard. The next morning a party from the mortar platoon and 10 Platoon found seven enemy dead, six makeshift rocket launchers and nine rockets. On 5 March eight more bodies, some partly buried, and another rocket were found nearby, making 15 enemy killed.

D Company, 9 RAR, moving west, ran into a large bunker system of 21 bunkers held by enemy soon reinforced to squad size or more. 11 Platoon was fired on and hit by rocket-propelled grenades, and 12 Platoon, sweeping to the south, was held up by fire from bunkers; when a medical evacuation helicopter hovered, the enemy opened up with a heavy machine-gun, rockets and rifles and drove it off. The company withdrew with its casualties, one Australian killed and five wounded, and the camp was hit by artillery, air strikes and gunships; the company found it abandoned the next day, and four enemy bodies were found two days later. The company commander warned against manoeuvring near a suspected bunker system before the ground is carefully examined, noted that the enemy waits quietly for its best chance such as a hovering medical evacuation helicopter, and advised against being drawn into a bunker fight without heavy artillery, air and tank support. He also noted that in dense bush the enemy's rocket-propelled grenade worked better than the Australian M72 light anti-tank weapon, whose fuse set off on foliage.

8 Platoon, C Company, 9 RAR, had just entered a re-entrant when it saw and fired on an enemy soldier, and came under rifle and rocket-propelled grenade fire from a bunker system held by what was thought to be at least an enemy platoon. The company commander swung 9 Platoon round to the north and used artillery to block the south; pushing down from the north, 9 Platoon also came under fire and then withdrew so the bunkers could be shelled. Over the five-hour battle five Australians were wounded and six enemy were killed; the enemy's fire was well controlled and aimed about a metre above the ground. Helicopter gunships covered the disengagement, the area was hit by artillery and mortars, and the bunkers were destroyed the next day after the enemy had gone; packs lost in the fighting were recovered.

At first light 5 Platoon, B Company, 9 RAR, ambushing a creek crossing on a well-used track, caught eight of about 20 enemy moving in quietly and well spread out from the west. Claymore mines and rifle fire killed three; the rest fired back and tried to escape, and three more were killed as the area was systematically raked, while artillery and mortars hit the escape routes. Six enemy were killed in all and more were hit by shrapnel, and an AK-47 and five submachine-guns were captured. The platoon commander credited concealment and good fire discipline, and said maximum firepower must be used once contact starts.

While elements of A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, with A Company, 5 RAR, were escorting a convoy of US trucks up Route 15 in Bien Hoa province, two trucks hit mines 50 metres apart. Accounts differ: one records ten Australians and two Americans wounded, with ten more Australians wounded who stayed on duty; another records seven Australians and one American wounded and one troop-carrying vehicle damaged.

Three Australians of the 4 RAR Mobile Advisory Team and 22 Vietnamese of 1 Platoon, 612 Regional Force Company, laid an ambush in paddy fields 150 metres from the tree line of Dat Do. Within 15 minutes the enemy opened fire from the trees with machine-guns, automatic weapons and B40 rockets, killing the leader of the rear protection squad and pinning the patrol behind the paddy banks. As the platoon withdrew two more Vietnamese were killed, and an Australian corporal was killed by a machine-gun burst while the Australians sheltered behind a bank. The enemy advanced until mortar fire from 4 RAR at the Horseshoe stopped them, and they retreated leaving one dead. The platoon had ambushed regularly from this spot and the enemy had come to know its movements; the Australians thought the mortars would have driven the enemy off with fewer casualties had the Vietnamese not withdrawn.

Minutes after 3 Platoon's ambush fired, the machine-gunner of 1 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, saw an enemy soldier appear on the track in front of him and opened fire; no one else fired, as they could see nothing. A sweep soon after found four bodies on the track, and a tracker dog followed a blood trail 400 metres to another body covered in leaves. The dead did not appear to be armed and, from the money they carried, were thought to be tax collectors. The daylight sweep also found another body, with a submachine-gun, from the contact the night before; six enemy are recorded killed and documents were recovered.

The leading section of 9 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, moving to high ground, saw five enemy grouped round a hammock and a bunker. The two other sections were deployed to the flanks and the platoon attacked through the bunker system, where 10 to 12 main-force enemy were seen; caught by surprise, the enemy were driven out and withdrew north-north-east. Three enemy were killed, possibly, and one or two wounded, and an AK-47 and two rocket-propelled grenade rounds were captured. There were no Australian casualties.

11 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR, in ambush, made contact with four enemy dressed in green moving south along a track. All four were killed, and three AK-47s, magazines, a grenade, ammunition and rice were captured.

C Company, 4 RAR, in ambush, made contact with an estimated enemy squad, killing one and possibly two more, and capturing an AK-47 and a pack. One Australian was shot in the shoulder. A sweep of the area on 22 March found two more bodies, bringing the enemy dead to three.

11 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, ran into a platoon of enemy in a bunker system and, spread out along the objective, found every part of the platoon under fire at once, leaving the commander no reserve. It was hit by claymore mines, heavy small-arms fire and rocket-propelled grenades, which killed one man and wounded seven; two Australians were killed in all. 12 Platoon, helicopter gunships and air strikes joined in, and after four hours 11 Platoon disengaged and carried out its wounded. Artillery did not contribute effectively. A Company later found graves with four recently killed bodies, believed to be from this contact.

12 Platoon, D Company, 9 RAR, found a latrine and was fired on by what proved to be an enemy platoon in a bunker system with a 200-metre front, well-cut fire lanes and snipers, using small arms, automatic weapons, a claymore mine and rocket-propelled grenades. With helicopter gunships in support, the platoon withdrew by fire and movement after 45 minutes, and artillery and mortars hit the bunkers. Seven Australians were wounded, three of whom were evacuated and one of whom died; one was slightly hit by spent shrapnel from Australian artillery. The rest of D Company joined the platoon and by evening had cleared 25 bunkers with grenades; one enemy sniper was shot and fell from a tree. It was noted that the enemy's fire seemed to follow the platoon's machine-guns, which should be moved during a long contact.

The Anti-Tank Platoon, Support Company, 4 RAR, in ambush, fired claymore mines and machine-guns at movement, using hand-held flares, artillery illumination and mortars. Moaning and movement were heard again later and the area was hit with grenades and machine-gun fire. A sweep at first light found seven bodies, two blood trails and a drag mark, and six AK-47s were captured.

5 Platoon and B Company headquarters, 5 RAR, in ambush, heard movement behind the position. A rifleman went a few paces forward and killed an enemy soldier 25 metres from the perimeter, but the enemy replied with automatic fire and a rocket-propelled grenade that killed him and wounded three others with shrapnel. Fire suppressed the enemy and dragging noises were heard; movement on the east flank was engaged with small arms and artillery, including 105 Field Battery. The medical evacuation helicopter was fired on. The claymores were not fired, as they could not be seen and the enemy might have tampered with them. Three enemy are recorded killed and one wounded.

2 Section, 2 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, in ambush, fired on two enemy groups totalling about 20 moving south to north, with 161 Field Battery in support. Six enemy were killed and five wounded, and the rest withdrew south-east.

Enemy approaching 11 Platoon, D Company, 9 RAR, from the south-east were seen by a sentry, but they heard the platoon talking as it adjusted mortar fire and fired rocket-propelled grenades and machine-guns into platoon headquarters. Fire was returned, with an AC-47 gunship and helicopter gunships in support, and enemy movement continued near the night position for over two hours. One enemy was killed. Four Australians were evacuated, three with gunshot wounds and one in severe shock, and three more were wounded by grenade splinters but stayed on duty.

2 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, with 14 to 16 armoured personnel carriers including mortar carriers, and D and E Platoons on foot, laid a combined ambush on either side of the remains of Thua Tich village on Route 328. D and E Platoons warned that a large body of enemy with heavy packs was coming; after three scouts were let through, about 50 enemy entered the killing grounds and both ambushes opened fire with claymores and heavy machine-guns. Mortars fired on the expected withdrawal route and an AC-47 gunship later ringed the ambush sites with fire. Eleven enemy were killed and three wounded, and rifles, a rocket-propelled grenade launcher, grenades, ammunition, medical supplies and 14 packs were captured.

W Company, 4 RAR, supporting elements of the US 11th Armored Cavalry Regiment, made contact with an estimated enemy company. Six armoured personnel carriers formed a fire base and fired .50 calibre and M60 machine-guns and grenade launchers, supported by helicopter gunships; the force then withdrew to let air strikes hit the area. Eighteen enemy were killed, four of them by Australian forces, and rifles, rocket-propelled grenade rounds, bangalore torpedoes, documents, a telephone, a pistol, grenades and mortar rounds were captured.

An engineer vehicle set off two of a cluster of four M16 mines in Dat Do, wounding seven soldiers of the Assault Pioneer Platoon, Support Company, 9 RAR; six were evacuated. The road had been swept with mine detectors the day before and by bulldozers that morning, but the mines were missed. 10 Platoon, 30 metres away, went to help.

6 Platoon, B Company, 9 RAR, had found an enemy camp and a seven-man engineer team from 1 Field Squadron was checking a track into it when about four enemy, who had followed a patrol into the camp, ambushed them from behind an anthill and from trees with rocket-propelled grenades and small arms. Two engineers and two members of the platoon were wounded; one engineer died of his wounds. The platoon and an armoured personnel carrier swept the area; one enemy was wounded and the enemy withdrew west.

A Task Force reaction force moved with 9 RAR to Dat Do to support Regional Force, Popular Force and South Vietnamese Army troops, who had been fighting an estimated enemy company since early that morning. By afternoon the enemy were contained within a set area. South Vietnamese losses were seven killed, 26 wounded and 12 missing; two enemy were possibly killed and a carbine and a pistol captured.

After 1 Platoon's contact 800 metres away, 2 Platoon, A Company, 9 RAR, was on full alert when ten enemy walked into its killing ground. Claymores were fired at the first three, who had bunched up, and at the rest, and the killer group opened heavy fire; the enemy did not fire back, though 60mm mortars supported them. Mortars and artillery fired on escape routes and lit the area through the night, and grenades were thrown at any movement. Despite this the enemy removed their dead and wounded, leaving drag marks and blood trails; the platoon thought it had killed three and wounded seven.

From late morning to evening, B and D Companies, 5 RAR, with tanks of B Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, armoured personnel carriers of B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, Duc Thanh district Regional and Popular Force troops, helicopter gunships and 105 Field Battery, fought an estimated 90 enemy in the village of Binh Ba. B Company, with tanks, formed a blocking position while the village was swept. At least 27 enemy were killed and two captured, with 43 killed and six wounded recorded in all. One Australian was killed and eight or more wounded, and two Centurion tanks were moderately damaged.

A company of 1 Battalion, 33 North Vietnamese Regiment, attacked Duc Trung and overwhelmed the local defence platoon, and B Company, 5 RAR, was sent to restore the situation. Artillery was brought down to within 20 metres of the houses and helicopter gunships attacked the north and west of the village, then B Company attacked from the south with a troop of tanks and armoured personnel carriers. The enemy were routed, and the Popular Force took over clearing the rest of the village to avoid civilian casualties. Forty enemy are recorded killed.

On the south edge of Dat Do, a soldier of D Company, 5 RAR, stepped on an M16 mine that leapt two metres and exploded among 12 Platoon and company headquarters. Three Australians were killed, one of whom died of wounds, and 20 to 24 were wounded. Another M16 mine, laid in the previous two or three days, was found nearby. The district chief had been told three days earlier that D Company would be operating there.

10 Platoon, D Company, 6 RAR, had been in ambush for two days in thick bamboo beside a plantation track in the Courtenay rubber when about 60 enemy, a porter party, a stretcher party and a protection party, walked into it. The claymores were fired when most were in the killing ground, followed by three machine-guns and rifles; the enemy fired a few wild shots and withdrew south and west. The sweep found 22 enemy dead and many blood trails, and captured six AK-47s, a rocket-propelled grenade launcher, 26 grenades, small arms, documents and medical supplies. Five of the 11 claymores failed because of faulty detonators, but the platoon's daily cleaning of its machine-gun ammunition paid off, as none of the three guns stopped. Mortars fired in support.

After spotting an enemy sentry sheltering under a plastic cape in heavy rain, 6 Platoon and half of 5 Platoon, B Company, 6 RAR, attacked what was thought to be a small camp, surprising and killing the sentry. The camp proved to be a large bunker system, and the enemy counter-attacked; the rest of the company was fed in, with artillery, helicopter gunships and an AC-47 gunship in support. After taking ten casualties, seven of them serious, the company was ordered to withdraw, made difficult by heavy rain and eight to ten enemy snipers in trees; two of 6 Platoon's machine-guns failed and it lost all its packs. Radio communications were poor, and the artillery forward observer was the only link to battalion. The enemy left overnight; a search of the camp found nine enemy dead.

After its ambush and evacuating its wounded, the combined force of ten Australians from 3 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, and 55 South Vietnamese soldiers was moving to a new ambush site when a platoon of main-force Viet Cong attacked it with heavy AK-47, grenade-launcher and rocket-propelled grenade fire from all directions. Poor communications delayed artillery until a Possum aircraft relayed the requests, and the enemy then closed in to avoid the shells, but two teams of helicopter gunships fired to within 25 metres of the force and the enemy withdrew. Seven South Vietnamese were wounded by rocket-propelled grenades. Two enemy were killed and possibly six more, going by many blood trails.

C Company, 5 RAR, found a bunker system containing anti-vehicle mines, a claymore and a command-detonated 105mm mine on the south-east edge of the Long Hai hills. That night 7 Platoon hit an M16 mine, and another went off while the wounded were being moved; a third was found nearby. Three Australians were killed and 14 wounded, one of them an engineer.

3 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR, was clearing a harbour position about half a kilometre south-east of Hoi My when the platoon commander stepped out of the cleared area and set off an M16 mine. He was killed and 18 others were wounded, one of them a sapper. 750 pounds of rice in 15 drums were found.

An enemy force of 40 to 50 attacked local forces at Thai Thien, and the Task Force provided artillery support. Fourteen Viet Cong were killed, and a rocket launcher, six AK47s, an M16, a pistol, and mortar ammunition and parts were captured.

Following up an earlier contact, the forward section of 7 Platoon, C Company, 9 RAR, came under heavy rocket-propelled grenade and rifle fire from about a platoon of enemy in a large bunker system. The forward scout was killed and eight men were wounded, one of them trying to rescue him, and the section lost a machine-gun and several rifles and grenade launchers; the pinned-down sections were pulled out with difficulty. 9 Platoon's move round the left flank eased the enemy's pressure, and low cloud prevented air strikes, but helicopter gunships were very effective and artillery fired through the night. After a heavy bombardment C Company attacked next morning, but the enemy had gone; blood trails and cut bamboo poles suggested they had suffered casualties.

B Company, 6 RAR, planned a three-platoon attack on a bunker system, but 5 Platoon was delayed by an earlier contact, so 6 Platoon ambushed the track out of the camp while 4 Platoon attacked. Twenty metres from the camp, 4 Platoon's right flank was hit by rocket-propelled grenades, a light machine-gun and about ten automatic rifles, and five men were wounded, one seriously. The support section sent to help swung too far right, but 4 Platoon's other sections moved up, killing two enemy, and 5 Platoon pushed through the south of the camp; by then the enemy had withdrawn, and two more enemy dead and a large amount of equipment, including rocket launchers, were found. The company concluded that a bunker system could be taken by fire and movement, provided a thorough reconnaissance had first found the enemy's size, positions and escape routes.

An M16 mine went off in 2 Platoon, W Company, 6 RAR, about 100 metres west of Lo Gom, killing one New Zealander and wounding five, two of whom later died of their wounds. The mine was on a track the platoon had used earlier while looking for an ambush position; the enemy had seen them and laid mines where they expected the New Zealanders to go.

The assault pioneer platoon of Support Company, 5 RAR, preparing a harbour position, heard noises ahead, and after 105 Field Battery shelled the area, it and 3 Platoon, A Company, led by A Company's second-in-command, moved in to assault an enemy bunker system. They were met by very heavy rocket-propelled grenade and automatic rifle fire from the bunkers and flanks, with rockets landing behind them too, and withdrew to a base nearby to evacuate the wounded, with helicopter gunships firing in support. When the medical evacuation helicopters arrived, a large enemy force counter-attacked the base with 60mm mortars, rifles and rocket-propelled grenades, landing fire among the wounded, and most casualties came then; gunships suppressed the fire and the base was moved so the wounded could be flown out. One Australian was killed and more than 30 wounded; enemy losses were later amended to nine killed, four killed by artillery and air attack, and 25 wounded. The company commander said the company radio net had been a shambles, with every supporting element joining in, and suggested a forward air controller control all aircraft on a separate net.

Four armoured personnel carriers of 3 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, in ambush near the beach, fired on 20 to 25 enemy in the killing zone. Eleven were killed and two more bodies were found later, making 13 killed; four were wounded, one was captured or surrendered, and one was reported taken by a crocodile. Weapons, documents and a large quantity of food, clothing and other supplies were captured.

12 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, was in two half-platoon groups 70 metres apart when an enemy force moved north along the track through the southern group towards the northern one. The northern group opened fire when the leading enemy were in its killing ground, and the southern group fired on those still passing; 45 enemy had been counted and more were still coming. The enemy withdrew hastily east and south-east without firing back, dragging away bodies and helping wounded, and were fired on whenever they were heard; helicopter gunships, artillery and mortars covered the area, and at first light a sweep found seven enemy dead, possibly five more, and signs of nine wounded. One Australian was wounded in the head by a grenade fragment but stayed on duty, and weapons, ammunition, food and documents were captured.

After a briefing by a prisoner, 3 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR's anti-tank platoon, called in artillery and attacked a bunker system held by an estimated enemy company, on a broad front with two sections forward to stop being outflanked. The attack pinned the forward enemy in their bunkers, but machine-guns on the flanks and snipers in trees pinned the platoon down, and the undergrowth was too thick for grenades; a helicopter gunship could not fire closer than 50 metres because the vegetation hid the battlefield. The platoon broke contact and the area was hit by artillery, gunships and air strikes with napalm, rockets and 250-pound bombs. Seven enemy were killed by the platoon and four blood trails found; two Australians were wounded, one of them evacuated.
Tanks of 2 Troop, B Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, saw five enemy 100 metres away. A searchlight sweep showed lights, which were engaged with canister and 105mm artillery at Duc Thanh.

After 9 Platoon's contact, C Company, 5 RAR, concentrated to reconnoitre the bunker system and called artillery onto the camp, but one shell fell short and wounded three Australians of 7 and 8 Platoons; this is recorded as friendly fire. Helicopter gunships covered their medical evacuation, and when enemy following a reconnaissance party tried to interfere with it, three were seen to fall; a strong blood trail led away, and a grave was found next day. Early next morning, after more shelling and gunship fire, C Company swept through three new bunker systems of 8, 24 and 7 bunkers, occupied by a regular enemy unit, and took the camp without casualties.

Enemy got through the defences of Dat Do past Regional Force bunkers and came up against a small mobile advisory team from B Company, 9 RAR, firing rocket-propelled grenades. The team fought back, supported through the night by a Spooky gunship aircraft, and tanks, armoured personnel carriers and a platoon of B Company assembled for a dawn attack, but the enemy withdrew at first light. Figures differ: four or three Australians were wounded, with fragment and shrapnel wounds, and four Regional Force soldiers were killed and four wounded; one enemy killed was credited to the Regional Forces, and the enemy were thought to have suffered further casualties.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's ambush beyond the patrol commander's name; five enemy were recorded killed and one wounded.

6 Platoon, B Company, 6 RAR, made contact with three Viet Cong moving south-east and killed all three. Automatic rifles and a compass were captured, and two Australians were wounded and evacuated; 101 Field Battery fired in support.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's contact beyond the patrol commander's name; four enemy were recorded killed and two wounded.

2 Platoon, V Company, 6 RAR, in ambush, made contact with 12 or more main-force enemy carrying cooking pots and rice. Four were killed, and two AK47s, 350 rounds, four packs, 100 pounds of rice and North Vietnamese webbing were captured; 101 Field Battery fired in support.

The scout of 10 Platoon, D Company, 6 RAR, smelt smoke on a track just as the enemy opened fire from a bunker system with rifles, automatic weapons and rocket-propelled grenades. Before artillery could be used, a rocket-propelled grenade fired down the track wounded four men of the leading section, which was pulled back through the rest of the platoon; the platoon broke contact and rejoined the company. The bunkers were hit by an air strike and artillery, including 101 Field Battery, and the company then cleared the area, finding 38 bunkers.

A Company, 9 RAR, ambushed a large enemy group of 50 to 60 at night. 1 Platoon let five leading enemy pass, and they were followed by a group of 20 and then another of 30; 2 Platoon, 200 metres away, let the vanguard through and ambushed the group of 20. Artillery was then called down on the larger group and a Spooky gunship aircraft fired on the enemy. Reports vary on the result, from three possibly killed and six wounded, shown by blood trails, up to six killed and six wounded; 100 pounds of rice were recovered.

Men of 6 RAR's mortar platoon and D Company, with the South Vietnamese 3/52 Battalion, set off an M16 mine near houses north of Lo Gom. Two Australians were killed, an engineer and a D Company soldier, and six wounded, two of whom stayed on duty.

A patrol of 2 Platoon, A Company, 9 RAR, came under fire at five metres from an estimated 60 enemy in a bunker complex more than 200 metres deep; the forward scout was killed and a man trying to reach him was wounded. 1 and 3 Platoons came up in support, backed by artillery, including 161 Field Battery, and helicopter gunships, but the enemy replied with intense fire: five aircraft were fired on, a helicopter was shot down, and a gunship and a medical evacuation helicopter were hit. The record shows one Australian killed and three wounded, the wounded being helicopter crew; enemy casualties were thought minimal, and they withdrew overnight.

An armoured personnel carrier of 1 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, sweeping past a bunker complex with D Company, 6 RAR, was ambushed by about three enemy, and two rocket-propelled grenades both hit it, causing serious damage and casualties. One Australian was killed and three wounded, one of whom died three weeks later.

The rear protection group of 8 Platoon, C Company, 9 RAR, in ambush, engaged five enemy in blue shirts and shorts who were following small groups of civilians returning to Thai Thien. Two enemy were killed, and a sweep found three blood trails. The record shows one Australian wounded.

8 Platoon, C Company, 9 RAR, with a section of armoured personnel carriers, let several groups of civilians returning to Thai Thien pass along an ox track, then ambushed with claymore mines a party of four enemy trying to slip by with the last group. A second group of six enemy, 40 metres behind, opened fire on the platoon, and the enemy withdrew by fire and movement. One enemy was killed and three blood trails found; one Australian was shot in the upper body and evacuated by helicopter.

C Company, 5 RAR, was being carried by armoured personnel carriers of 2 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, when soldiers riding on top of a carrier saw three enemy and opened fire. The full firepower of two carrier sections and two platoons was brought to bear on about ten enemy hiding in a grassy swamp, who returned inaccurate fire; the platoons swept round the flanks and rear while the carriers held the front, and artillery cut off escape routes. Six enemy were killed, two wounded and one captured, and weapons, documents, ammunition and packs were taken; an enemy soldier who surrendered next day said he had seen eight bodies, and 9 Platoon found four more. The company commander said all carrier sections needed to be on the company radio net, and praised the usefulness of high-explosive and white phosphorus rifle grenades.

4 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, on a fighting patrol, heard noises and found a bunker system 35 metres away, then waited on a footpad leading into it for about two hours. When 12 enemy came down the track, two machine-guns and rifles opened fire; the enemy replied with about 12 rocket-propelled grenades, automatic rifles and possibly 60mm mortars, and the platoon fired a large number of rifle grenades that punched through the bamboo into bunker openings, killing five enemy within 20 metres. Artillery cut off the south, helicopter gunships hit the whole complex and an air strike followed; one enemy was captured wounded, and two Australians had minor shrapnel wounds. The platoon commander commented that it was better to ambush the likely exits of a bunker system than attack it, and that the quick follow-up threw the enemy into complete confusion.

Armoured personnel carriers of 1 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, and tanks of 1 Armoured Regiment helped a Regional Force platoon attack 15 to 20 enemy in a bunker complex. Four enemy were killed and an AK47 captured; four Regional Force soldiers were wounded and there were no Australian casualties. The record, however, shows four Australians wounded.

6 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, was ambushing inside an enemy bunker system when two enemy, followed by a larger group, came to get water from the well. The sentry fired a claymore mine, blowing down the first two, and the machine-gun fired on the rest; a sweep was then fired on with rocket-propelled grenades and automatic rifles, and two Australians were wounded by rocket fragments. The enemy also fired on a helicopter gunship and on the platoon with a light machine-gun, which was silenced by machine-gun and rifle-grenade fire. Intelligence concluded four enemy were killed, one wounded and one killed from the air; a grave with three bodies was found the next day.

A section of 2 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, with D and E Platoons of 1st Australian Task Force headquarters, was in ambush at night when it heard movement ahead and opened fire with automatic weapons. Groaning and dragging sounds were engaged with claymore mines, automatic weapons and mortars, and a sweep next morning found six enemy dead; two AK47s and a pistol were captured.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's ambush beyond the patrol commander's name; five enemy were recorded killed and one Australian wounded.

The forward scout of 5 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, saw a bunker and two enemy and opened fire, and heavy fire came back. The platoon fanned out to find the flank of the bunker system but was itself outflanked, and its weapons could not suppress the enemy fire, so it called for artillery and held on until tanks of B Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, and armoured personnel carriers of 3 Cavalry Regiment arrived. As they did, the enemy who could get away did so, at least 24 of them, and the rest were destroyed by tank and carrier fire or crushed in their bunkers. In the two-hour battle six enemy were killed, two by the infantry and four by the armour, and one Australian was killed; the record notes the artillery had little effect but the tanks destroyed the enemy.

3 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, was in ambush when three or more enemy in camouflage clothing, carrying rocket launchers, were heard pushing through the scrub into its rear. The rear machine-gun had a double-feed stoppage after one round, and a claymore mine failed to fire because of a faulty firing device; the enemy fired three rocket-propelled grenades and withdrew east. Eight Australians were wounded, four of them evacuated by helicopter and the rest staying on duty, and a pack of clothing, food and documents was recovered.

D Company, 8 RAR, found 30 to 40 well-trained enemy occupying six bunkers; 10 Platoon was first fired on by two enemy in a well-built trench, and an engineer was wounded. Supported by 11 Platoon, 10 Platoon assaulted the bunkers for 2 hours 40 minutes, putting one out of action and beating off a counter-attack; one soldier was shot dead in the chest while trying to recover the wounded man and another was grazed on the head. Helicopter gunships and artillery supported, and at dusk the company withdrew with its dead soldier and his weapon; it returned next day with tanks, but the enemy had gone, leaving one dead and an AK47. At least one enemy was killed and one wounded, though losses were probably higher.

8 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, had seen signs of enemy and was looking for an ambush site, with sentries and some claymore mines out, when a sentry fired on the forward scout of about 30 enemy in black armed with AK47s, rocket launchers and grenade launchers. The enemy were hit by a claymore as the sentry withdrew, then returned fire and attacked twice, being beaten off each time. Two enemy were killed and one wounded, and an AK47 was captured; four Australians were wounded by rocket-propelled grenades. Artillery, mortars and helicopter gunships supported.

An armoured personnel carrier of 2 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, moving from fire support base Picton to Discovery just north of Thua Tich, hit an anti-tank mine of 30 to 60 pounds of explosive, which set off two more. The carrier was heavily damaged; a crewman and a passenger, a sapper, were killed, and a crewman and another passenger, also a sapper, were injured. During the medical evacuation the helicopter landed on another mine, which damaged it and injured another soldier.

1 Platoon, A Company, 8 RAR, was in a harbour and ambush position on a track, still arming its claymore mines, when two enemy appeared. The machine-gun sentry opened fire, and the second enemy fired a rocket-propelled grenade at the belt-feeder kneeling beside the gun, seriously wounding him; others were also wounded. The record gives four or six Australians wounded, four of them evacuated; one enemy was thought wounded by the machine-gun. 161 Field Battery fired in support.

A patrol of 10 Platoon, D Company, 8 RAR, in the Task Force's area, was ambushing a track junction near the Suoi Hoa Nuoc beside paddy fields when the machine-gun sentry heard a radio playing and waited until it was in the killing area. The claymore mines were fired and the machine-gun and grenade launchers raked the killing ground; after five minutes moaning was heard, and flares were fired and grenades systematically fired into the area for ten more minutes, with 161 Field Battery firing nearby. Of 11 enemy, eight were killed, one of them a woman, and two were captured wounded; a rocket launcher, rifles, carbines, pistols and grenades were captured. The patrol commander said fire must be kept low with interlocking arcs, and all the killing group must pour maximum fire into the killing area once the ambush is sprung.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's ambush beyond the patrol commander's name; seven enemy were recorded killed and two wounded.
A mine exploded among 3A Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR, killing two Australians, both engineers, and wounding four.

The sentry of 7 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, ambushing a track, heard eight enemy approaching from the west, and a section engaged them; the enemy fired back with AK47s and a rocket launcher to get their wounded out. When the firing died down, a sweep went out and was fired on by wounded enemy, and three Australians were wounded and evacuated by helicopter before the sweep resumed. Two enemy were killed, one possibly killed and one wounded, and two AK47s were captured; artillery and helicopter gunships supported. The platoon commander said the Australian casualties should have been left until the sweep was finished, and noted that the three M16s used all had continual stoppages.
The record gives no account of this SAS patrol's ambush beyond the patrol commander's name; five enemy were recorded killed and two wounded.

Following blood trails from its earlier contact, 2 Platoon, W Company, 6 RAR, broke into a large clearing and saw six enemy dressed in black running down a track, and engaged them. An enemy soldier hidden in long grass opened fire from two metres, wounding one soldier, and the machine-gunner was wounded while changing a belt; another soldier loaded the gun and opened fire, killing that enemy. Two enemy were killed, two wounded and two AK47s captured; two New Zealand soldiers were wounded.

Near the Long Hai hills, the headquarters of C Company, 8 RAR, met three Viet Cong and captured one, who said about 40 enemy were in a nearby bunker system surrounded by anti-personnel mines. The company attacked with armoured personnel carriers of B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, and tanks of A Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment; a carrier was destroyed by two rocket-propelled grenades, and two Australians were killed and several wounded. After artillery and air strikes a second assault led by tanks fought through the bunkers, but was stopped by a deep creek and an anti-tank minefield and ordered to withdraw, coming under heavy fire again from enemy who had reoccupied the bunkers and suffering more wounded; in all 13 Australians were wounded. That evening tanks recovered the lost carrier's casualties, and 12 enemy were killed, mostly by tank canister and high-explosive rounds, with many blood trails found; the system, held by 30 to 40 enemy or perhaps a battalion, was struck by B52 bombers before 8 RAR returned two days later.

1 Platoon, A Company, 8 RAR, moving carefully through a known minefield south-east of the Long Hai hills with engineers clearing the way, had reached its ambush site when a member of the engineer team set off an M16 jumping mine while the platoon was gathered around its headquarters. Seven Australians were killed and 13 wounded (one account gives eight killed, probably including a man killed by a second mine soon after).

9 Platoon, C Company, 8 RAR, set a carefully planned ambush on a track north of the Long Hais, inserted by tanks that then made a diversion, with 15 claymore mines and close artillery and mortar support. An enemy force of about a company, some 100 or more in four groups, came through; the platoon let the first group pass and blew the claymores on the second and third, and the first and fourth groups counter-attacked. With the platoon running short of ammunition, tanks of 2 Troop, 1 Armoured Regiment, came out from Fire Support Base Isa within 40 minutes, cleared the killing ground and stayed all night, while mortars, several artillery batteries and helicopter gunships fired in support. Three Australians were wounded and evacuated; ten enemy were killed, including two in small contacts during the next morning's sweep, and 22 drag marks suggested many more killed or wounded. Weapons, grenades and documents were captured.

Following C Company's heavy contact, B Company, 8 RAR, was being rushed into blocking positions by armoured personnel carrier. 4 Platoon had just dismounted and was moving forward with the carriers when it came under heavy fire from a bunker position, and rocket-propelled grenades hit a carrier, wounding its two crew, and a tank. A sweep was stopped ten metres into the jungle when claymore-type wires were seen, and the platoon was pulled back. Eight Australians were wounded by the rocket-grenades; six enemy were recorded killed, and three bodies were later found.

3 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR/NZ, searching for the D445 Battalion camp, found a well-used track and a poncho when both forward sections came under intense rocket-grenade, machine-gun, heavy machine-gun and rifle fire. The rest of the platoon helped them pull back, and nine Australians were wounded. The platoon withdrew 100 metres and artillery, mortars and helicopter gunships engaged the area, where C1 and C4 Companies and the headquarters of D445 Battalion were present; 2 Platoon then joined them. The commanders noted that dense undergrowth limited the use of rockets and grenade launchers, and that navigation errors made supporting fire less effective. Four enemy were recorded wounded.

2 Platoon and the headquarters of A Company, 5 RAR, in ambush, saw about 20 enemy approaching and waited until they were five metres from the machine-gun before firing claymore mines and the machine-gun. The Viet Cong returned heavy fire for about 20 minutes, with helicopter gunships and artillery supporting the Australians. A sweep found two enemy dead, drag marks from two more probably killed and four blood trails; one Australian was wounded and evacuated by helicopter. Two AK47s, a pistol, packs and documents were captured.

D Company, 6 RAR/NZ, under command of 8 RAR, was moving in column with 10 Platoon leading when it found bunkers, and 10 Platoon was sent to check them. Five to ten enemy in the bunkers opened fire with AK47s and rocket-propelled grenades, and the company took heavy losses; artillery was called in and most of 12 Platoon came forward, and the combined fire of the two platoons suppressed the enemy, while company headquarters covered the rear and evacuated the wounded. 10 Platoon's right flank machine-gun had been malfunctioning. After two and a half hours the enemy withdrew along well-prepared routes; three Australians were killed and six wounded, one of them accidentally. The nine bunkers guarded the northern approach to a more important system 200 metres away, which 11 Platoon occupied with tanks; artillery support for that attack was delayed because the guns were busy with another mission.

5 Platoon, B Company, 8 RAR, in the jungle 6 kilometres south of Xuyen Moc, found an old rusty M16 mine. While it was being destroyed, the platoon began looking at some old bunkers and formed an all-round defence, and someone set off another M16 mine, killing two Australians and wounding six.

The headquarters of V Company and 3 Platoon, V Company, 6 RAR/NZ, were fired on by an estimated 30 to 50 Viet Cong in a bunker system with mortars, rocket-propelled grenades and machine-guns; the enemy then withdrew, direction uncertain. The system was in two parts, one with fighting pits, one-man bunkers and shelters, the other with five or six large bunkers, possibly a headquarters. One New Zealand soldier was killed and three wounded; one Viet Cong was killed and three blood trails found. 101 Field Battery fired in support.

The Anti-Tank Platoon of 6 RAR/NZ, 24 strong, sprang an ambush on the advance guard of a larger enemy party of 10 to 15, killing one. The enemy fell back and were attacked by D Company and 3 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, placed across their main escape route, and four more were killed. An AK50 rifle, eight packs, eating utensils and documents were captured.

1 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR/NZ, made contact with 13 people, ten adults and three children, who were foraging for food; they withdrew north-west. Three were killed, recorded as Viet Cong, and there were no Australian casualties, though one Australian is shown as wounded in the casualty figures. Equipment and digging tools were recovered. The record lists this as a contact with civilians.
6 Platoon, B Company, 8 RAR, in the jungle 7 kilometres south of Xuyen Moc, set off what was probably an M16 mine, which exploded without jumping. Four Australians were wounded.

To let 5 Platoon get clear and evacuate its wounded, a patrol from B Company headquarters, 7 RAR, went into a bunker system of 18 bunkers along the Song Rai and came under intense rifle and rocket-grenade fire for an hour, taking three casualties. A section of 4 Platoon and platoon headquarters then attacked the line of bunkers so the wounded could be evacuated, and also met intense fire; helicopter gunships fired to within 10 to 15 metres ahead of the troops. All troops were withdrawn and an air strike hit the bunkers; tanks could not get through the jungle before dark, and next morning the enemy had gone. One Australian later died of a head wound and five were wounded; four enemy bodies were later found and credited to this contact, and the company commander rated the grenade spigot a good answer to the RPG-2.

An armoured personnel carrier of 3 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, carrying troops of 5 Platoon, B Company, 8 RAR, on a track off Route 23, hit an anti-tank mine of about 40 pounds of Chinese-made explosive. The carrier was heavily damaged; one crewman was killed and ten others riding in it were wounded, one of them an engineer.

An ambush patrol of 9 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, saw 12 enemy, and through its night-vision scope the patrol leader counted more than 50 still coming. The ambush was sprung, and 12 to 15 enemy were seen to fall, but others carried them away as fast as they went down; the enemy fired back with many rocket-propelled grenades, machine-guns and rifles. Helicopter gunships, a Shadow gunship aircraft firing 28,000 rounds and flares, tanks and artillery supported the patrol. Eight enemy bodies were positively identified, including one found later, and one Australian was wounded by a rocket-grenade; an M16 rifle and a rocket round were captured.

7 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, after a 1,000-metre night move, was setting claymore mines for an ambush when a section leader's cover man moved towards a paddy bund and found seven enemy crouched behind it watching the platoon. He shot the first from one metre, and the gun groups and a recoilless rifle firing splintex rounds supported him as he and his section leader got back. The enemy returned rocket-grenade and AK47 fire, and an AK47 round hit a grenade mounted on a weapon, which exploded, killing one Australian and wounding four. Later an enemy seen trying to drag away a body was fired on; next morning no bodies remained, though two enemy were recorded killed and documents found showed elements of D445 Battalion. 101 and 161 Field Batteries fired in support.

A section of 1 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, had dropped 9 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, at an ambush position near Phuoc Hai and was returning through an established gap in the minefield when an armoured personnel carrier hit an anti-tank mine of 60 to 70 pounds of explosive in the swamp north of Lo Gom. The carrier was wrecked and an infantry officer killed; the two crew and four other members of the squadron thrown from the vehicle were wounded. A local Viet Cong had been watching the carriers deliver the platoon.

A half-platoon ambush of 9 Platoon, C Company, 8 RAR, on the main route into Hoa Long, fired its flank claymore mines at an estimated 20 to 30 enemy. The enemy fired back with rifles, rocket-propelled grenades and a grenade launcher and made three probing attacks from different directions at once over 40 minutes, driven off by claymores and rifle fire; one machine-gun failed with a broken firing pin and the other kept stopping. Seven armoured personnel carriers of 1 and 3 Troops, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, arrived and the enemy broke contact; three Australians were wounded by rocket-grenades. Three wounded enemy were captured by the carriers, and heavy drag marks, bloodstains and a blood trail were found next morning; 161 Field Battery fired in support.

1 Platoon, A Company, and the Reconnaissance Platoon, 7 RAR, were directed by an aircraft to an occupied bunker system 800 metres away and went in on armoured personnel carriers of 2 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, led by tanks of 3 Troop, A Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment. In the middle of the bunkers the two platoons attacked on either flank with the tanks in the centre, and met intense rifle and rocket-grenade fire; some bunkers were taken, but 1 Platoon took casualties and pulled back 75 metres, a rocket-grenade having killed a machine-gunner and wounded his number two and the forward scout. The Reconnaissance Platoon did not get the withdrawal order and fought on, losing four wounded, and a carrier hit by rockets was towed clear by another before the action was suspended. One Australian was killed and 12 wounded, four of whom stayed on duty; five Viet Cong were killed and three captured, and weapons and ammunition were taken.

3 Platoon, A Company, 8 RAR, moving to an ambush position, made contact when its leading section saw and fired on 40 to 50 Viet Cong armed with AK47s, rocket-propelled grenades, machine-guns and grenade launchers. The platoon formed a fire base; enemy parties attacked from both flanks and, using fire and movement, came within ten metres to recover their wounded and some dead. After an hour's fighting armoured personnel carriers of 3 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, arrived, and the enemy broke contact soon after. Six Australians were wounded by rocket-grenades and grenades; two Viet Cong were recorded killed and five wounded, with blood trails and drag marks leading south, and intelligence later claimed over 50 enemy killed. Artillery, aircraft, mortars and 161 Field Battery supported the platoon.

3 Platoon, A Company, 8 RAR, set its ambush in groups of four in a rectangle, and a party of about 15 Viet Cong moving in single file about seven metres apart walked into the south-west group. Machine-guns and M72 rockets opened fire, killing six in the first burst and a seventh as he tried to run. A rocket launcher, a grenade launcher, two SKS rifles and two M16s were captured; 106 Field Battery fired illumination.
8 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR/NZ, set off a claymore-type mine with a pressure or electric switch, possibly an M16 mine according to intelligence. Two Australians were killed and three wounded.

After the Regional Force post at Ap Lo Voi was attacked by D445 Battalion, the retreating enemy walked into the ambush of the Assault Pioneer Platoon, Support Company, 8 RAR. They came in three groups; the first stopped and bunched in the killing ground to wait for the others, and when the second joined it, some 45 men in all, the ambush was sprung. The third group at once counter-attacked twice with rifles, rocket-propelled grenades and machine-guns and was held on both flanks, and the groups in the killing ground pulled out by fire and movement with accurate, heavy fire. Armoured personnel carriers of 3 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, came to spend the night with the platoon; two enemy were killed, and a sweep next morning found eight heavy blood trails and 14 drag marks. Two rifles, 100 phials of penicillin and clothing were captured, and US artillery probably fired cut-off fire.

An armoured personnel carrier of 3 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, in the jungle east of Highway 15, hit a booby-trapped shell, possibly 155mm. The carrier was badly damaged and five or six soldiers, including its two crew, were wounded.

Two sections and headquarters of 2 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR/NZ, investigating smoke, saw three enemy sitting around a fire near a bunker system, and the forward scout opened fire, wounding two. As the leading section pressed forward, the enemy set off a command-detonated 105mm shell, causing heavy casualties, and machine-gun and AK47 fire from the bunkers down prepared fire lanes hit more. Helicopter gunships suppressed the bunkers so the platoon could pull back, and artillery and mortars hit the camp; the platoon withdrew because of the danger of more mines, and the enemy, a force of nearly a platoon, withdrew north-east. One New Zealand soldier was killed, one died of wounds and five were wounded; three blood trails and two drag marks were found.

Following up the blood trail from its ambush the night before, in the sandhills south-west of Phuoc Hai, a patrol of 9 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, set off an M16 mine. Two Australians were killed, one died of wounds and one was wounded. The enemy had come back and laid the mine where he could be fairly sure an Australian follow-up would go.

8 Platoon, C Company, 8 RAR, following a new track, saw two enemy near a bunker and killed one; heavy fire from two bunkers then pinned the forward section, wounding two men, who were taken back for evacuation. The enemy began to pull out but then reoccupied the bunkers and fired again, hitting two more, who were evacuated under cover of helicopter gunships while ammunition was flown in; the casualties were caused by a grenade, a rocket-grenade and AK47 fire. After holding the enemy for an hour, the platoon withdrew 800 metres for an artillery bombardment and joined a tank troop and an armoured personnel carrier troop, and the assault later that day met no resistance. One Australian was killed and three wounded; documents were captured, and 161 Field Battery and two US batteries fired in support.

An armoured personnel carrier of 2 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, carrying troops of 7 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, south-west of Long Phuoc Hai, hit an anti-tank mine of 80 to 100 pounds of explosive. The carrier was badly damaged; a soldier of an engineer team riding on it was killed, and others were wounded, with broken legs, a broken nose and burns.

8 Platoon, C Company, 8 RAR, moved into its ambush at dusk to keep it secret, and the gunner later saw four enemy moving into the killing ground. A bank of four claymore mines was fired but only two went off; both machine-guns raked the area, illumination was fired, and two groups moved forward to secure the killing ground while grenade launchers covered escape routes. Four enemy bodies were recovered, with a pistol and two grenades; the enemy were possibly from a group in contact with Regional Forces earlier that evening. A US battery fired illumination.
The Anti-Tank Platoon, Support Company, 7 RAR, 6 kilometres south of Xuyen Moc, set off an M16 mine, wounding four Australians. Another mine was found four feet from the first.

3 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR/NZ, following Viet Cong tracks for several days, came on caves with old enemy signs, and its reconnaissance element saw signs of mines and heard voices before being attacked with grenades. The platoon moved up, came under grenade and AK47 fire, and replied with grenade launchers as the rocky ground allowed nothing else; while helicopter gunships engaged the enemy, the platoon was hit by rockets, possibly B40s, from the valley, bringing its casualties to six, five New Zealanders and one Australian. Checking the caves later, it was hit by two command-detonated mines, wounding more men. 107 Field Battery and a US battery fired in support.

An armoured personnel carrier of 1 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, west of Cam My and Highway 2, hit a Chinese-made pressure mine of 10 to 15 pounds. The carrier was lightly damaged, but its two crew and four passengers were injured. A 105mm shell rigged as a mine was also found.

8 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, saw an enemy at the edge of the scrub gazing across the paddy towards Dat Do and set an ambush at once; six local force enemy then crossed the paddy 30 metres apart. The platoon fired for three minutes at 150 metres and then advanced by fire and movement; the enemy in the paddy went to ground and fired back, and about nine others who had stayed in the scrub hooked round the platoon's left rear, wounding one Australian in the leg. The platoon saturated the area with fire and grenades and pulled back to the wounded man. The enemy left four dead and dragged away two wounded; one body had an M16 mine attached, and an M16 mine and an M16 rifle were captured.

C Company, 8 RAR, less one platoon, with a troop of tanks of A Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, was sent to seize a bunker system identified by an enemy defector, who led them there. The tanks lost direction and the defector had to be called back to redirect them, and his party came under rocket-grenade and rifle fire.
