The tanks attacked with two platoons in close support; the intense enemy fire soon stopped, and the tanks, hampered by very dense vegetation, crushed several bunkers, possibly killing several enemy, before the light failed. The defenders were a small delaying party for a main body 100 to 150 metres away; artillery fired on the retreating enemy, and there were no Australian casualties.

1 Platoon, W Company, 2 RAR/NZ, fired on at least four Viet Cong, who fired back a rocket-propelled grenade that wounded three New Zealand soldiers, and withdrew. Mortars and artillery, including 161 Field Battery and two US batteries, fired on the withdrawal route. A sweep found one dead enemy, an AK47 and a pack; another enemy was also wounded.

The Reconnaissance Platoon, Support Company, 7 RAR, in a night harbour, saw a Viet Cong approaching, and the sentry waited until he was a metre away and shot him dead. A second, unseen Viet Cong opened fire with an AK47, and the dead man's pack of explosive blew up, wounding two Australians in the shoulder and eye; the platoon killed the second enemy with machine-gun fire and a grenade. Following a track, the patrol found an M16 mine, another that had been triggered but failed to go off, and bunkers used a day or two earlier, with ammunition, documents, an M16 mine and a training mine.

8 Platoon, C Company, 8 RAR, ambushing Route 2 as a supply route into Hoa Long, watched 50 to 60 Viet Cong move carefully into the village, well spaced and crouching, but not through the killing ground, so it let them pass and shifted the ambush to catch them on their return, with armoured personnel carriers of 1 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, on standby. At about 3 am they came back in two groups of about 25, closely spaced, carrying packs and much less alert, and headed straight for one group, so the ambush was sprung early; claymore mines and a crossfire from all four machine-guns, rifles and M72 rockets killed or wounded the whole first group. The second group counter-attacked briefly, then withdrew south-east with the first group's wounded as the carriers arrived; the carriers pursued, killing more and capturing five who had hidden in scrub 800 metres away. Nineteen Viet Cong were killed and six captured, and one surrendered; one Australian was wounded. Weapons, ammunition, documents and large quantities of food, including 550 pounds of rice, were captured; three batteries fired blocking fire west of Hoa Long.

An armoured personnel carrier of 1 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, reversed onto a 30-pound anti-tank mine, which threw it into the air onto the fuel tank of a nearby Centurion tank, killing a Vietnamese scout sitting on the tank. The carrier's two crew and eight passengers from D and E Platoon were all injured. It was the first time a carrier fitted with new belly armour had been mined; the hull was not pierced, and casualties would otherwise have been much worse.

The Anti-Tank Platoon, Support Company, 2 RAR/NZ, examining an enemy camp, set off a Chinese-made mine, recorded as 2 or 20 pounds of explosive. Seven Australians and one South Vietnamese soldier were wounded (another report adds a New Zealander).

2 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, was relieving 1 Platoon in the bunker system taken the day before, and the commanding officer was showing his counterpart around with a protection party, when a booby-trapped 155mm shell went off. One soldier was killed and four wounded, one of whom died soon after; both commanding officers were among the casualties and lost legs.

The Anti-Tank Platoon, Support Company, 7 RAR, looking for a harbour, saw an enemy and the platoon commander opened fire, but eight enemy then hit the platoon from several directions, wounding the scout and the forward section leader. The other two sections swept through and found a camp of eight shelters, where the enemy were beginning to build bunkers, and drew more bursts of fire; an incoming burst set off a grenade about to be fired, lightly wounding three more Australians. One Australian was killed and four wounded in all; a small quantity of arms, food and clothing was captured, and 106 Field Battery fired in support.

D and E Platoon, 1st Australian Task Force, in ambush on a trail fringed by thick jungle, heard movement and Vietnamese voices and, warned they might be civilians, lay low until the group was seen at 15 metres carrying packs and all armed. The enemy, a food party of about 20 from Hoa Long supplying Viet Cong cadres, stopped to rest in front of the ambush; when two moved into the jungle and saw the soldiers, fire was opened at once. The enemy fled in all directions under covering fire and the ambush pursued them for 150 metres, while artillery and Bushranger gunships hit likely escape routes; a tracker dog team found the area deserted. Two enemy were killed and three heavy blood trails found; 21 packs holding 400 pounds of rice, 100 pounds of other food, clothing and cigarettes, and two carbines and a submachine-gun were captured. The platoon commander was disturbed that his men had shot high, but his superior, noting how new the unit was, thought it the best result that could have been expected.

A patrol from 3 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR/NZ, ambushed six or more enemy, the M60 sweeping the killing ground, and the enemy withdrew north-east. A sweep was driven back to the ambush position by automatic fire, and mortars and Bushranger helicopter gunships then attacked, the gunships also firing on movement 300 metres away; a second sweep met no resistance, and artillery fired in support. Five Viet Cong were killed and one wounded and captured, and two more were possibly killed by the gunships; weapons, webbing, food and documents were captured.

An ambush party of the Assault Pioneer Platoon, Support Company, 7 RAR, in position on a track since dusk, had its sentry see two enemy on the right flank without firing; they moved back onto the track into the killing ground. When he could see four of them, the ambush was sprung with claymore mines and rifles. Four enemy were killed and two wounded, one of whom was captured by Regional Forces at Dat Do; four AK47s and five grenades were captured. 106 Field Battery fired in support.

3 Platoon, W Company, 2 RAR/NZ, moving along a track, got a signal from its rear element that Viet Cong were crossing a swamp to the north, and two minutes later the lead section opened fire on movement to its front. Of about six enemy, two were killed and two wounded; an AK47, grenades, ammunition and documents from D65 Battalion were captured. 107 Field Battery fired in support.
SAS Patrol 31, 1 SAS Squadron, made contact with three Viet Cong, killing two and capturing a Garand rifle and a carbine. The third withdrew west, and the patrol suspected more Viet Cong were nearby.

3 Platoon, W Company, 2 RAR/NZ, following a recently used track, smelled cooking and wood smoke, and 60 metres from the contact the M60 gunner covering the lead scout saw an enemy sentry stand up by a bamboo clump and shot him just before he could shoot the scout. The platoon advanced under covering fire, the enemy firing a B40 rocket, and found a camp of about ten enemy who had gone: 13 bunkers with overhead protection, 12 fighting pits and 40 sleeping places, about a year old and wired for booby traps, though none were found. The dead man was from D65 Battalion's liaison section; an AK47, documents, cooking gear and clothing were recovered and the camp was destroyed. 107 Field Battery fired in support.

2 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR, moving out from its base in a heavy rainstorm, saw people moving along a track and engaged them with a machine-gun, killing one and wounding and capturing another. They were an unarmed Viet Cong supply party, 5 kilometres inside the free-fire zone, returning from near a suspected Viet Cong camp; both the dead and the wounded were women. The wounded woman was evacuated and treated, and questioning showed she was part of a resupply party from Ngai Giao. The record notes this was possibly a contact with civilians; a US battery fired in support.

8 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR, with a tracking team following a fresh enemy track, saw an enemy in a grassy clearing, challenged him and fired when he ran. The main enemy body of 20 to 30, digging in in thick bamboo beside the platoon's flank, opened fire with AK47s, automatic rifles and rocket-propelled grenades, catching the platoon in open ground; one Australian was killed and two or three wounded. Artillery, including 107 Field Battery and a US battery, and helicopter gunships supported the platoon, and aircraft engaged the enemy's escape routes as they withdrew south. Fifteen shelters, hammocks, tools, clothing, webbing, a B40 round and a grenade were recovered.

9 Platoon, C Company, 8 RAR, ambushing Route 2, saw the silhouettes of six Viet Cong armed with a rocket launcher, an AK47 and a grenade, and fired the claymore mines, three of which failed, followed by M60 fire. Machine-guns, M72 rockets and grenade launchers kept up suppressive fire until aircraft illumination and armoured personnel carriers arrived. Four Viet Cong were killed and one North Vietnamese wounded and captured; 106 Field Battery fired illumination.

1 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR/NZ, was crossing a river when the second group was hit by machine-gun fire, apparently from the far bank; one New Zealand soldier was killed and two wounded. The contact report described four enemy with automatic weapons and a blood trail, and artillery and helicopter gunships supported. The official history records that the casualties were in fact caused by an accidental discharge of the platoon's own machine-gun and that the contact report was fabricated.

7 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, on operations around Xuyen Moc, had split into two ambush parties when it was warned of enemy moving along the tree line towards it, apparently following one party into its ambush. As the commander went to warn his groups, three enemy appeared 15 metres away and he opened fire; the other party then saw movement to its west and fired, and both swept the area. Two bodies of members of the Xuyen Moc company were found next day, and a third, a secretary cadre of Xuyen Moc district, was found by Regional Forces later. Two AK47s, an RPG-2 and an M16 were captured; 161 Field Battery fired illumination.

A patrol of 3 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR, moving west along a track, saw one unarmed person and then two armed enemy; the scout opened fire, and one enemy was wounded and captured. Five packs were also captured and artillery fired in support. The platoon commander noted a heavy blood trail and drag marks suggesting at least 12 people and probably four more enemy casualties.

A patrol of 7 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR/NZ, beside the Suoi Chau Pha, heard firing from an 8 Platoon contact across the river and moved into position; three Viet Cong in black came running towards it across a small swamp, and it opened fire at 20 metres, killing two. The third withdrew and was probably wounded. A carbine and documents were captured. US artillery probably fired in support.

A patrol of 3 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, in ambush was caught during a sentry change by four enemy moving north along a creek bed, who opened fire first at five metres. Two Australians were wounded, one in the thighs and one in the leg, which was later amputated. The platoon's second machine-gun replied quickly and accurately, killing two enemy, local guerrillas, and weapons, ammunition, packs and documents were captured. Artillery fired illumination.

A patrol of 12 Platoon, D Company, 7 RAR, moving to its lying-up position, heard enemy ahead and let them come on until they were level with the patrol commander, who opened fire with the rest of the patrol. The two to four enemy fired back with rifles, an AK47 and a rocket-propelled grenade, which wounded one Australian in the forehead. The sweep found one enemy dead and one wounded, who was shot and killed as he tried to escape, and a heavy blood trail; weapons, a claymore, an M16 mine, ammunition and documents identifying a mortar section commander of the Long Dat unit were captured.

The sentry of an ambush by 3 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR/NZ, fired on two Viet Cong moving fast from west to east and the ambush then engaged the area. One enemy was killed and another wounded and later captured, and an AK47, rifle grenades, 310 detonators and two packs of food and clothing were captured; artillery and helicopter gunships supported. The prisoner said his group of three had been going to collect rice, and that he belonged to the Ba Ria city sapper unit.

At night defensive position Garth, a platoon of Support Company, 2 RAR, heard an enemy soldier moving along the perimeter wire; he was engaged with a claymore mine and grenade launcher as he withdrew, and moaning was heard. A sweep next morning did not find him but found his tracks and a small hole by the perimeter, possibly dug for a mine.

A patrol of the Assault Pioneer Platoon, Support Company, 7 RAR, following enemy tracks, made contact with about 10 enemy in black, heavily camouflaged with foliage and armed with a rocket-propelled grenade launcher and AK47s, who tried to outflank the patrol. Helicopter gunships fired on the area and were fired on from the ground. The enemy withdrew and a sweep found nothing, though one enemy was recorded killed.

An enemy light machine-gun fired on the observation post of a half-platoon ambush of 5 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, at the base of the Long Hai hills, slightly wounding the observer. Two machine-guns and a grenade launcher fired back into the enemy area, with unknown result. The company commander thought the ambush had been given away by poor camouflage and unnecessary movement.

About 45 Viet Cong walked into an ambush laid by 6 Platoon and B Company Headquarters, 7 RAR, with a section of B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment; the ambush held fire until the killing ground was full, then fired all its claymores and weapons. The enemy fought back with rifles, rocket-propelled grenades and machine-guns and made many attempts to recover their dead. There were no friendly casualties; 21 Viet Cong were killed and nine wounded, and a large haul of weapons, ammunition, mines, a radio and very significant documents, at least one of strategic value, was captured. The dead included the second-in-command and political officer of D445 Local Force Battalion and several of its platoon and section leaders.

6 Platoon, B Company, 2 RAR/NZ, in ambush in a rubber plantation covering the house of a known Viet Cong food supplier, first saw 10 unarmed people, who ran and were not fired on. Later, after signals with torches and a lantern, enemy crept towards the position and the ambush was sprung when whispering was heard in front of the machine-gun; the enemy threw a grenade and fought back with AK47s and a rocket-propelled grenade until armoured personnel carriers were heard approaching. Two Australians were wounded and 10 enemy were killed, dressed in black; two AK47s and two packs were captured. A prisoner later said 14 were killed and five or six wounded.

6 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, searching for a suspected bunker system, followed a track showing about 20 enemy nearby, found an old bunker and was fired on by hidden enemy with machine-guns and rocket-propelled grenades, wounding three soldiers; as the sections moved to contact another was hit, and he later died. When the enemy began to work around the flanks, helicopter gunships attacked with miniguns and rockets, and armoured personnel carriers of 2 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, came in, engaged the enemy and evacuated the wounded. The platoon then cleared the bunker area, but the enemy had gone, leaving two blood trails. The company commander said casualties would have been heavier had the battalion commander not controlled the air support from a helicopter overhead, and the gunships arrived quickly because the battalion command post had ordered them up in advance.

A half-platoon ambush of 4 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, three days in position near a new D445 Battalion bunker area, was mortared and then attacked by 25 to 30 enemy with machine-guns, AK47s, rocket-propelled grenades and grenades. The enemy's first assault went the wrong way, missing the position by 50 metres, and the patrol's fire brought down four of them; helicopter gunships broke up the attack, one being shot down and another hit, though the downed helicopter was recovered. Two Australians were wounded; one enemy body and heavy blood trails, suggesting at least seven wounded, were found, and later patrols found a 55-bunker complex. The company commander credited good fire control, and the platoon commander thought the enemy gave themselves away by talking.

A soldier of 11 Platoon, D Company, 7 RAR, moving from its day position to a night ambush in the north-east Long Hai hills, trod on what was possibly an M16 mine, which exploded in the ground and wounded four Australians, including two engineers.

A patrol from 5 Platoon, B Company, 2 RAR/NZ, setting up an ambush, fired claymores at eight or nine enemy moving in two groups, and armoured personnel carriers of B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, came to support. A sweep under artillery illumination found two enemy dead, a grenade launcher, a rifle and two packs. Back in the ambush position, the carriers fired at movement outside the perimeter, and a dawn sweep found a fresh enemy grave and two enemy weapons; three enemy were recorded killed.

6 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, in ambush, let a party of 15 pass because the ambush was badly aligned, then re-sited it on the track; shortly after, about 20 enemy, a Viet Cong food party of the Long Dat district force, came the other way and the platoon opened fire on the first seven at five metres. The enemy fought back with grenades and rifles, and a dying enemy soldier threw a grenade into the machine-gun pit, killing one Australian and wounding another; the official history says a machine-gun also jammed. Five enemy were killed and seven blood trails found, and an M16, packs and a large quantity of food were captured. Artillery fired in support.

A lying-up ambush patrol of 5 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, ambushed about 20 enemy approaching from the Long Hai hills, who fired back with rifles, a rocket-propelled grenade and two grenades. One Australian was killed and three wounded; the medical evacuation helicopter was briefly fired on and left with the most badly wounded man, and armoured personnel carriers withdrew the rest. The carriers' arrival revealed two enemy dead and six blood trails. US and Australian artillery fired in support.

A Vietnamese Bushman Scout set off a 30-pound mine at the same place as the earlier mine blast on Route 329 that day. He was killed and seven Australians were wounded: a carrier crewman and infantry of D and E Platoons riding on a nearby armoured personnel carrier of 3 Cavalry Regiment; five had ear damage and were evacuated by helicopter.

9 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR, getting ready to ambush, saw three enemy emerge from thick undergrowth 10 metres away, heading for a house in the rubber; the sentry opened fire and they scattered. A section of 2 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, sent to cut off their retreat, found enemy lying in the grass, killing two and wounding one, who later died; a sweep next morning found two more killed by the platoon, and an AK47 was captured. Five enemy were killed in all. The record notes the platoon had moved in near dark and so was not seen by civilians, who usually warned the enemy.

A patrol of 8 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR, in ambush on a track between two houses, heard talking and saw torches coming towards it, and fired claymores and two machine-guns when about eight enemy, a food party, were in the killing ground. A sweep under artillery and mortar illumination found five enemy dead, and an AK47 and four packs of food were captured.

9 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR, in an ambush set after dark to watch some houses, fired on two enemy; the first bank of claymores failed to go off, so a grenade and rifles were used, then a second bank was fired. The sweep found one enemy dead, killed a second crawling away, and was fired on by five or six enemy in two houses, four of whom broke out when illumination was fired. The next morning's sweep found another body and a wounded enemy, who led the patrol to three more who wished to surrender, and did. One Australian was wounded.

While the Anti-Tank Platoon, Support Company, 7 RAR, was in an ambush position in jungle south of Xuyen Moc, a machine-gunner rolled over onto an M16 mine, which exploded. Five Australians were wounded, two of whom later died.
A Land Rover of 131 Divisional Locating Battery drove over a 30-pound pressure mine at the edge of the Cam My rubber plantation, wounding four Australians.

A patrol of 2 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, was hit by two mines, one a US claymore; one Australian was killed and one wounded, apparently an engineer. The record says one was command-detonated, though the battalion commander and his staff thought both had been set off by pressure switches.

A patrol of B Company Headquarters, 7 RAR, ambushing near fresh enemy tracks in the Binh Chau area, saw two armed enemy; the sentry shot one in the head, killing him instantly, and the other in the chest. The second ran 200 metres before dying and his body was found in the follow-up. An AK47 and an SKS rifle were captured.

A New Zealand SAS patrol, Patrol 42 of 1 SAS Squadron, saw four enemy approaching at 60 metres and another four from a different direction at 30 metres, waited until they were 25 metres away and opened fire, possibly killing or wounding three. Reinforced by two more patrols, it swept the contact area and captured a carbine, two packs and documents. Two enemy were recorded killed.
An armoured personnel carrier of 3 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, hit a 30-pound anti-tank mine in the Cam My rubber. The vehicle was badly damaged and two crew were injured.

1 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR/NZ, under command of 3 RAR, following a freshly used track, fired on a group of five enemy 10 metres ahead, who seemed to be hit, and ran into the headquarters of D445 Battalion and its C2 Company. Heavy fire came from three sides with machine-guns, mortars, rocket-propelled grenades, grenades and satchel charges; gunships struggled to identify friendly positions, and several helicopters, including a Possum and a medical evacuation helicopter, were hit and forced to land. After two hours, low on ammunition, the platoon broke contact with its own fire and withdrew, abandoning packs and the weapons of the wounded, and was relieved by the Assault Pioneer Platoon of 3 RAR; a helicopter evacuation attempt was hit and a crewman mortally wounded. The contact report lists nine Australians wounded, two of whom died, one of them an RAAF crewman; enemy losses were two killed, including a body found later in a grave, and six wounded, and the enemy recovered a machine-gun, rifles, claymores and explosives left behind.

D Company, 3 RAR, in a circular harbour beside a strip of rice paddy during its in-country training, fired claymores and machine-guns at enemy 20 to 30 metres away, then at about 10 enemy trying to recover bodies, while more enemy attacked 10 Platoon's perimeter with heavy AK47 fire. A satchel charge thrown inside the perimeter killed the platoon commander and wounded a soldier, who stayed on duty, and rifle fire killed another soldier and wounded one more. C Company nearby was also probed; the enemy signalled with tin whistles and fired rifles and rocket-propelled grenades. Helicopter gunships, artillery illumination and fire on withdrawal routes, and a tank of C Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, supported, and casualties were evacuated by helicopter. Two Australians were killed and two wounded; three enemy were recorded wounded.

A half-platoon of 8 Platoon, C Company, 3 RAR, patrolling a track, heard chopping, digging and a dog barking, fired grenades at the sound and swept forward into a bunker system; two explosions, possibly grenades, wounded the platoon commander, who later died, and the machine-gunner, and heavy fire pinned the patrol down. It withdrew, leaving the two wounded at first, and another soldier was hit. Gunships could not pick out the friendly troops because the smoke grenades had run out, and one gunship was hit by ground fire, its co-pilot later dying; the Assault Pioneer Platoon in armoured personnel carriers, the rest of the company and a troop of tanks converged, and the enemy, thought to be a stay-behind group, withdrew. The camp was new and possibly a headquarters. The dead platoon commander was criticised for attacking without a reconnaissance, and most ammunition and smoke had been in packs dropped at the start of the contact; artillery could not fire because the platoon's location was uncertain.

The Assault Pioneer Platoon, Support Company, 3 RAR, sent to help 1 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, joined it and helped evacuate the wounded, then covered its withdrawal. As it withdrew downhill it was followed by four to six enemy with heavy weapons and rifles and drove them off with fire and movement. One Australian was wounded; one enemy was recorded killed and four wounded.

A sentry of 1 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR/NZ, ambushing a track, killed an enemy soldier with two rifle shots and captured his AK47, and the machine-gun and grenade launcher fired into the area. During the sweep, a grass fire started by the machine-gun's tracer set off a claymore mine, wounding two New Zealand soldiers, one of whom, the platoon commander, died. The sweep was abandoned.

The forward section of 5 Platoon, B Company, 2 RAR, heard enemy talking 30 metres ahead, crept forward, and opened fire with a machine-gun when three enemy saw them. A sweep found one body and heard moaning from a bunker already grenaded, which was grenaded again, killing the man inside; the rest of the four to six enemy had withdrawn. Two enemy were killed and two wounded, and an AK47 and documents were captured. The platoon had not known a bunker system was there. Artillery fired in support.

After its earlier contact, 8 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR/NZ, called in helicopter gunships and began clearing the bunker system, but the 8 to 10 enemy there, armed with AK47s, rocket-propelled grenades, grenades and claymore mines, were too strong and well dug in, and three Australians were wounded. Gunships and artillery then fired on the bunkers. The recently renovated system held 11 bunkers in a line 150 metres long; US claymores, a radio aerial and cooking gear were captured.

A soldier of 2 Company, 302 Regional Force Battalion, stepped on a mine, possibly an M16, wounding four Vietnamese. A medical evacuation helicopter came from the Task Force, and members of Mobile Advisory Training Team 3, Australian Army Training Team Vietnam, supervised the evacuation on the ground. As the helicopter hovered it was hit by a rocket-propelled grenade and crashed on top of the evacuation party, killing two Australians, an American and a Vietnamese and wounding three Vietnamese; the helicopter was destroyed.

A patrol from the Jungle Warfare Training Centre made contact with 10 to 15 Viet Cong in a base camp, supported by RAAF gunships. One Viet Cong was killed by air and three were wounded, leaving blood trails; an M16, three pistols, a typewriter, medical equipment and documents were captured. One Vietnamese soldier was wounded.

SAS Patrol 24, 2 SAS Squadron, ambushed three enemy on a track, killing two and capturing two rifles, three packs averaging 50 pounds and documents. The third kept going through the ambush site and was fired on, but withdrew with unknown result.

1 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, moving through familiar ground, heard movement in an old bunker system and its forward elements fired on the enemy on sight; the enemy fired back, and a reserve element outflanked them to create a crossfire. With the platoon fully committed, artillery and helicopter gunships were called in; the enemy fired a grenade launcher high to give a mortar effect and after 25 minutes withdrew by fire and movement. One Australian was wounded. The platoon commander noted the enemy, of D445 Battalion, seemed to know when the support would arrive and left as it appeared.

An armoured personnel carrier of A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, set off an anti-tank mine of 20 to 40 pounds on Route 328 just south of Thua Tich, apparently recently laid with a pressure switch. The carrier was badly damaged and two crew were wounded.

SAS Patrol 14, 2 SAS Squadron, ambushed four enemy, killing all four, and captured an M16, an AK47, documents and equipment. Personal letters among the documents suggested they might be members of 274 Viet Cong Regiment, but this could not be confirmed.

An armoured personnel carrier of 1 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, set off an anti-tank mine of 60 to 80 pounds in the Cam My rubber. The carrier was badly damaged and two Australians were wounded, one of them an engineer.

An armoured personnel carrier of 1 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, set off a Chinese pressure mine near a village north-west of Cam My, wounding a crewman and an engineer and moderately damaging the carrier. A second mine of 15 pounds, about a year old, was found nearby and recovered.
SAS Patrol 23, 2 SAS Squadron, fired on two enemy in bunkers armed with a light machine-gun and an automatic rifle. One Australian was wounded; enemy casualties are not known.
SAS Patrol 11, 2 SAS Squadron, fired on four enemy thought to be moving away from the earlier contact that afternoon, killing one and capturing a weapon and documents.
3 Section, 1 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, fired on a Viet Cong approaching from the north, killing him and capturing an M1 rifle, ammunition, a grenade and detonators.

After a night of artillery and mortar fire on the bunker system it had found the day before, 5 Platoon, B Company, 3 RAR, advanced up a spur and ran into heavy fire at 15 metres from bunkers held by part of 3 Battalion, 33 Regiment, with machine-guns, heavy machine-guns and rocket-propelled grenades; the rest of B Company came up in support. The fight went on for most of the day: helicopter gunships and later US Cobras attacked with miniguns and rockets within 30 metres of the platoon, the company's artillery forward observer was killed, and a helicopter dropping ammunition was shot down, two of its RAAF crew dying. Tanks of C Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, attacked the bunkers from the rear and, with D Company and cavalry, secured the system by late afternoon; packs, documents, food and a radio were found. Three Australians were killed, including the two RAAF crew, and about 12 wounded, four of whom stayed on duty; five enemy were recorded killed. The company commander noted that smoke grenades dissipated under the 150-foot canopy while a marker balloon worked well, rifle grenades were effective, and machine-guns failed badly, three having to be replaced during the fight.

Three armoured personnel carriers of A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, carrying D and E Platoons, were patrolling a track when the lead driver saw an artillery illumination canister he suspected was part of a mine and stopped; the enemy, of 274 Regiment, then opened fire with rifles and rocket-propelled grenades. A grenade hit a pile of claymore mines on the back of the last carrier, which exploded, killing its crew and five soldiers of D and E Platoons and wounding three others, one of whom later died. Eight Australians died in all. Australian and US artillery fired in support.

1 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, set a series of ambushes along the southern edge of the Courtenay rubber plantation on a dark night of heavy rain; four armoured personnel carriers of 11 Section ambushed an enemy force at 10 metres with claymores and machine-guns, and when they swept the area the enemy counter-attacked with grenades. The other sections left their ambushes and swept the area with spotlights, and light contacts went on until about 3 am, with further prisoners taken the next morning. Twelve enemy were killed and three Viet Cong captured, one of them wounded; weapons, 22 packs, a large quantity of documents, food and a field surgical kit were captured. Another body was found in July. Artillery fired illumination.

Following up 2 Platoon's contact, 1 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR/NZ, under command of C Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, advanced with tanks and armoured personnel carriers on a large bunker system held by 1 Battalion, 274 Regiment. A rocket-propelled grenade hit the forward tank; when a second was fired, the platoon engaged and was met by heavy fire from enemy who had moved out onto its left flank, and for 15 minutes the infantry, tanks and carriers fought back with canister and machine-guns. The enemy used heavy and light machine-guns, rocket-propelled grenades and claymores, and CS gas was noticed; Cobra gunships and artillery supported, and the carriers and tanks came under fire again during the evening, including during a medical evacuation. The record lists seven Australians and New Zealanders wounded, including two cavalrymen hit by a rocket grenade or claymore; three bodies were later found, and the armoured report estimated five and possibly 12 enemy casualties. The area was not swept, so the true enemy losses are unclear.

Tanks of 5 and 3 Troops, C Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, with armoured personnel carriers of 2 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, moved to support 5 Platoon, B Company, 3 RAR, and attacked the bunker complex; the lead tank was fired on by rocket-propelled grenades and rifles, and two tanks were hit, one slightly damaged and the other by a round that failed to explode. The tanks destroyed at least five bunkers with their guns, canister and machine-guns and, after waiting for D Company, swept on to find more bunkers, by then deserted. Three Australians were slightly wounded by grenade fragments and stayed on duty. Three enemy were counted killed, though the record suggests at least six is a conservative estimate.

2 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR/NZ, found signs of a bunker system and probed forward on a broad front with three sections; at the edge of the area an enemy soldier walked towards the platoon and was shot at 15 metres. The machine-guns fired on enemy voices and were answered with rocket-propelled grenades, machine-guns, rifles and claymores along a 50-metre front, and the platoon withdrew under helicopter gunship cover with two wounded; the enemy followed, wounding a third. The platoon commander complained the artillery was unacceptably late because of repeated check-fires, and that he had to keep insisting the gunships fire closer. Lessons drawn were that advancing on a broad front revealed the enemy's main killing area, machine-guns must support each other because the enemy concentrated on them, and a plan for withdrawal was needed when attacking bunkers.

D Company, 4 RAR/NZ, on a search-and-destroy operation for 1 Battalion, 274 Regiment, and just parted from its tanks, came under rocket-propelled grenade fire from a bunker; the fire grew intense, with machine-guns and AK47s, and 10 Platoon took casualties and was pinned down. 12 Platoon assaulted a bunker, killing three enemy as they tried to escape, and a troop of tanks of C Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, returned and, slowed by thick vegetation and the need to identify friendly troops, came level with the infantry and then advanced through the bunker system, clearing it with guns and machine-guns. One Australian was killed and four or five wounded; eight enemy were killed and four more bodies found the next morning. The nine-bunker system yielded a rocket launcher, ammunition, rice and documents. Australian and US artillery fired in support.

7 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR, following a track from an unoccupied bunker system across a steep gully, saw a bunker; as the section commander moved forward, an enemy came out and the contact began. The enemy fired rifles from the bunkers, claymores from nearby trees and, after 15 minutes, rocket-propelled grenades; after about an hour the platoon withdrew by fire and movement, with three Australians wounded, while at least three enemy were heard crying out. Many artillery shells with delay fuzes failed to explode in the soft ground, but quick-fuzed rounds kept the enemy in their bunkers while the platoon withdrew. About half the grenade-launcher rounds failed and two machine-guns broke down; rifle grenades were judged far more effective. Three enemy were recorded killed.

9 Platoon, C Company, 3 RAR, about to move to an ambush position, saw three people approaching whom it first took for civilians until, at 25 metres, it saw they were armed; the machine-gun killed the first, and the second fired a rocket-propelled grenade into the perimeter, slightly wounding three Australians. The other two escaped into the jungle, leaving weapons and packs, though two sections went after them. An AK47, rocket rounds, a field telephone, three packs, rice, salt and documents were captured.

7 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR/NZ, ambushed three alert but fast-moving enemy on a track with claymores, killing all three, and a machine-gun then fired into the area. Three AK47s, packs, torches, documents and batteries were captured. Company and battalion commanders were impressed by how little ammunition was used. Artillery fired in support.

The rearmost soldier of 6 Platoon, B Company, 4 RAR/NZ, following a track north, saw three enemy approaching from behind and fired two aimed shots and a burst. A sweep found one dead and two blood trails; documents, medals and a belt were captured, and what looked like a cache was seen hanging in a tree. A second body found nearby some days later by 10 Platoon was almost certainly from this contact.

11 Section, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, moving to an ambush position, saw two people in rubber 600 metres away and went to investigate, finding about 10 armed enemy, apparently a porter party, running away. They ignored a warning burst and scattered, and the carriers opened fire, killing one and wounding two, one of whom died; the other was captured, with two AK47s and a pistol. During the sweep that followed, two shots hit two carriers and the area was fired on.

SAS Patrol 24, 2 SAS Squadron, ambushed a party of at least 10 enemy moving tactically along a track with two scouts ahead. Four or five enemy were killed and three wounded; AK47s, pistols, packs, radios, maps, documents and 100,000 piastres were captured, and artillery and four air strikes followed, uncovering an old base camp. The documents identified the party as part of the headquarters of 3 Battalion, 274 Regiment; one body was the regiment's deputy chief of staff.

8 Platoon, C Company, 3 RAR, patrolling along the Song Hoa, entered thick jungle and was fired on from hidden bunkers with AK47s, a light machine-gun and rocket-propelled grenades; a grenade hit the left machine-gun, wounding the scout, section leader and gunner. The platoon fought back with grenade launchers as the enemy began to work round its flanks, and artillery and helicopter gunships were called in; firing went on for over two hours before it went quiet and the platoon pulled back to join the armoured vehicles. Two machine-guns failed, one not feeding at all and the other stopping after 600 rounds.

10 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR/NZ, having found a large cache of rice and food, set an ambush; three enemy approached through long grass and were allowed to come close enough to be identified, then the machine-gun and other weapons opened fire, severely wounding two, who called out to surrender. The enemy fired back and more movement was heard. The two wounded were brought inside the perimeter but both died; documents suggested they were senior local cadres of the Binh Ba and Ba Long area.

The forward scout and section commander of 6 Platoon, B Company, 3 RAR, investigating a track, saw two enemy but were seen by 12 more; they opened fire and were met by heavy fire from rocket-propelled grenades, AK47s, carbines, grenades and grenade launchers, though few of the grenades exploded. Artillery, mortars and a helicopter gunship, guided by a marker balloon and phosphorus rounds, reduced the enemy fire, and 4 Platoon and company headquarters joined, but the enemy could not be dislodged from their bunkers until the approach of armoured personnel carriers of A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, seems to have made them withdraw. The carriers secured the freshly used bunker complex of D445 Battalion; there were no friendly casualties and one enemy was possibly wounded. Rocket rounds, claymores, radio batteries and medical supplies were captured.

1 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR/NZ, harboured for lunch while following fresh Viet Cong tracks, was warned by company headquarters that three enemy were coming its way; the sentries saw them 30 metres away and a machine-gun and rifle opened fire, joined by others. One enemy was killed and one wounded, leaving a blood trail; an AK47, packs, documents and equipment were captured. The record notes the enemy had used a track heavily used by Australian troops.

The forward scout of 8 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR/NZ, patrolling through light scrub, heard movement and saw a man in black in an overnight camp; he challenged him, and when the man ran he was shot dead and his AK47 captured. Accounts differ on how many escaped: one says three, the other that the second was a woman in green with an AK47. Documents identified the dead man as a platoon second-in-command of a requisitioning and purchasing company of a rear services group.

12 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR/NZ, deploying from its night position, was fired on from a well-established bunker system of 3 Battalion, 33 North Vietnamese Regiment, and one Australian was killed and two wounded; artillery and a wide range of aircraft attacked the position to within 40 metres, and 11 Platoon fought off an enemy probe. In the afternoon D Company assaulted, but 15 metres short of the bunkers it came under intense fire from the flanks, and the leading section lost three killed and one who died of wounds; the company withdrew, leaving its dead, while napalm was dropped. The enemy followed up and D Company, having bumped into a second bunker system, fought a heavy contact until dark, with artillery brought to within 100 metres. Two days later, with V Company, it recovered the dead and all lost equipment. Five Australians were killed and nine wounded; the enemy lost 18 dead, nine of them to air attack. The commander noted how hard it was to find and indicate targets in close country.

6 Platoon, B Company, 4 RAR/NZ, still following the telephone wire, fired on a man rolling it up and followed his tracks; later a reconnaissance party looking for a night position fired on enemy on three sides and fell back, and the main body came under rifle and 60 mm mortar fire and took many casualties. 4 Platoon, sent to help, killed one of three enemy on the way and joined 6 Platoon at a helicopter winch point; B Company Headquarters was also mortared. Artillery, three US Pink Teams and airstrikes with napalm and bombs hit the area. Fifteen Australians were wounded, three of whom stayed on duty; the enemy were thought to be headquarters and support elements of 33 North Vietnamese Regiment, and seven enemy were recorded killed. Two bunker complexes were later found around the contact area.

Four enemy entered the killing ground of an ambush by the Anti-Tank (Tracker) Platoon, Support Company, 4 RAR/NZ; low scrub hid whether they were armed, so they were challenged, and they bolted. The claymores killed two, a third was found shot dead 10 metres into the scrub, and the fourth left a blood trail. An AK47, two pistols, packs, maps, documents identifying them as members of the Chau Duc district, and 42,000 piastres were captured.

11 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR/NZ, checking a track, met about 20 North Vietnamese soldiers coming round a corner 20 metres ahead and opened fire, killing the leading man; the enemy quickly deployed and returned automatic fire, then were ordered by their commander to withdraw. Artillery and a US Pink Team helicopter team followed them up, though the artillery was interrupted while the helicopters got organised. A body and an AK47 were found, and a second partly buried body the next day. The enemy were believed to be from 3 Battalion, 33 North Vietnamese Regiment.

11 Section, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, escorting a vehicle along Route 2, ran into an ambush about 100 metres long by around 20 enemy, who fired rifles and rocket-propelled grenades; the rockets all missed, but the second carrier was hit by rifle fire. The enemy dispersed under continuous machine-gun fire, and a sweep found one enemy dead and an AK47. One Australian was slightly wounded above the eye. The ambush was well designed and would have been very effective had the first carrier been hit and blocked the road; the enemy were probably of 33 North Vietnamese Regiment.

The day before, 5 Platoon, B Company, 3 RAR, had found an enemy camp of about 20 and, under cover of heavy rain, reconnoitred to within 10 metres, seeing enemy sheltering under plastic sheets; the company commander decided to attack at first light with air and artillery support. The two air strikes missed because of very poor weather, and after artillery fire B Company and 3 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, assaulted but found the camp empty. A large quantity of documents, a rocket launcher, ammunition, a claymore, rice and medical supplies were found; the enemy were C2 Company of D445 Battalion and headquarters elements.

A Popular Force platoon at Ngai Giao fired claymores at enemy approaching the village, and a Regional Force company in ambush nearby joined in; 50 to 60 enemy fired on the village in a semicircle and eight mortar rounds landed in it, wounding one Popular Force soldier. Armoured personnel carriers of A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, fired machine-guns and artillery from fire support base Robin and Ngai Giao fired cut-off missions, and the enemy broke contact and withdrew north. An AK47 and bloodstains were found, and three enemy bodies were found in graves the next day, killed by claymores and grenade launchers.
6 Platoon, B Company, 4 RAR/NZ, fired on an enemy soldier moving on its perimeter, and moaning was heard. A search at first light found tracks of one or two people moving north.

2 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR/NZ, halted in an area open to civilians, saw three people coming along a track it had made earlier but could not identify them as enemy; a little later another section did and fired, but by then they were sprinting away. There were no casualties on either side.

A sentry of 6 Platoon, B Company, 4 RAR, held his fire as someone approached very cautiously along the platoon's track, thinking it might be a friendly soldier who had wandered outside the perimeter. When challenged, the enemy moved off, and the movement and sounds were fired on.

Sentries at fire support base Robin fired on two people believed to be local guerrillas, and armoured personnel carriers of A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, fired machine-guns. The two withdrew south; a first-light search found nothing.
The Mobile Advisory Training Team at Hoa Long had a contact, and flares were fired from the Hoa Long compound. The record gives no further detail.
5 Platoon, B Company, 4 RAR/NZ, was fired on by two or three enemy in green and black, who withdrew with unknown losses. There were no friendly casualties.

2 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, found a camp of three huts, and while destroying it a grenade hidden in a hut roof exploded. One Australian and two New Zealand members of the artillery forward observer party received minor shrapnel wounds.

3 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, was fired on by a sniper, and one Australian was killed. The sniper fired again later; contact drills failed to find him, but a section sent to circle back onto the track caught him running away at about 100 metres. The next day another sniper, seen wearing a camouflage suit, fired on the platoon at a creek crossing and escaped a cordon and sweep. The platoon commander recommended trying to block a sniper's line of withdrawal once it was known, and found the grenade launcher extremely useful.
B Company, 1 RAR, had a contact with a Viet Cong, who was wounded but escaped, leaving a blood trail. A French bolt-action rifle was captured.

The forward scout of 22 Section, 8 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, on a search-and-destroy patrol, came upon three local-force Viet Cong standing in a clearing. Shots were exchanged, and one Viet Cong fell; the other two ran off, one apparently hit. When the two tried to come back for the body, fire from the section commander, scout and grenade launcher drove them off, and the body, a home-made rifle and ammunition were recovered.
C Company, 1 RAR, came upon a local-force Viet Cong, who escaped north.
B Company, 1 RAR, had a contact with a local-force Viet Cong, who escaped.
C Company, 1 RAR, had a contact with a local-force Viet Cong, who escaped south.

C Company headquarters, 1 RAR, and a section of 9 Platoon were securing a landing zone for the commanding officer's arrival when movement was seen in the bush and a Viet Cong was spotted moving fast through the scrub. The company sergeant major and half the section chased him and fired several rifle shots, but he escaped south. The lesson drawn was that the section must be more alert.

On Operation Iron Triangle, men of 8 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, riding in armoured personnel carriers, hit an anti-tank mine made from a 105mm shell. Nine Australians were injured, with shrapnel wounds, a broken ankle, bruising and shock, and the American driver of the carrier was killed.

On Operation Iron Triangle, 8 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, leading the company along an unused track, set off a grenade booby trap with a trip wire tied to a branch; the forward section had passed it safely, but a member of platoon headquarters triggered it. Four Australians were wounded, including the platoon commander. Carriers with the medical officer and the commanding officer arrived within ten minutes. The lesson drawn was that troops must be well spaced at all times.
On Operation Iron Triangle, two booby traps went off near A Company, 1 RAR, injuring two Australian soldiers, a New Zealand gunner and a Vietnamese policeman.

On Operation Iron Triangle, the machine-gun group of 7 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, standing to in the company harbour, saw three Viet Cong creeping up to probe the perimeter, perhaps for a grenade attack. It waited until they were near the forward pits, then opened fire, killing two and wounding the third as he tried to escape; his body was found the next day. An M1 carbine and nine grenades were captured.

On Operation Iron Triangle, 6 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, leading a company patrol in single file ten metres apart, halted while the platoon commander went back to look at a booby trap A Company had found. On his return a booby trap exploded, wounding two soldiers in the neck and legs; no trip wire or mine could be found. He recommended wider spacing than the usual ten metres in areas with a high booby-trap threat.

On Operation Iron Triangle, 5 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, followed fresh tracks past an empty sentry post into a defended Viet Cong village, where the forward scout got within seven metres of a machine-gunner before opening fire and the section assaulted straight in. The rear section chased the Viet Cong out of the far end, but with their strength and many tunnels the pursuit was called off, and a Viet Cong trying to return shortly afterwards escaped under fire. The village, an administrative headquarters covering 5,000 square metres with 23 tunnels, weapon pits, a trench, 11 huts, a bell alarm and booby-trapped approaches, yielded a Browning automatic rifle, two carbines, packs, helmets and documents. Artillery failed to damage it, so an air strike was called in after the platoon withdrew; the platoon commander stressed the value of a stealthy approach, surprise and heavy fire from the lead section.

On Operation Iron Triangle, a soldier of 6 Section, 2 Platoon, 1 RAR, was shot in the throat and killed while reconnoitring a track system. A contact drill failed to find the enemy, though his tracks were found leading away from an anthill.

On Operation Iron Triangle, 16 Section, 6 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, clearing a booby-trapped area in extended line, set off a grenade half-buried in the ground with a trip wire. One soldier was wounded in both legs and the section commander injured in the ankle; both were evacuated.

On Operation New Life, 1 RAR moved into Vo Xu village with little trouble; 52 Viet Cong were captured and several rallied. Clearing the rest of the village that afternoon, 4 Platoon, B Company, part of the cordon, came under machine-gun and rifle fire from across the La Nga river from a force of just under a platoon, apparently covering other Viet Cong escaping by boat. The platoon returned fire, and mortars, artillery and helicopters engaged the enemy; the platoon commander estimated four enemy were killed, though no bodies were recovered. Two Australians were wounded, one of whom later died of his wounds.

On Operation New Life, after securing the road from Vo Dat to Chanh Duc, 1 RAR attacked Vo Xu village. C Company, mounted in 1 APC Troop's carriers, made a frontal assault down the road, with A Company in support and B and D Companies giving diversionary fire. It met light fire entering the village but quickly secured its objective; two Viet Cong were thought to have escaped through tunnels. Four Viet Cong were recorded killed.
On Operation New Life, 1 RAR assaulted the Brass Monkey feature after air and artillery bombardment, with B Company leading. The feature was deserted, with no sign the Viet Cong had ever occupied it.

On Operation New Life, after Vo Xu village had been cleared and handed to a South Vietnamese Army unit, 1 RAR returned to Chanh Duc. The next morning the northern part of Chanh Duc, known as Duc Hanh, was cleared of Viet Cong using helicopter Eagle Flights and an advance down the road through the village. Thirty-nine Vietnamese were detained, 20 of them confirmed Viet Cong and six ralliers, and clearing patrols found a workshop making sharpened bamboo stakes and two tons of rice.

On Operation New Life, D Company, 1 RAR, attacked Chanh Duc village. 12 Platoon, crossing the moat to seize a foothold, was fired on from the front and flank; it fought off 14 to 20 enemy near the church and pinned down an enemy section crossing a road, on which artillery was brought down, and detained seven suspects. With C Company in support and mortar and artillery fire on enemy positions, the company cleared down the line of the road, using tear gas on tunnels, and the Viet Cong fled north. Seven Viet Cong were killed. The platoon commander noted that ammunition carried was barely enough, and that the road made it easy to adjust artillery fire. The battalion, joined by the armoured personnel carrier troop, harboured in the village, where there was light enemy fire and sniping over the next nights.

On Operation New Life, D Company, 1 RAR, cleared Vo Xu, detaining 40 Viet Cong suspects who were sent to battalion headquarters. C Company found a cache of 20 tons of rice, which was taken to Vo Dat for distribution to the local people.
On Operation New Life, B Company, 1 RAR, saw three suspected Viet Cong but could not catch them.

On Operation New Life, a Viet Cong rallied to C Company, 1 RAR, handing over a shotgun. The next day US military intelligence staff, with the battalion intelligence officer and an interpreter, took him to higher headquarters.

12 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, clearing ground for a battalion harbour, walked into open country covered by a Viet Cong ambush of about four to seven men firing grenades and automatic weapons from well-built bunkers. Several soldiers were wounded, including the platoon commander, and two medics going forward to help the wounded were killed. A flanking attack by the company support section met no opposition, and the contact ended after 80 minutes; in all two Australians were killed and six wounded. Engineers later recovered clothing, rice, four Russian bolt-action rifles, ammunition and grenades from the bunkers, and the lessons drawn were to avoid open areas and keep medics back until it was safe to send them forward.

B Company headquarters, 1 RAR, was moving forward to meet a C Company patrol when a command-detonated mine exploded beside the main track, killing an officer and wounding a lance corporal. The company fired into a bamboo clump thought to hide the Viet Cong, and a second mine was set off. A radio operator taking over the wounded man's radio was then shot in the chest by a sniper from the same clump, and later a 4 Platoon machine-gunner passing the area was shot dead from there too.

Engineers used a Mighty Mite air blower to force smoke and tear gas into tunnels found by B Company, 1 RAR, to reveal other entrances and deny the tunnels to the enemy. An engineer corporal inspecting a shaft between tunnel levels lost his respirator and was asphyxiated by the gas and lack of oxygen, and was dead when rescuers reached him; two others were badly affected trying to reach him and were evacuated by helicopter. Important documents, including a well-produced propaganda photograph book, were found in the tunnels, and other caches of food, documents and medical stores were found inside the company perimeter. One cache had a hinged trapdoor wired to two grenade booby traps, which had failed because the grenade pins had been left splayed.

10 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, was moving to block for a sweep by 12 Platoon when the platoon commander and a section commander were fired on while investigating voices in some scrub. The area proved to be heavily fortified with trenches and was slowly cleared; during the sweep a sniper in another trench system hit a lance corporal and was himself shot, though his body was not found. The three or four enemy, armed with a sub-machine-gun and a French rifle, withdrew through the trenches into a tunnel. Two more Australians were wounded in the incident, and one Australian was recorded killed.

12 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, in ambush, saw about ten Viet Cong (two seen, others heard) coming to collect information from women in huts in the ambush area. The platoon let them come as close as possible before the stop group opened fire, killing two, whose bodies were later dragged away by the others; a search next morning found blood stains and drag marks. The lesson drawn was that safety catches must be off when a platoon is in ambush.

12 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, sweeping towards a blocking force, came into an area of widespread booby traps. The forward section accidentally set off a grenade booby trap, lightly wounding two men, while two or three enemy riflemen sniped at the platoon, which fired back. The lesson drawn was to beware of vines, cord and wires, as they are often connected to grenades.

While 2 Section, 4 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, was moving along a track, its machine-gunner was shot dead by a Viet Cong sniper, thought to be using a light weapon such as an M1 carbine. Elements of C Company sprayed the area with fire but found no trace of the sniper.

While 2 Section, 4 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, was moving along a track, its machine-gunner was shot dead by a Viet Cong sniper. Elements of C Company sprayed the area with machine-gun fire but could not find him.

On Operation Rolling Stone, later that night the same 1 Section, 4 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, ambush opened fire on about 15 enemy approaching the track, and the leading group went down. Ordered to withdraw, the patrol fired on another group of about ten as it pulled back, and then shot dead a Viet Cong who walked out of the rubber trees and tried to join them, even speaking to them, thinking they were his comrades. In all four Viet Cong were killed and two wounded and captured, and an AK-47, seven Chinese rifles, 15 grenades, a flare pistol, documents and equipment were taken. The company commander called it a highly commendable display of good soldiering: the patrol engaged 28 Viet Cong and inflicted considerable casualties without receiving fire in return.

On Operation Rolling Stone, a standing patrol from C Company headquarters, 1 RAR, opposite the company water point, saw a Viet Cong moving across its front, and every weapon opened fire at once. He was seen to drop and was heard going into the bush. A sweep next morning found nothing, but engineers found three bodies two days later.
On Operation 4/66, A Company, 1 RAR, made contact with two Viet Cong, killing one. Grenades and shovels were captured.
On Operation 4/66, A Company, 1 RAR, fired on five Viet Cong, apparently wounding one, as a hat and sandal were later found. Later two more Viet Cong were contacted in the area.

On Operation 4/66, a machine-gunner of 9 Section, 9 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, on picket duty, heard movement on the track he covered and waited until a group of Viet Cong stopped and squatted behind a bush about 20 metres away before opening fire; the rest of the platoon fired at where his tracer showed. A clearing patrol next morning found two bodies, which were buried, from a group of at least four. A Chinese carbine, an AK-47, an SKS carbine, four sets of webbing, food, documents and ammunition were captured.
On Operation Rolling Stone, C Company, 1 RAR, saw three Viet Cong probing its perimeter and fired on them, with no result.

On Operation 4/66, 9 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, clearing north of an engineer base camp, came under fire from two Viet Cong, apparently sentries for a group of about six digging an ambush position of eight pits covering a track. The platoon swept through on a three-section front, and the Viet Cong fled, leaving a good deal of equipment. One Viet Cong was killed and buried, and an SKS carbine, ammunition, grenades, entrenching tools, water bottles, wallets and documents were captured. The platoon commander credited quick action and accurate fire by the forward section.

On Operation Rolling Stone, amid the night's heavy firing, a Viet Cong who had crept up to 9 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, ran through the scrub between two weapon pits into the platoon area, and a burst fired at him in the dark missed. He tripped over a shelter cord and dropped his weapon, ran behind three pits, turned away from a machine-gun pit, and ran into another pit, where a lance corporal killed him at about three metres. An AK-47, webbing, a pack of rice and ammunition, and documents were captured. The platoon commander thought he was confused by the night's fire and trying to get away, and noted that by staying silent and still, troops can spot an intruder inside the perimeter without much risk.
On Operation Silver City, the US armoured unit attached to 1 RAR made contact with about a squad of Viet Cong. An air strike on the place was estimated to have killed six and wounded six more.

On Operation Silver City, B Company, 1 RAR, reported that three men, two Australian engineers of 3 Field Troop and a US soldier, were wounded when a Claymore mine went off in front of a Mule, a light transport vehicle, carrying rice out of a captured cache.

On Operation Silver City, 2 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, was guarding engineers clearing booby traps from a cache of about 420 bags of rice before blowing it up. 6 Section, with two machine-guns, saw enemy approaching in open formation and held fire until they were eight to ten metres away; the enemy fired back at once, pinning down the section and platoon headquarters, until 1 Platoon's machine-gun fire across the front relieved the pressure. The five-minute fight was with about 25 Viet Cong of the mobile force. A sweep found two bodies and signs of a third being dragged away, and three Viet Cong were recorded killed; a Chinese light machine-gun, an AK-47, ammunition, equipment and documents were captured. One Australian was wounded and later flown out.

On Operation Silver City, 2 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, was setting a night ambush on a well-used track when 20 to 25 enemy arrived just before last light. The first group spotted the machine-gunner of the stop group, which opened fire before the enemy reached the main killing group, and for seven or eight minutes held them off as they tried a counter-ambush drill. The stop group then withdrew into the main position, and the patrol moved 40 metres back across the track, settled for the night and called artillery onto the enemy's escape route. At least three Viet Cong were killed, their bodies dragged away by their comrades.

On Operation Silver City, a patrol of the US armoured unit attached to 1 RAR made contact with a squad-sized group of Viet Cong. One American was killed; two Viet Cong were believed killed and two wounded.

On Operation Silver City, a 13-man patrol of 7 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, acting as a cut-off party, stopped to check its location when its lead machine-gunner saw two Viet Cong and fired. A tremendous volume of fire came back from right across the front, pinning the patrol down for five minutes until the Viet Cong suddenly broke contact. One Australian was killed. The enemy, estimated at more than 25 and well armed with automatic weapons, had been in an L-shaped ambush position, and mortar fire was called onto their line of withdrawal.
On Operation Silver City, the US armoured unit attached to 1 RAR had a contact with enemy probing its position. One man was wounded and evacuated, and two were slightly wounded by their own grenades.

On Operation Silver City, the Assault Pioneer Platoon, Support Company, 1 RAR, crossed the Song Be to secure the landing zone for US infantry and artillery. At the crossing, one Australian was killed by Viet Cong on the eastern bank; the platoon made contact with two snipers but completed the crossing, helped by heavy fog over the river. By mid-morning the battalion and its attached US units had been flown in, and artillery began arriving by Chinook helicopter.

On Operation Abilene, a ten-man ambush from 11 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, was sprung by its machine-gun when five Viet Cong walked into the killing ground. Four fell and one escaped; grenades were thrown at two who seemed to be crawling away, and meanwhile another apparently crawled off. The patrol withdrew 100 metres for the night and searched at first light. Three Viet Cong were killed, one of them a woman, one was possibly killed and one escaped wounded; two weapons were recovered.

On Operation Abilene, the deputy commander of the US 1st Division, landing at the Binh Ba airstrip, reported Viet Cong moving away south-west. B Company, 1 RAR, and 1 APC Troop gave chase, and with company headquarters mounted in carriers caught about 12 Viet Cong fleeing into the jungle east of the rubber plantation. Two were killed by fire from the carriers and a third was hit and dropped his rifle, later found bloodstained; the Viet Cong did not fire back, and an air strike was put on their escape route. Grenades, a grenade launcher, two Garand rifles, documents, equipment and ammunition were captured. Lessons drawn were the value of quick follow-up and the need for better communication between carrier commanders and the infantry riding with them.
On Operation Abilene, two soldiers of A Company, 1 RAR, were wounded when they accidentally set off a booby trap.

On Operation Abilene, C Company, 1 RAR, made contact with three Viet Cong; one was wounded and captured and another wounded but escaped. Sweeps around the Binh Ba airstrip continued, with C Company capturing three suspects and B Company detaining 28, who were sent to the prisoner cage for questioning.

On Operation Abilene, 1 Section, 8 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, in a three-group ambush sited 15 metres off a moonlit track, opened fire as five Viet Cong hurried through the killing ground, followed closely by four more. Two were seen to fall before dust obscured the area; the Viet Cong did not fire back, and a quick search found no bodies, so the patrol moved to its alternative position. Next morning four heavy blood trails were found, and a wounded Viet Cong found along them was shot dead at about ten metres. A pack, hats, webbing, a magazine and trousers were captured; the section commander recommended siting all pits to fire into the killing ground and considering Claymore mines for ambushes.

On Operation Abilene, 4 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, set a night ambush on a track junction with machine-guns on each flank firing across the track. Six Viet Cong with slung rifles came along it, with another group about 30 metres behind, and the platoon opened fire as they reached the killing ground; two were seen to fall. Hearing movement to his right, the platoon commander thought the second group was trying to outflank him and moved his men 100 metres to ambush them, but there was no further contact, and he called in artillery. The Viet Cong never fired back, and a search at first light found many fresh tracks but no bodies.
On Operation Abilene, C Company, 1 RAR, fired on four or five Viet Cong, possibly wounding one, and captured five Viet Cong.
On Operation Abilene, the US 1/4 Cavalry had an armoured personnel carrier destroyed by recoilless-rifle fire near Long Tan and two soldiers wounded, and also came under some rifle fire.

On Operation Denver, as B Company, 1 RAR, moved into a harbour position, the leading section of 5 Platoon saw three Viet Cong coming up the ridge towards it. At about 60 metres they realised they were walking into an Australian patrol and turned to escape, and the platoon opened fire. One was killed at once, one was wounded and died within three minutes, and the third escaped wounded. A Garand rifle and an M1 carbine were captured.

On Operation Denver, 12 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, clearing a ridge, saw two armed Viet Cong moving parallel 50 metres away. 9 Section followed and met about five Viet Cong, and the section commander fired a burst into them at about eight metres, wounding three, who fled west; at the same time three unarmed Viet Cong came up behind the section and were all wounded by the second-in-command, and one of them was killed by a stop group as they fled north. The Viet Cong had clearly not known the patrol was there. Friendly troops nearby prevented a follow-up, and the dead man was buried. The platoon commander noted that the M16 rifle lacked stopping power at close range: men hit in the chest and stomach ran as if unhurt.
On Operation Denver, B Company, 1 RAR, made contact with three Viet Cong, and saw three more that afternoon. A sweep of the area found no Viet Cong.

A clearing patrol of D Company, 1 RAR, on Operation Denver, made contact with eight Viet Cong armed with three automatic weapons. One Australian was shot in the thigh and evacuated. The Viet Cong got away without casualties, and artillery fired on their line of withdrawal.

On Operation Denver, 4 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, was fired on by five Viet Cong on its right front. The forward elements of 6 Platoon, on the left, got off a little fire before 4 Platoon moved into the area and it was no longer safe for 6 Platoon to shoot. The incident lasted about five minutes.
On Operation Denver, two sentries guarding 1 RAR's tactical headquarters challenged four Viet Cong walking down the road, and fired on them as they fled. One Viet Cong was claimed wounded.
On Operation Denver, 7 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, detained two Viet Cong and two suspects. Medical supplies, clothing and Viet Cong supply lists were found in huts in the area.

On Operation Denver, the forward section of 6 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, the left forward platoon in a company advance, was fired on by a Viet Cong as it moved into a gully. He withdrew south when fire was returned.

A patrol of 10 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, was hit by enemy 120 mm and 82 mm mortar fire, killing two Australians and wounding four. Artillery fired on the 82 mm mortar positions, and an air strike hit the 120 mm mortar's.

D Company, 5 RAR, sweeping the north-east of Hoa Long for enemy mortar positions, came under light mortar fire, and one Australian was killed and three wounded, from D and E Platoon, 1 APC Squadron and 1 Field Squadron. Radar placed the mortars at Long Phuoc village, and artillery fired on them with unknown results.
A platoon of D Company, 5 RAR, made contact with eight enemy soldiers, killing three and recovering two rifles and an automatic weapon.

A patrol from A Company, 5 RAR, met an enemy soldier who opened fire on them with an automatic weapon. 6 Platoon, B Company, which was collecting water nearby, was drawn into the contact. One Australian soldier died of his wounds; he had been shot by his own side during what may have been a contact with the enemy.
9 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, made contact with four Viet Cong, killing two. One grenade was thrown at the Australians, and there were no Australian casualties.
7 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, set off an enemy grenade booby trap, and two Australians were wounded and evacuated by helicopter.

The leading section of 3 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, was examining a recently used track when about six armed enemy approached. They spotted the section's boot marks and its leader, who opened fire, and the riflemen joined in before the machine-gun could be set up. One enemy was killed and carried away, another was wounded, and a rifle was captured; the section leader was critical of his Owen gun, whose rounds would not go through the bush.
A platoon of B Company, 5 RAR, made contact with five enemy soldiers, killing one and wounding another. A rifle was found.

The Battle of Long Tan. D Company, 6 RAR, 108 strong, was following fresh tracks east of Nui Dat when 11 Platoon met a few Viet Cong and then a much larger force. From about 5.30 pm the company was attacked by at least a company, later found to be far more, under heavy machine-gun and mortar fire in heavy rain, and held on until A Company arrived in armoured personnel carriers after 7 pm. Close artillery fire broke up many of the attacks; low cloud ruled out air strikes, and helicopters flew in ammunition and took out the wounded. Seventeen Australians were killed and nineteen wounded; 245 enemy were recorded killed. The company commander afterwards reported that the M60 machine-guns jammed in the mud and that the men needed to carry more ammunition.

During the Battle of Long Tan, A Company, 6 RAR, rode out from Nui Dat in the armoured personnel carriers of 3 Troop, 1 APC Squadron, to relieve D Company. On the way it clashed with the support company of the D445 Battalion, causing about 15 casualties, and then with two companies of the 275th Regiment, causing about 45 more, before joining D Company as the enemy withdrew. Four Australians were wounded.
A platoon of A Company, 6 RAR, made contact with six Viet Cong, wounding one. The unit's log has no record of it.

During the Battle of Long Tan, B Company, 6 RAR, heading back to Nui Dat, stopped when it heard D Company's firing and was ordered to help. It reached the battlefield as the enemy were retreating, and joined D Company that evening.

10 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, found two well-hidden huts, surrounded them and opened fire on a group of 18. Five escaped downhill, and ten, nine men and a woman, were killed; six rifles and two other weapons were captured.

5 RAR's Assault Pioneer Platoon was investigating inhabited, booby-trapped caves when a lone sniper shot a sentry in the back. One Australian was killed and two wounded, the two by ricochets of their own fire off the rocks. An enemy was wounded and retreated into a cave, which was attacked with a flamethrower, and he was believed killed.
A soldier of 1 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, tripped a booby trap, wounding four. A Chinese grenade and an 81 mm mortar-round booby trap were found nearby and destroyed.

5 RAR's Anti-Tank Platoon, sent back to free men of the battalion headquarters pinned down by a sniper, was itself pinned down in ground the enemy had chosen well, by snipers in the trees and machine-guns in the gullies. A section leader was shot and killed. With A Company's machine-guns firing in support, the platoon got out, and a helicopter gunship raked the area. The commanders were struck by the enemy's fire control: probably no more than ten men, firing from four or five directions and never twice from the same spot.
5 RAR's Anti-Tank Platoon, trying to clear a spur, was pinned down by enemy fire, and one Australian was killed. The firefight lasted until late afternoon.
Two men of 5 RAR's Assault Pioneer Platoon trod on a buried anti-personnel mine near the caves, and both were wounded, one seriously. Ten huts were destroyed in the area.
B Company, 5 RAR, made contact with five Viet Cong, possibly wounding two; one was dressed like an Australian and carried an Armalite rifle.

The Anti-Tank Platoon, guarding 5 RAR's battalion headquarters, was pinned down by a skilful sniper, who fired well-aimed shots whenever anyone moved, and by an enemy machine-gun. One Australian was wounded.

A command-detonated mine exploded against D Company, 6 RAR, killing one Australian and wounding ten, with three civilians also wounded. About half the casualties, including the man killed, were caused by an Australian Claymore mine carried by an NCO, which went off in the blast. The record also notes evidence that a Vietnamese woman who ran to the scene was wounded or killed by soldiers who mistook her for an enemy.

Five enemy approached 6 RAR's Assault Pioneer Platoon in harbour at night and opened fire when a sentry challenged them. One Australian was killed and two wounded; the record notes the dangers of the rules of engagement.
In the afternoon the enemy fired more command-detonated mines at 2 Troop, 1 APC Squadron's carriers, wounding three infantrymen inside and slightly damaging a carrier.

A reconnaissance patrol of 9 Platoon, C Company, 6 RAR, was fired on with a machine-gun and grenades by local Viet Cong in ambush pits along a track. It flanked them, and its fire set off an enemy Claymore; a sweep found a camp with booby-trapped tunnels and a dead section commander of the D445 Battalion, with blood trails from others.
The rear platoon of A Company, 6 RAR, saw two Viet Cong coming towards the column; the column went to ground and shot both dead at 20 metres. A rifle was recovered.

The enemy fired two command-detonated mines at 2 Troop, 1 APC Squadron's carriers. The carriers followed the Viet Cong north and killed two, and ammunition and a grenade were captured. There were no Australian casualties.
A patrol of 10 Platoon, D Company, 6 RAR, caught a squad of about eight enemy crossing a river and wounded three, with the help of helicopter gunships.

A patrol of 10 Platoon, D Company, 6 RAR, moving in single file through thick bamboo, saw an enemy step out 60 metres away and opened fire with everything. Three blood trails were found, and one of the enemy was a woman; artillery fired on their escape route.
