During a battalion cordon and search, C Company headquarters, 5 RAR, set off a booby trap while holding an orders meeting. Three Australians were killed and five wounded. The record says the mine was probably a booby trap laid by friendly forces.

After A Company, 6 RAR, ran into a dug-in enemy position, B Company was ordered to assault it with A Company's support. Following artillery fire, B Company attacked and was pinned down by fire from all sides, including heavy machine-guns, Claymore mines and light mortars, revealing a heavy weapons company supporting well-hidden positions of D445 Battalion. With casualties mounting, four air strikes were made, and 2 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, came in to recover casualties; one carrier was disabled by three recoilless rifle rounds, killing its driver and wounding its commander and the wounded inside. After a four-hour battle the companies withdrew into a night position 200 metres away, and the enemy withdrew overnight; eight Australians were killed and 21 wounded, with 50 enemy recorded killed. The commanding officer said he had not launched a full battalion attack because he was ordered to finish at last light, and that the action showed the need for tanks.

6 RAR was flown in by helicopter to cut off enemy forces withdrawing from an attack on Phuoc Hai. As 2 Platoon, A Company, pushed into the jungle to secure the landing zone, its sergeant shot a sniper in a tree, and enemy automatic weapons opened up; the right-hand section swept to within 20 metres of one gun when another opened fire, wounding five men. The platoon had run into a dug-in company of D445 Battalion, with its heavy weapons company, in bunkers with overhead cover. Six Australians were wounded and three to six enemy killed, and the platoon withdrew 150 metres, at a time when it had no mortar support and artillery fire had been interrupted.

A Company, 6 RAR, moving in support of B Company's attack on the main enemy position, came under sniper fire, and two enemy were killed. A Company supported B Company and guided the armoured personnel carriers in to recover its casualties; one of the guides was wounded doing so.

B Company, 5 RAR, was being carried by 3 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, into position for a Task Force attack on the Viet Cong stronghold of the Long Hai Hills when the leading carrier hit a powerful mine on a dirt track. Two cavalrymen and two infantrymen were killed, the rest aboard were badly wounded, and the carrier was thrown on its side. When no ambush followed, soldiers ran from their carriers to help the medics and set off more anti-personnel mines, killing or wounding most of the medics and the company headquarters; normal mine drills had been ignored. Engineers ordered everyone to keep still while they cleared the mines, medical help came by helicopter, and Operation Renmark was cancelled. In all nine Australians were killed and 26 wounded.

Following up its earlier contact, the Reconnaissance Platoon, Support Company, 5 RAR, met the same group again and killed a Viet Cong woman. Artillery was fired at the fleeing enemy, and an M2 carbine was recovered.

4 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, made contact with two Viet Cong near a platoon-sized camp. They threw a grenade, fired rifles and fled after eight others from the camp. One Australian was shot in the right upper arm and walked out to be evacuated by helicopter.
4 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, was destroying the camp it had found earlier when a booby trap went off, wounding one Australian in the right thigh. He was carried out for evacuation by helicopter.

The Reconnaissance Platoon, Support Company, 5 RAR, made contact with four Viet Cong, carrying an automatic weapon and three carbines, who fled through a camp. The platoon swept the area and met them again later, and artillery fired in support.
A Company, 5 RAR, saw lights on the northern slopes of Hon Vung mountain, and they were engaged by artillery throughout the night.
An engineer of 1 Troop, 1 Field Squadron, set off an M16 mine while laying it in the barrier minefield. Six soldiers were wounded, two of whom later died.

The Reconnaissance Platoon, Support Company, 5 RAR, in ambush, made contact with four enemy, killing two and wounding two. One Australian was wounded in the leg by a burst of automatic fire. Claymore mines had not been used because the paddy field gave little cover and they would have been too close to the platoon. Artillery supported, and a search next morning found blood trails, sandal marks, field dressings, drag marks and scattered rice.

A soldier of 4 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, set off an anti-personnel mine after the engineers had swept for mines up to a line of pickets; the platoon commander, following the mine detector, had stepped outside the line. One Australian was killed, the platoon commander was very seriously wounded in both legs and later died, and another soldier suffered severe shock. The mine, not an M16, blew a hole a metre wide and half a metre deep.

While mines were being laid in the barrier minefield, a member of a mine-arming party from 7 RAR's Assault Pioneers set off an M16 mine, killing a sapper of 1 Field Squadron and wounding two others. It is recorded as a friendly-fire incident.
Two engineers of 1 Field Squadron were killed when an anti-lift device exploded while they were laying M16 mines in the barrier minefield.

4 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, ambushing the road bridge on the Suoi Sau near the Horseshoe, saw ten enemy on the road beside the bridge while four more came down a track into a machine-gun's field of fire; it opened fire and the enemy went to ground and fired back, and another ten appeared along the creek line. The platoon commander said 20 to 30 enemy in three groups milled around until 2 am searching for their casualties, and took away a wounded man who could be heard moaning. Two bodies were found in the morning, buried just outside the Horseshoe, along with a blood trail; five grenades and a submachine-gun were captured. Artillery engaged the area.
A clearing patrol of 1 ARU, under the command of 7 RAR, made contact with one enemy armed with an automatic weapon, and two Australians were wounded.

Two Viet Cong walking along a paddy bund were fired on by 5 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR's machine-gun, and one, a woman, was killed. The other fled towards 6 Platoon, which opened fire with a machine-gun and grenade launchers, but escaped, leaving a heavy blood trail. A grenade was recovered.

6 RAR was set to intercept enemy forces withdrawing from the attack on Lo Gom. As 2 Platoon, A Company, left its lunch position, the forward scout heard a rifle being cocked, and the platoon engaged a well dug-in enemy platoon, then pulled back 50 metres while artillery and mortars hit the position. The enemy replied with 60mm mortars, lightly wounding two Australians. A Company then attacked behind heavy artillery and mortar fire and took the position as the enemy withdrew; one enemy body, 20 to 30 fighting pits and an AK-47 were found. The enemy were the rear of 2 Battalion, 275 Regiment, covering the battalion's withdrawal across the Song Rai.

B Company, 6 RAR, with 2 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, was sent to ambush boats supplying the enemy, and at dawn engaged five motorised sampans 250 metres offshore. Three were sunk and two badly damaged, mostly by the armoured vehicles' .50 calibre machine-guns. Six enemy were recorded killed.

Half of 6 Platoon, B Company, 6 RAR, was sent to check a sandhill covered in dense 2-metre scrub where movement was suspected. After 120 metres, fire from a hidden pit 5 metres away hit the machine-gun's number two, and the gunner was hit from another hidden pit after one burst. The half platoon withdrew; the full platoon then attacked with armoured personnel carrier support and rescued the two wounded, and 5 Platoon swept the area as the enemy withdrew. Six to eight enemy of 2 Battalion, 275 Regiment, had been in three bunkers and five other positions, and were hit by a large airstrike and heavy artillery fire. Three Australians were wounded, two of whom died; there were no known enemy casualties, and an SLR rifle was captured.

A soldier of 4 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, set off a US M16 mine north of Phuoc Loi, killing one Australian and wounding two. The mine had been set beside the road in line with a fence; the local sub-sector said it had laid no mines there, engineers found no others, and it could not be told how long it had been there.
C Company, 6 RAR, found a cache of 80 tons of rice. It was booby-trapped, and three Australians of 8 Platoon were wounded.

2 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR, was returning from night activity astride Route 23 south of Xuyen Moc when a soldier crossing the road set off an anti-vehicle mine. He died of his wounds, and one other Australian was wounded.

A figure jumped out in front of a scout of 6 Platoon, B Company, 6 RAR, who fired one shot at 25 metres. A woman was killed, and a man with no identity card was detained. The record classes it as a contact with civilians.

A Company, 5 RAR, carried by 3 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, was deploying around two bogged armoured personnel carriers when it made contact with four or five Viet Cong, three of whom broke cover and fled south-west. Artillery and helicopter gunships engaged the area, with no known result.

9 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, found enemy tracks in a creek bed near a partly destroyed bunker system and was deploying when three enemy were seen. Two were shot dead immediately and the third escaped. One Australian was slightly wounded by shrapnel from a grenade launcher.

C Company, 7 RAR, heard firing 70 to 100 metres away, and a section found four Vietnamese bound with wire and shot, three of them still alive. They had been executed by the enemy, who went off in the direction of A Company.

3 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, found enemy tracks, and the forward scout signalled that three enemy were approaching. Before the section could deploy the enemy saw the scout, who opened fire and killed one. Another was wounded and tried to escape but was tracked by the dogs and killed beneath a bush.

3 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, made contact with three Viet Cong, killing one and wounding another. The blood trail was followed with tracker dogs, and the wounded man was found and killed about an hour later. Artillery fired on enemy withdrawal routes.

11 Platoon, D Company, 7 RAR, stopped for a rest when the last man heard noises behind, and the rear section improvised an ambush. Eight to twelve enemy, who had been tracking the platoon without realising it had stopped, walked into it; an inexperienced rifleman opened fire too early, and the section fired on four targets. The enemy returned fire, threw a grenade and withdrew after two of them were knocked down, and tried to recover a body but were driven off. A sweep found no enemy, and artillery fired illumination and on escape routes.

2 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, in ambush on a track, fired a Claymore mine when three Viet Cong walked into the killing ground, killing the first. The other two escaped and a sweep found no sign of them. The Claymore had not been properly sited.

1 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, was searching a camp and bunker system when an enemy soldier walked up towards a sentry post. The machine-gunner told the section commander, who shot him in the stomach as he turned to run; he fell, then got up and ran off, and the tracker dogs could not find him. Artillery fired on likely escape routes.

A section of 2 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, investigating cut trees near a track, found four enemy in a prepared position. The platoon was setting up crossfire when the enemy saw them and the section's machine-gun opened fire; the enemy fired back but withdrew hastily as a second section swept towards them, leaving one wounded. A blood trail was followed for 150 metres, and 3 Platoon took over the bunker system so 2 Platoon could follow the trail with a tracker team flown in.

After its ambush, A Company, 7 RAR, sent 2 Platoon along the track towards a suspected enemy squad; about 100 metres on it ran into heavy automatic fire from a defensive position, and 1 Platoon's right flanking attack was stopped by an enemy platoon, with seven enemy machine-guns firing at 30 metres. The rest of the company was committed with air strikes and artillery, and the enemy replied with rockets, grenades, machine-guns and rifles before withdrawing north under intense artillery and air attack after several hours. The enemy, C12 (2nd Company) of 3 Battalion, 274 Regiment, and a reconnaissance platoon, had been covering the withdrawal of their battalion from a camp a kilometre away. Six Australians were killed and 17 to 20 wounded, many slightly; an estimated 15 enemy were killed (five by body count) and 25 wounded, and artillery and air strikes were thought to have caused many more. AK-47s, an RPD light machine-gun, a B40 rocket launcher and ammunition were among the items captured.

During a search and destroy operation in the Hat Dich area, A Company, 7 RAR, was inserted by stealth to ambush trails to enemy camps. 2 Platoon set a simple ambush on a well-used track, and within minutes two enemy with rifles slung wandered into it and were shot dead with a machine-gun burst.

Two or three Viet Cong of the Chau Duc Company, dressed in black with green bush hats, walked along a trail into 4 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR's ambush. One was killed and one wounded, and an M1 rifle, a grenade and documents were captured. The wounded man's blood trail was followed without result, and artillery fired on escape routes.

4 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, in ambush, had two Viet Cong of the Chau Duc Company walk along a trail into its position from the east. One was killed, and an M1 rifle, rice, North Vietnamese money, ammunition, photos, exercise books and letters were recovered. Artillery fired in support.
4 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, made contact with three enemy at 30 metres. A blood trail and a Viet Cong base camp were found, and 106 Field Battery fired in support.

A sentry of A Company, 7 RAR, saw one Viet Cong, thought to be a scout, and fired, possibly hitting him. The sentry was withdrawn under covering fire, and a blood trail was found. Artillery fired on enemy withdrawal routes.

7 RAR's Assault Pioneer Platoon, working with D Company, made contact with two Viet Cong, neither armed, and captured one. He was dressed in green and carried two clips of ammunition, a week's rice and some Australian and US items. Artillery fired in support and on possible escape routes.
5 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, made contact with two Viet Cong, with no result. 106 Field Battery then fired on possible escape routes.

9 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR, surprised an enemy platoon in a platoon-sized camp of D445 Battalion and shot the leading man as the enemy fled, and it came under fire again as it followed up. Two enemy were killed and at least one wounded; documents identified them as C4 Company of D445, and a Mauser, an M1 Garand, a Chinese rifle and a Colt .45 pistol were captured. Artillery fired on two enemy escaping from the contact.

3 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, heard chopping 75 metres away and thought it was near a company-sized camp, then saw movement 50 metres off. The company pulled back 800 metres so that mortars, artillery, helicopter gunships and bombers, with 500-pound bombs and napalm, could hit the target. A Company then swept through the area but found nothing.

An SAS patrol set a Claymore ambush on a track, and four enemy in camouflage uniforms walked into it, the leader with his carbine ready and the others with weapons slung. The first three were knocked down by the Claymores and killed; the fourth opened fire with an automatic weapon and was engaged with rifles and another Claymore as he retreated up the track. The patrol then came under fire from two light weapons 30 metres up the track, withdrew and was lifted out.

Groups of 5 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, were protecting engineers blowing up a battalion-sized camp when three enemy slipped in and stole one of the engineers' rifles. A sentry saw movement and shot two dead, a 20-year-old woman and a 26-year-old man, both carrying Chinese assault rifles, sleeping gear and medical supplies, and wounded the third. The platoon followed the blood trail for 100 metres, and the forward scout shot the wounded man dead. Three weapons were captured, and the man's notebook held details of a meeting with another party.
A gun pit of 11 Platoon, D Company, 2 RAR, saw movement and fired two bursts, hitting two enemy at 20 metres. Both were killed; they carried an AK-47 and an M1 rifle.

C Company, 2 RAR, made contact on a well-worn track with three Viet Cong moving parallel to it, 5 metres off; nine more were seen following behind. One was killed and one wounded and taken prisoner, and a Thompson submachine-gun and two grenades were captured. Artillery fired in support.

Following up the enemy who had fled their camp, 9 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR, came under fire. It pulled back to let artillery hit the area and secured the camp; one enemy was recorded killed in this phase.

1 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR, heard talking and opened fire on five or six Viet Cong moving south, hitting one or two. The enemy split up and fled east and west; a sweep found a heavily bloodstained pack with drag marks beside it and three bags of rice. Artillery fired in support.

Enemy outside the perimeter of 2 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR's base fired a command-detonated Chinese Claymore-type mine from about 45 metres, probably aimed at the noise of the radio; its narrow blast reached 75 metres. Two Australians were killed and five or six wounded, one more suffering shock. A helicopter visit an hour earlier may have given the position away, and rain had masked the enemy's noise as they set the mine. The company commander noted that the men who ran to the wounded risked the blast of a second mine and should have waited for a sweep.

10 Platoon, D Company, 7 RAR, made contact with about seven people while crossing a creek. Three were killed and one wounded and captured; one escaped down a tunnel and two to the east. Although the enemy had fired on the patrol, those hit by its return fire were probably civilians: a boy and a girl were killed and an elderly couple wounded. The landing zone used for the medical evacuation was booby-trapped, but the booby trap was blown before the helicopter landed.

The Assault Pioneer Platoon, Support Company, 7 RAR, escorting an engineer team, came face to face with four enemy. The forward scout shot the first, the machine-gun had a stoppage, but supporting fire built up and the enemy stopped firing and withdrew. One enemy was killed and one possibly wounded, and a rifle was recovered; the enemy had used a Thompson submachine-gun. Two pioneers were slightly wounded by shrapnel, in the foot and the nose, and not evacuated; artillery and mortars fired in support.

Several enemy got through 108 Field Battery's defences during the night and set four Claymore mines aimed at the sleeping quarters. Two were fired, killing a gunner; the other two did not go off. Casualties would have been higher had most of the battery not been on duty.

8 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR, sweeping an extensive bunker system, made contact with four or five Viet Cong. A bunker was destroyed with rocket-launcher fire, one enemy was killed and an M1 carbine captured. Two Australians were wounded, one by shrapnel in the leg and one shot in the chest.

8 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, followed a track to a hut, crept up and opened fire on an enemy lying in bed and another inside; three bodies were found afterwards. An M1, an AK-47, a Thompson submachine-gun, a Browning automatic rifle and five packs were captured. A large camp nearby had 12 bunkers with overhead cover, holding documents, grenades, ammunition, military equipment and a radio. Artillery engaged escape routes.

3 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, ambushing nearby, saw movement heading towards 1 Platoon and warned it. When three enemy came towards 1 Platoon's position, its machine-guns killed two and wounded the third, and an AK-47 and a Thompson submachine-gun were captured.

A section of 1 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, part of an ambush on an enemy camp, was watching a main track when three or more enemy came along it and were engaged by the section commander. Two were killed and one wounded.

Acting on SAS information, D Company, 7 RAR, attacked an occupied enemy base camp while B Company ambushed escape routes. 10 and 12 Platoons drove the enemy from several bunkers, destroying one with a rocket launcher, and the company consolidated in the centre of the camp without loss. The enemy then circled around through communication trenches and counter-attacked from the east and north, getting between the reserve platoon and the others, and fired rocket-propelled grenades into the tree canopy to shower the Australians with shrapnel; grenade-launcher rounds failed to arm, a machine-gun jammed, and gunships and artillery could not be used so close. Fighting in heavy rain ended at nightfall. Two Australians were shot dead and about 20 wounded, mostly by shrapnel, ten of whom stayed on duty until the next day; three to four enemy were killed. The camp, prepared by the Chau Duc District Company, was probably used as a forward base by D445 Battalion.

A 12-man patrol of 2 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, was hit by a command-detonated mine, and the enemy also opened fire. One or two Australians were killed and seven or eight wounded. Fire was returned and artillery brought down.

An SAS patrol, in ambush, made contact with seven Viet Cong, five men and two women in mixed dress carrying a large amount of food. All seven were killed, and a Chinese rifle, a carbine and an M1 rifle were captured.
While 2 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, was searching an enemy camp 8 kilometres west of Xuyen Moc, a booby trap killed two Australians and wounded one.

12 Platoon, D Company, 2 RAR, in ambush, made contact with six Viet Cong, killing four and wounding one. An M1 Garand and two submachine-guns were captured, and a document showed one of the dead was the commander of the Xuyen Moc district platoon. A tracking team followed a blood trail until it was lost at a river, and artillery fired on escape routes.

1 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, in ambush, fired two Claymore mines at three enemy, followed by two machine-guns and rifles. Two were killed at once and the third, wounded, was killed in the sweep. Three SKS rifles were captured.

A platoon of B Company, 7 RAR, came at right angles onto a substantial ambush set on a track by 15 or more Viet Cong. The section leader saw the position and the enemy fired a Claymore mine, lightly wounding him in the face and leg and knocking four men unconscious; light machine-guns then opened fire from both flanks, pinning down a section. The company came up and sent platoons around each flank while artillery and gunships hit the surrounding area, but the enemy had gone. The company commander thought the enemy had fired the Claymore too soon when the scout appeared; one enemy was recorded wounded.

1 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, in ambush, made contact with four or five Viet Cong in black with packs, killing two and wounding one. A Thompson submachine-gun, a Chinese rifle, a 1917 Remington rifle and seven packs, mostly of food, were captured.

1 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR, in ambush, made contact with about ten Viet Cong, part of the same night's battle, supported by artillery and a Spooky gunship. Five enemy were killed at the time and later evaluation added more, for seven or eight in all; a heavy blood trail was found, and AK-47s, an M1, rifles, rocket-propelled grenade launchers and packs were captured.

2 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR, was resiting Claymore mines on a track when voices were heard and engaged, and the enemy left two rocket-propelled grenade launchers behind. During the sweep that followed, two New Zealanders and an Australian engineer were wounded, two shot in the arm and one in the head by a ricochet.

During the sweep, two or three enemy fired on 6 Platoon, B Company, 2 RAR, about 100 metres from its perimeter, and the platoon returned fire vigorously. A sweep next morning found one dead enemy and a wounded man trying to get away, who was shot dead. An automatic weapon and an AK-47 were captured.

2 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR, in ambush, made contact with about ten enemy, killing one and capturing three AK-47s, a machine-gun, three rocket-propelled grenade launchers and six packs. This began a four-hour battle in which two groups of about ten enemy clashed repeatedly with V Company.
2 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR, made contact with two enemy during a sweep and killed one, who was carrying medical stores and a grenade.

After contacts the night before, 6 Platoon, B Company, 2 RAR, swept the area in the morning and found one dead enemy and one wounded man trying to get away, who was shot and killed. An automatic rifle and an AK-47 were captured.
3 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR, sweeping the previous night's battlefield, found two enemy and wounded and captured one, who later died.
3 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, made contact with one enemy and wounded him, leaving a heavy blood trail. An AK-47 was captured.

During the Tet Offensive an enemy battalion seized much of Baria, a town of 15,000 with many brick and stone buildings, and 1 ATF sent A Company, 3 RAR (less a platoon), and nine carriers of 3 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, to protect key government buildings and drive the Viet Cong out. Rather than clearing their way on foot, the platoons were carried quickly in the carriers to the US compound and the administration and logistics compound, despite the threat of rocket-propelled grenades, with one section of carriers staying with Sector headquarters. Enemy infiltrators and rocket teams remained a constant threat for most of the battle, and the carriers were exposed from many directions because many houses had not been cleared. In heavy fighting one Australian was killed and 19 wounded; enemy casualties were put at 54, 42 of them killed.

Fire Support Base Anderson was attacked at night by at least a company of Viet Cong and a mortar platoon. The whole base was first hit accurately by 82mm and 60mm mortars and rocket-propelled grenades, and the enemy then assaulted from a high bund to the south-east in waves of grenadiers followed by rocket teams, breaking into the perimeter and causing casualties in the 3 RAR Mortar Platoon and the US B/2/35 Battery; a section of carriers from 1 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, with the battery's and mortars' fire, drove them back. Further fire and a probing attack from other directions were beaten off at the wire by machine-guns, and a second mortar attack covered the enemy's withdrawal; 3 RAR's mortars and 161 Battery engaged the enemy mortar positions, and gunships supported. Seven or eight Australians were killed and 22 to 27 wounded, including four engineers of 1 Field Squadron killed by a mortar bomb that hit their standing patrol; one American was killed and three wounded. Four enemy bodies were found, but blood, bandages and remains showed many more casualties.

V Company, 2 RAR, made contact with an enemy company and was attacked from the north, east and west with about 20 rockets and heavy automatic fire. Gunships and artillery supported. Ten New Zealanders were wounded; 13 enemy were killed and seven wounded, judging by drag marks and blood. Six AK-47s, two light machine-guns, 12 anti-tank grenades, 13 RPG-2 rounds, magazines and two sandbags of belted ammunition were captured.

10 Platoon, D Company, 7 RAR, unknowingly approached an enemy camp holding more than a company, and its forward section came under fire, three men being hit; the enemy then came forward and caused five more casualties as the platoon formed a perimeter. The company commander brought artillery and mortars onto the camp, and with 10 Platoon almost out of ammunition and enemy grenade launchers and mortars ranging onto it, gunships struck the enemy only 30 metres away. The rest of D Company came up, 11 and 12 Platoons assaulted on the flanks, and after an airstrike on the edges of the camp and escape routes the camp was cleared, the enemy withdrawing hurriedly and in some disorder. One Australian was killed and ten wounded, mostly by grenade-launcher and rocket-propelled grenade fire; enemy losses were heavy but uncertain, notionally five killed and five wounded. The enemy were C238 Battalion, concentrating for an attack on Long Binh, in a camp big enough for two companies.

After air and gunship strikes on the camp, 8 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, followed by 9 Platoon, made a wide flanking move to the right. The camp seemed deserted until four massive hidden bunkers opened fire at 10 metres, wounding three men and knocking out a machine-gun; rocket-launcher hits had little effect on a bunker, and the forward sections were pinned in crossfire and pulled back 15 metres. The company formed a perimeter and brought artillery and mortars in as close as 35 metres while the enemy probed its flanks with machine-guns and rockets; after a gunship strike 25 metres away the enemy fire slackened and they withdrew in good order. Three enemy were killed and five wounded, though the company commander said there were certainly more; 14 Australians were wounded, none seriously, six staying on duty overnight.

2 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, still holding the previous day's ambush, heard a large body of enemy approaching and stood to in its shell scrapes. When the first five entered the killing ground, Claymore mines, machine-guns and rifles opened fire and four of the five were killed, but 20 or more enemy fought back aggressively with AK-47s, RPD light machine-guns and rocket-propelled grenades. Many of the Australian casualties were caused by rocket-grenade shrapnel; the radio operator was incapacitated, and the platoon medic died of his wounds. One Australian was killed and seven wounded, and eight enemy were killed.
Australian and US artillery fired on an enemy mortar position. The next morning more than 18 enemy bodies were found, nine of them credited to the Task Force artillery.

During the Tet Offensive an enemy force of 20 to 30 men, with more than two platoons outside, occupied the village of Trang Bom, and D Company, 2 RAR, carried in armoured personnel carriers of A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, was sent with South Vietnamese forces to remove it. Heavy rocket-propelled grenade and automatic fire kept the infantry out of the village at first, and gunships were called in; the attack was repeatedly delayed by civilians still in their homes, who had to be moved to the market place. The enemy withdrew in good order north-west under the smoke of burning houses, with two killed by infantry and six by artillery, and no Australian losses. The enemy returned that night, and next morning, again hampered by civilians, the Australians attacked with carriers and artillery and drove them out by midday, killing 11; six civilians were also killed by artillery.

5 Platoon, B Company, 3 RAR, was moving along the road in Long Dien to protect 4 Platoon's flank while it searched for a missing South Vietnamese battalion commander when its forward sections came under heavy fire from an enemy platoon, and returned it. Nine Viet Cong were killed. Two or three Australians were killed and four or five wounded, and the enemy took a radio from an Australian signaller and may also have taken weapons from the casualties.

5 Platoon, B Company, 3 RAR, in Long Dien, made contact with five Viet Cong and cleared a house, and the enemy withdrew north. About an hour later it captured an armed Viet Cong who had been trying to avoid the clearing patrol, along with his M1 carbine.
B Company, 3 RAR, in Long Dien, made contact with five Viet Cong in black moving north. There were no known casualties.

B Company, 3 RAR's headquarters, in Long Dien, came under sniper fire from three trees, which were engaged. A Viet Cong was seen to leave one tree and run into a house, which was destroyed by two rounds from an 84mm anti-tank weapon. There were no Australian casualties.

After B Company, 2 RAR, seized the Dinh Co hill north-west of the Long Hai hills, an engineer set off a booby trap in the temple, killing himself and wounding 11 to 13 others. The area was infested with mines and booby traps, and the company commander believed the enemy were placing them in places likely to interest Westerners for their cultural value.

The forward scout of 7 Platoon, C Company, 3 RAR, patrolling in the south-east Long Hai hills, trod on an M16 mine that failed to jump and exploded in the ground, badly injuring him and another soldier. While the engineer team cleared the area, their protection party stepped outside the cleared area onto another M16 and was killed. 9 Platoon sent its engineer team with two escorts to help, and on the way down the ridge someone set off a third mine, killing the two sappers and seriously wounding the escorts. In all three Australians were killed and four wounded.
2 Platoon, W Company, 2 RAR, set off a second M16 mine north-west of the Long Hai hills, less than an hour after the first, wounding seven New Zealanders.

The commander of 9 Platoon, C Company, 3 RAR, following a path cleared by engineers in the south-east Long Hai hills, appears to have cut a corner and set off an M16 mine. The engineers, a soldier and the platoon commander were wounded, four in all, and the platoon commander, seriously wounded, died on the way to hospital.

The forward scout of 6 Platoon, B Company, 3 RAR, came within 5 metres of an enemy camp surrounded by barbed wire and was hit by light machine-gun and AK-47 fire; the platoon commander, trying to rescue him, was slightly wounded, and the whole platoon was pinned down. Artillery fired while tank T32 of C Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, was called; the enemy tried to encircle the platoon and one was killed. The tank fired canister and machine-guns, and the platoon was extricated with the scout, who had been killed; another man was grazed by a ricochet. The tanks returned with B Company the next day and found a large bunker system the enemy had abandoned.

A section ambush of 8 Platoon, C Company, 3 RAR, on a used track saw eight enemy approach from the north, and the rear sentry opened fire; three jumped into a ditch beside the track, and the machine-gun and a grenade launcher fired along it. The Claymore mines could not be fired because gunfire had cut their wires. The section moved to better ground and was joined by the rest of the platoon, and sweeps that night and next morning found four bodies; three AK-47s and an RPG-2 launcher were captured. One Australian was slightly wounded in the shoulder by shrapnel from a grenade-launcher round.

A section ambush of 12 Platoon, D Company, 3 RAR, saw six enemy walking along the track, waited until as many as possible were in the killing zone and fired the Claymores, and the machine-gun opened fire; the enemy withdrew, and groaning was heard. Automatic weapons then fired on the ambush from the east and south and were suppressed, and artillery and mortars fired through the night. At first light the platoon found four bodies and captured an AK-47, an AK-50, an M16 and an M14. The patrol had gone out without grenade launchers, which would have been invaluable, because no one checked.

Five enemy were seen by the perimeter defence of 2 Platoon, W Company, 2 RAR, and ambushed; three were killed and one captured, and W Company captured the last one about two hours later. Two M1 rifles, a Garand and a submachine-gun were captured, and artillery fired in support.

Fire support base Coral was attacked by an estimated enemy battalion with very heavy and accurate mortar fire, rocket-propelled grenades and a ground assault. The enemy overran a 105 mm howitzer position and tried to turn it on the Australians, and also overran the 1 RAR mortar platoon. The fighting ended at 8 am, supported by a Spooky gunship aircraft and helicopter gunships, with 161 Field Battery and 3 RAR's mortars firing from 1 km away. Nine Australians were killed and 28 wounded; 55 North Vietnamese were killed, one was captured, and seven rocket launchers were taken. 1 RAR's rifle companies were out ambushing 1 to 2 km away.

Fire support base Coral was attacked by an estimated enemy regiment. Heavy mortar and rocket-propelled grenade fire opened the attack, followed by a ground assault, and the base was defended by 1 RAR, the artillery and armoured personnel carriers of A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, supported by a Spooky gunship aircraft, helicopter gunships and an air strike on an enemy anti-aircraft machine-gun. Seven Australians were killed and 17 to 19 wounded, and two Americans were also wounded. Thirty-seven North Vietnamese were counted dead, ten more possibly killed, and one captured; later intelligence assessed that only 100 of the 790 attackers remained uninjured.

The North Vietnamese renewed their attack on fire support base Balmoral with mortar and rocket-propelled grenade fire followed by a ground attack by two battalions, recorded as the 2nd and 3rd Battalions of 165 Regiment (141 Regiment in another account). The attack broke up on the wire under helicopter gunship and artillery fire. One Australian was killed and six to eight wounded. Accounts give 47 to 55 enemy killed and six prisoners taken, one of whom died.

The North Vietnamese 165 Regiment attacked fire support base Balmoral, held by 3 RAR with tanks and armoured personnel carriers. Heavy mortar fire was followed by a ground attack supported by rocket-propelled grenades and light machine-guns; an enemy battalion group was thought to be present, with one company making the ground assault. Three Australians were killed and 16 wounded; six enemy were recorded killed and 30 wounded.

C Company, 1 RAR, on a reconnaissance in force, met three enemy and then came under heavy mortar, machine-gun and rocket-propelled grenade fire from a bunker system held by an estimated enemy company, and was pinned down. Helicopter gunships and artillery silenced the enemy mortars but could do little more because most of the fighting was at 10 to 15 m, and armoured personnel carriers could not push through the jungle; one carrier was hit by a rocket while evacuating wounded. When two tanks arrived from Coral an assault was made and eight bunkers destroyed, and the company then broke contact for air strikes. One Australian was killed and seven wounded; 24 enemy were killed, with more probably or possibly killed by air strikes and artillery. Returning on 2 June, the company found five more bodies and signs of many more buried by the bombing and shelling.

D Company, 1 RAR, with tanks of 1 Troop, C Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, returned to the site of B Company's contact of the day before, after an air strike, and came under rocket-propelled grenade, machine-gun and AK-47 fire from a well-built bunker system big enough for a company. The infantry protected the tanks while they cleared the jungle with canister and blew up or crushed bunkers, and the infantry also used flame-throwers; enemy RPG-2 rounds had no effect on the tanks. 10 and 12 Platoons destroyed 14 bunkers, probably closer to 18, and killed at least seven enemy, with an unknown number more crushed in their bunkers. The force broke off in fading light and withdrew behind accurate artillery and mortar fire, without loss.

To draw the Task Force's attention from Balmoral, the enemy made a 30-minute attack on fire support base Coral with about 60 rounds of 82 mm mortar and 20 rounds of 75 mm recoilless rifle fire, and rocket-propelled grenades. One Australian was killed and two wounded; enemy casualties are not known.

D Company, 1 RAR, was in an ambush position 800 m north of fire support base Coral when three enemy moved in front of 11 Platoon. The record gives no further account, though its figures show two Australians killed and nine wounded, and one enemy killed.

A 15-man patrol of 1 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR/NZ (ANZAC), set up a base at the limit of mortar support, and nine men went out to reconnoitre for a night ambush. They tracked, stalked and killed three enemy heard talking and laughing, not knowing they were at the edge of an enemy camp, and were at once attacked by at least 30 enemy at 10 to 15 m; one New Zealander was mortally wounded and three more, including the patrol leader and the machine-gunner, were wounded by rifle grenades, and the machine-gun was lost. Mortar fire was brought in 15 to 20 m from the patrol, and an assault by 17 enemy backed by a heavy machine-gun and 15 more was stopped 10 to 20 m away by rifles and grenade launcher, with mortars, helicopter gunships and 155 mm artillery adding to the enemy's losses. Short of ammunition, the patrol held off a further attack with gunship support until sections of V Company were flown in to secure the area and evacuate the casualties. At least five enemy were killed and nine wounded.

An enemy squad ambushed the first vehicle of a two-vehicle convoy from C Company, 2 RAR, at the Horseshoe, bound for Dat Do, with Claymore mines and automatic weapons at the eastern checkpoint. Three Australians were killed, one of them dying of his wounds, and two interpreters were wounded, one of whom later died; four weapons were lost. A sweep by C Company and South Vietnamese troops found only three AK-47 magazines and a squad-sized hiding tunnel near the fence. A woman living nearby said the Viet Cong had been there four days, and residents near the site were taken to 1 ATF for processing.

1 Platoon, W Company, 6 RAR/NZ, in ambush, made contact with four or five enemy moving north to south, and four or five Viet Cong were killed, two of them women. A carbine and documents were captured.

The northern checkpoint at Dat Do was attacked by an unknown number of enemy, and a section of C Company, 4 RAR, went to help. A small group of four or five Viet Cong mingled with civilians and opened fire, and the Australians could not return fire for fear of hitting civilians. One Australian was killed; enemy casualties are not known.
1 Platoon, W Company, 2 RAR, engaged five people at the northern checkpoint of the Horseshoe. About an hour later mortars engaged four or five people.

2 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR, following tracks north through a defoliated area, saw three enemy and fired, killing two; the third jumped into a bunker. The enemy, estimated at two platoons, replied with three rocket-propelled grenades, three claymores and AK-47 fire down fire lanes cut through a fence, and 1 and 3 Platoons, which came up in support, were also fired on. The company withdrew so that artillery, helicopter gunships and two air strikes could hit the bunkers, and prepared to attack the next day. Three enemy were possibly killed.

2 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR, sweeping near the previous day's contact, followed a track to a log-walled bunker system. The forward scout shot an enemy at 7 m and grenades were thrown into the bunkers, but the forward section then had three claymores fired at it and the platoon was pinned down by fire from rocket launchers, automatic rifles and 10 to 15 AK-47s at 7 m. Artillery called in close wounded one New Zealander with shrapnel from a tree burst, a friendly-fire incident, and did not relieve the platoon. Under helicopter gunship fire and smoke it broke contact, killing another enemy as it went; three enemy were killed in all. B and W Companies attacked the next day after artillery and air strikes, but the enemy had gone.

2 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR, reconnoitring upstream from the company base, realised an enemy camp was near and sent three scouts forward, who killed two enemy. The enemy fired back with an automatic rifle and six to eight AK-47s, and began to outflank the platoon once the scouts were back, until the leading man was shot by a machine-gun. Artillery was brought down within 75 m, and two helicopter gunships came up in support. Three enemy were recorded killed; the rest of the account is cut off.

The point section of 10 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR, following up an earlier contact, saw an enemy soldier on the track and the forward scout shot him. About four enemy armed with AK-47s fired back from several places, and as the section moved forward by fire and movement an enemy claymore mine was fired, wounding two or three Australians. One enemy was killed; the rest withdrew west, taking the dead man's weapon.

The commander of D Company, 3 RAR, saw two enemy crossing the engineer trail 150 m away and fired, and 12 Platoon swept the area, finding packs, tripods and body parts. On a second sweep the platoon was fired on from old pits at 25 m by six to ten enemy in grey-green uniforms and Chinese caps; the forward scout was shot in the arm and the platoon was pinned down. 11 Platoon took 30 minutes over hard ground to attack the enemy flank, and artillery was held up 40 minutes waiting for air clearance; 11 Platoon hit one enemy, who was dragged away, and grenaded the pits, freeing 12 Platoon. One enemy was killed and another possibly killed, and two theodolites were captured.

3 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR, had been in ambush on a track for 30 minutes when two Viet Cong in black came cautiously down it. Two claymores and rifle fire killed both, and two AK-47s and documents were captured.

A section machine-gun group of 10 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR, guarding the north side of an enemy camp that engineers were preparing to demolish, saw two Viet Cong coming down the track and opened fire at 10 m, killing both. The machine-gun stopped after one round because the belt lying across the top of the gun caused a bad extraction. An AK-47 and an SKS were captured.

3 Platoon, A Company, 3 RAR, in ambush near a previous contact, was alerted when a sentry saw three enemy moving cautiously towards it. They had just reached the killing ground when they turned and began to retreat; the sentry shot the rear man and called on the machine-guns, which possibly hit another. The enemy fired back, and mortars were called onto their likely escape route. The platoon commander thought it a mistake to arm a sentry with a self-loading rifle rather than an M16 or machine-gun.

The scout of 6 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, saw an enemy with an AK-47 on top of a bunker and fired; the enemy replied with rocket-propelled grenades, claymores and AK-47s and set off a command-detonated mine, wounding four Australians, and the company withdrew and brought artillery down on the bunkers. When it returned, 4 Platoon, struggling through dense scrub, drew heavy fire, believed killing two enemy, and had to pull back. After two air strikes, 5 Platoon tried again and was hit by another command-detonated mine and fire from bunkers the air strikes had missed; five more were wounded, one of whom died, and the company withdrew. The company commander admitted it had not at first realised what it had met or how strong the enemy was; it was also noted that helicopter gunships would have helped, and that the artillery observer was repeatedly cut out by the battalion radio net.

With air support restricted, the rifle companies of 1 RAR were relying on 3 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, for resupply along two trails, and the enemy had noticed. While deploying D Company, 1 RAR, an armoured personnel carrier hit a pressure mine of 75 to 100 lb of explosive laid in the previous two days, which threw it into the air. One trooper and one infantryman were killed, and others were wounded, one of whom later died; the carrier was badly damaged.

C Company, 1 RAR, made contact with an enemy squad, possibly killing one, and a sweep found a bunker system and a cache of an SKS, two 12.7 mm heavy machine-guns with seven spare barrels, three claymores, oil and personal equipment. An enemy soldier ran from a shelter and set off a claymore, wounding three Australians with shrapnel; he was killed. Tall trees delayed the helicopter evacuation of the wounded.

Following its earlier contact, 11 Platoon, D Company, 3 RAR, found an enemy camp and had cleared half of it when it was pinned down by heavy fire, with one man wounded. The right flank was on a steep slope and could not be turned, and 10 Platoon, sent round the other flank, was pinned by six bunkers and a sniper; its platoon sergeant was shot while organising the leading section and died of his wounds. The company withdrew for the night. An air strike hit the bunkers the next day, and when the camp was swept a day later the enemy had gone.

3 Platoon, A Company, 3 RAR, was in ambush on a track about 20 m from a stream when the sentry heard four or five enemy approaching. The machine-gun let them come to 7 m before opening fire, the sentry set off the claymore, and rifle fire swept the killing ground; the enemy did not fire back. Two were killed in the killing ground, and a third was wounded and crawled away, his body found later. Three AK-47s were captured, and mortars fired on the likely withdrawal routes.

5 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, was in a company harbour 5 m from a track when torches and voices came along it towards the machine-gun pit. The gunner waited until an enemy torch was about to light him up at 3 m and opened fire, then fired up the track at more movement. The enemy, who had been holding a torch about a foot above the ground and following the company, did not fire back. Two were killed and one wounded, and an AK-47 was captured.

2 Platoon, A Company, 3 RAR, made contact with 20 enemy in mixed green and grey uniforms moving south-east to north-west, killing one and possibly another, and capturing a pistol. Artillery and mortars fired on the area. 3 Platoon later found a body believed to be from this contact.

6 Platoon, B Company, 1 RAR, in a temporary position overlooking a clearing and ox-track, saw two Viet Cong in black with packs cross its front at 75 to 100 m. A section sent to outflank them missed them, but they turned and walked back past the platoon at 50 m and were killed by a long burst of machine-gun, rifle and grenade-launcher fire without firing back. A Chinese rifle and an M1 were captured.

An armoured personnel carrier of 3 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, set off a mine on a track off Highway 15. Three 4 RAR soldiers were slightly wounded and one member of A Squadron was also wounded.

Four or more enemy crept up to the perimeter of 3 Platoon, W Company, 4 RAR, which was guarding working bulldozers, and were seen by a sentry. The machine-gun opened fire, and the enemy replied with automatic weapons and an RPG-2, wounding two New Zealanders. The platoon swept the area without result, and the enemy withdrew south with unknown losses.

A bulldozer of 17 Construction Squadron hit an electrically fired pressure mine of 15 to 20 lb of TNT on a track off Highway 15. Two Australians were wounded, one with bleeding ears and one with shrapnel wounds to the shoulder and arm, and the bulldozer was slightly damaged.

While 3 Platoon, W Company, 4 RAR, was in the camp it had found earlier, two enemy walked down the track into it. The machine-gun killed one; the other tried to drag the body away and escaped, leaving a blood trail. Two SKS rifles, grenades and cooking gear were captured.
The Tracker Platoon, Support Company, 4 RAR, made contact with three enemy, killing one and capturing an AK-47. There were no Australian casualties.

6 Platoon, B Company, 4 RAR, looking for a company position, came on an old enemy bunker system, and a small reconnaissance group went forward. A Viet Cong jumped up and shot a corporal from about a metre away, and he fell behind dense scrub where he could not be seen, so the section could not at first fire back for fear of hitting him. The enemy fled south into thick jungle.

As 12 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR, moved into an ambush position, a flank sentry saw two enemy and shot one, who was dragged away by the other. A section following up was met by automatic fire from six to ten enemy, pulled back and called in artillery, and then followed the blood trail until it was lost among bamboo. One enemy was possibly killed.

A land-clearing team of 1 Field Squadron working around Nui Thi Vai and the Nui Dinh hills was attacked by two enemy with an RPG-2 and rifle fire. The D8 bulldozer caught fire and its driver was wounded in the head, chest and legs. The engineers could not put out the fire, so pushed the dozer into a cutting and buried it in soil; it was recovered to Nui Dat the next day.

An estimated 100 enemy, identified from captured documents as from C1 Company of D445 Local Force Battalion, attacked Long Dien with recoilless rifles, rocket-propelled grenades, automatic weapons and rifles. B, C and D Companies of 1 RAR, with armoured personnel carriers, tanks and helicopter gunships, were sent in; C Company and the armour fought a company-sized force in black inside the town, and B Company fought another group on Route 23. Sporadic fighting went on until late afternoon, and artillery fired five missions in support. Eleven or twelve Australians were wounded, seven of them in C Company by a 60 mm mortar; 29 to 40 enemy were recorded killed.

9 Platoon, C Company, 3 RAR, coming down a hill, met about 20 enemy in green uniforms coming up. The enemy fired AK-47s and rocket-propelled grenades into the trees, causing several minor splinter injuries; a dog handler wounded in the head and forearm and the forward scout, shot in the thigh, were evacuated. Six enemy were possibly killed, and the rest withdrew north.

9 Platoon, C Company, 3 RAR, coming out of grass into bamboo by a large clearing, saw five enemy sitting down. The forward scout fired and missed, then fired again and hit one who had just stood up. Two ran north, and another picked up the wounded man and fled south. One enemy was possibly killed, and an M1 carbine was captured.
B Company, 3 RAR, had one rifle round fired at it by an unknown number of enemy. There were no Australian casualties.
A sentry of 8 Platoon, C Company, 3 RAR, saw an enemy soldier in long grass 15 m away and opened fire. The enemy ran away; the result is not known.

12 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, made contact with about 60 enemy in a large bunker system of 14 large and 10 small bunkers covering 200 by 250 m. The platoon pulled back for an air strike and artillery, and D Company then attacked and cleared all but three still-occupied bunkers, which were ambushed overnight, though most of the occupants got away. Five Australians were wounded. Six enemy bodies and two blood trails were found.

7 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR, searching for bunkers, found a company-sized system of 20 interlocking covered bunkers in thick jungle that seemed to be empty, and quickly attacked with two sections. The first bunkers were cleared easily, but halfway in both sections came under very disciplined AK-47 fire from enemy in green uniforms and pith helmets, and the casualties came in clearing three main bunkers: two Australians were killed, one died of wounds and six were wounded. Two enemy were killed and the rest withdrew east; an AK-47, 600 lb of rice, packs, medical kits and documents were captured. The platoon considered it should have reconnoitred the bunkers more carefully before attacking.

1 and 2 Platoons, V Company, 4 RAR, were in ambush on a track system. Thirteen enemy, unarmed porters carrying packs guarded by three armed men, walked into 1 Platoon's heavy claymore ambush on the main track and were hit by nine claymores and rifle fire; four were killed, two blood trails led away, and four ran down the track into 2 Platoon's ambush. Across both ambushes seven enemy were killed and three wounded, and an ID card indicated the presence of the D2014 infiltration group.

Eight enemy in black carrying weapons and packs ran into a section of 12 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, holding a firm base. One Australian died of a head wound. Three enemy were killed, and one or two AK-47s were captured.

Four enemy fleeing 1 Platoon's ambush ran down the track into 2 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR. The sentry's first pair of claymores failed, but the second pair went off, and machine-gun and rifle fire followed; two enemy were killed at once and a wounded man was killed in the follow-up, while another escaped leaving a blood trail. Two AK-47s were captured.

7 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR, had only just reached its ambush position when two enemy were seen and killed. As the platoon began digging in, two more enemy travelling well behind heard the digging and turned to escape, but one was shot dead.

6 Platoon, B Company, 4 RAR, following a well-used enemy track, heard noises ahead, and the forward section commander and a scout went forward and saw two enemy sitting on a pit edge and one in a hammock. They opened fire and were fired on by two heavy machine-guns, one of which the forward section silenced, and then about ten AK-47s opened up from well-hidden bunkers further back. The platoon pulled back and artillery hit the bunkers, but the enemy were still there when it returned, and again the next afternoon after an air strike failed to come; only on the following day had they gone. Two enemy were killed and one wounded; there were no Australian casualties.

3 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR, had been in ambush for many hours on a heavily used north-south trail when three enemy came cautiously along it. The claymores and two machine-guns were fired, killing all three, and three AK-47s and documents were captured; the documents identified 3 Battalion, 84A Rocket Regiment. Both machine-guns jammed from dirt thrown up by the claymores, showing the need to keep linked ammunition clean. Artillery was then adjusted onto the area around the ambush.

7 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, searching for camps after its earlier contact, swept unsupported into a bunker complex and was pinned down at 20 m by intense automatic and sniper fire from an estimated enemy company. Two Australians were killed and five wounded; the fire was too heavy to recover the bodies, and the platoon was extracted under helicopter gunship fire at 50 m, the enemy being too close for artillery. The company, also under sniper fire, killed one enemy. A medical evacuation helicopter was hit and had to withdraw, and after gunships directed by the battalion commander suppressed the fire, all casualties were evacuated from another winch point. The camp was then hit by artillery, mortars and two air strikes.

4 Platoon, B Company, 3 RAR, harboured north of the Firestone Trail, had six claymores covering 200 m of the trail, with a three-man killing party on duty. When 80 or more enemy began filing past, the party fired the claymores, one of which failed, and withdrew to the rest of the platoon, and artillery was brought down around the killing ground. A sweep next morning found two bodies and eleven drag marks, and rocket rounds, a grenade and a pack were captured.

A Company, 1 RAR, was ambushed while crossing a creek by two or three enemy who opened up with claymores and AK-47s at 30 m; 1 Platoon, already across, could not help because of thick bamboo. Five Australians were wounded by shrapnel, one of whom died two days later. 102 Field Battery shelled the area, and a sweep found a covered bunker.

Four enemy, one with an RPD machine-gun, fired on the leading elements of 11 Platoon, D Company, 3 RAR. The platoon returned fire; one enemy was possibly killed and drag marks showed at least one wounded, and the enemy withdrew north. One Australian was shot in the head and later died of his wounds. Packs, ammunition, rice, a transistor radio, clothing and cooking utensils were captured.

3 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, ambushed three or four enemy at 5 m with a claymore, machine-gun and grenades; they did not fire back. Two bodies were seen on the track and the moaning of wounded was heard, and two bodies were found in the morning sweep. Two AK-47s, 1000 feet of cable, a field telephone and grenades were captured.

Four enemy with webbing and packs walked into a cut-off group of 7 Platoon, C Company, 1 RAR, which opened fire at 30 m with its machine-gun, and fired again a few minutes later at noises. A sweep found one body and a blood trail, and the wounded enemy tried to escape and was shot dead. An M1 carbine was captured.

A Company, 3 RAR, was in harbour, and two sentries of 2 Platoon on a track to the north fired on a Viet Cong. When the body was checked, they found that a second enemy following close behind had also been killed. Two AK-47s, webbing and packs were captured.

5 Platoon, B Company, 3 RAR, in ambush on the south side of the Firestone Trail, fired claymores and a machine-gun on a bunched group of three enemy, part of an estimated five, and then grenades at movement heading west. A sweep next morning found two dead and the tracks of one who had crawled and then run west. An AK-47, three packs and documents were captured.

2 Platoon, A Company, 3 RAR, in ambush on a track 400 m from the company base, shot dead an enemy soldier, and ten minutes later was attacked by at least an enemy platoon with rocket-propelled grenades and at least three machine-guns; accurate rocket fire into a machine-gun position killed two Australians, and the enemy seemed to be enveloping the platoon. Under artillery fire, 1 Platoon came up to cover the right flank and withdrawal and was drawn into the fight, and with helicopter gunships firing very accurately the platoons withdrew to the company base. The enemy then tried to envelop the company; casualties were evacuated, a second gunship team was called in, and the company broke contact and withdrew. Two Australians died of wounds and six were wounded, mostly by rocket-propelled grenades; seven enemy were killed and up to nine more possibly killed.

The machine-gunner of 1 Platoon, A Company, 3 RAR, covering a track into the company position, watched an enemy group approach to 15 m and then opened fire along it, hitting two; the rest went to ground and briefly fired back. One body and several heavy blood trails were found; the record gives two to three enemy killed. An AK-47 and an RPG-7 round were captured, and one Australian was wounded.

Two sentries of 1 Platoon, A Company, 3 RAR, watching the approaches to the company position, let three enemy come to 10 m and then each fired a magazine, hitting two. They then pulled back so the machine-gun could fire on the area. A later search found three dead enemy, and an AK-47 was captured.

2 Platoon, A Company, 3 RAR, was setting up an ambush on a track when three enemy came down it. The first turned, saw the half-prepared position and was shot dead; the other two left the track and fired back, and the platoon advanced by fire and movement and killed them. Two AK-47s, a pack and webbing were captured.

11 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR, reached a small creek and sent a section 100 m ahead to reconnoitre; it found a squad-sized bunker camp held by about six enemy and had to open fire before the rest of the platoon could close up. The platoon swept the system and followed several blood trails; two enemy were killed and one wounded, and an SKS rifle, medical supplies and documents were captured. The rest withdrew north.

11 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR, found fresh footprints on an east-west track and harboured across it with its machine-guns pointing up it. When movement was seen, the machine-gunner opened fire, killing two of five enemy, and his number two threw a grenade. An AK-47 and an SKS were captured, and the rest withdrew south-west.

A section of 12 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR, sent along a track to pick up fresh tracks, had its forward scout killed by a single shot. The platoon swept the area and called in artillery, and found signs of four enemy.

11 Platoon, D Company, 1 RAR, moving with company headquarters, heard voices and chopping and sent a reconnaissance party forward. It was seen, so it rushed the enemy in their camp, killing one and badly wounding another, who later died. A Browning automatic rifle, a Chinese rifle, two transistor radios, a sewing machine and documents were captured, and 18 bunkers were found in the area.

After its earlier contact, 2 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, found it was on the edge of a large camp, and the company commander sent 1 and 3 Platoons round the left flank to move in. 1 Platoon saw a claymore just before it exploded, wounding two Australians. After artillery fire it moved forward again and was pinned down by heavy fire; the platoon commander and a section commander were killed and another soldier was shot in the shoulder. 3 Platoon was ordered forward to 1 Platoon; the rest of the account is cut off. Two enemy were recorded killed and one wounded.

2 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR, moving west through sparse bush, was ambushed from dense cover 15 to 30 m away by enemy with about ten weapons, including a machine-gun, firing heavily and low. One New Zealander was killed and three wounded, two by gunshots and one slightly by shrapnel from artillery fire. The forward scout shot one enemy; artillery was brought in and a section swept the area, but the enemy had withdrawn. An enemy camp was found nearby.

2 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, following a well-worn track, surprised about 15 enemy hastily preparing an ambush and opened fire, killing one and badly wounding another. One Australian was shot in the head and later died, and another was wounded in the arm. The enemy withdrew to a bunker complex of about 30 bunkers, around two years old, which A Company then attacked; women's and children's clothing was found there.

Up to five enemy approached 7 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR, along a track; two were killed and the platoon swept west down the track. Meanwhile another enemy approached the perimeter from the east and was shot by a sentry. Artillery was adjusted onto the first group's escape route. Two AK-47s, an M1 carbine, magazines, webbing and grenades were captured.

A sentry of 8 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR, investigating a track, fired on three enemy moving quickly down it, joined by the machine-gun, wounding one in the shoulder. A section sweeping forward came under fire and killed one enemy and possibly another whose body could not be recovered, and after fire from the left another was killed. About 15 North Vietnamese packs were seen on the track and the enemy could be heard organising an attack, so the platoon went into all-round defence and called in close artillery. Eight packs and two AK-47s were captured.

1 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, moving into an ambush position, saw five enemy in green uniforms with packs 150 m away and fired at once. Two were killed and one left a heavy blood trail; an M16, a pistol and three packs were captured.

3 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR, was circling an enemy camp of five, only one armed, preparing to attack, when one called out and walked towards the leading soldiers. The machine-gunner shot him dead and hit the two behind, and the camp was fired on; a tracker dog team followed a heavy blood trail and found another body. Two enemy were killed and one wounded, and an AK-47 or SKS, grenades and two packs were captured.

A sentry on a track in front of 7 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR's position waited until approaching enemy were within 20 m and fired, killing one; the rest went to ground. A section sweep met and killed another. An AK-47 and an M1 carbine were captured, and artillery fired into the area.

During a sweep, 3 Platoon, A Company, 9 RAR, came under fire from an unknown number of enemy in a large bunker system using heavy and light machine-guns, rocket-propelled grenades and claymore mines. The contact lasted three and a half hours and drew in 2 Platoon. It was broken off at last light after small arms, artillery, mortars, helicopter gunships and air strikes were used. Ten enemy were killed; one Australian was killed and six were wounded and evacuated.

1 Troop, B Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, and B Company, 4 RAR, were fired on by enemy in bunkers and attacked them, meeting rocket-propelled grenades, machine-guns and claymore mines, with air strikes and helicopter gunships in support. Two Australians of B Company were killed and eight wounded, five from the tanks, mostly by rocket-propelled grenades, and three from B Company, mostly by claymores. One tank was seriously damaged by four or five rocket-propelled grenades. W Company joined B Company, both withdrew to let 155mm artillery hit the bunkers, and the force needed an ammunition resupply. Six enemy were recorded killed.

D Company, 9 RAR, moving west, ran into a large bunker system of 21 bunkers held by enemy soon reinforced to squad size or more. 11 Platoon was fired on and hit by rocket-propelled grenades, and 12 Platoon, sweeping to the south, was held up by fire from bunkers; when a medical evacuation helicopter hovered, the enemy opened up with a heavy machine-gun, rockets and rifles and drove it off. The company withdrew with its casualties, one Australian killed and five wounded, and the camp was hit by artillery, air strikes and gunships; the company found it abandoned the next day, and four enemy bodies were found two days later. The company commander warned against manoeuvring near a suspected bunker system before the ground is carefully examined, noted that the enemy waits quietly for its best chance such as a hovering medical evacuation helicopter, and advised against being drawn into a bunker fight without heavy artillery, air and tank support. He also noted that in dense bush the enemy's rocket-propelled grenade worked better than the Australian M72 light anti-tank weapon, whose fuse set off on foliage.

2 Platoon, A Company, 1 RAR, moving parallel to a track, had its second section hit by two claymores fired by about six enemy near a bunker system, and the leading and rear sections came under rifle fire. The company quickly reinforced the platoon and brought artillery onto the bunkers, and the casualties were moved to a winch point for helicopter evacuation. One Australian was killed and nine or ten wounded, including a gunner and engineers attached to the battalion. The company secured the camp, but the enemy had left; claymores, a 105 mm shell rigged with a tripwire, rice and medical supplies were recovered.

8 Platoon, C Company, 9 RAR, had just entered a re-entrant when it saw and fired on an enemy soldier, and came under rifle and rocket-propelled grenade fire from a bunker system held by what was thought to be at least an enemy platoon. The company commander swung 9 Platoon round to the north and used artillery to block the south; pushing down from the north, 9 Platoon also came under fire and then withdrew so the bunkers could be shelled. Over the five-hour battle five Australians were wounded and six enemy were killed; the enemy's fire was well controlled and aimed about a metre above the ground. Helicopter gunships covered the disengagement, the area was hit by artillery and mortars, and the bunkers were destroyed the next day after the enemy had gone; packs lost in the fighting were recovered.

A Company, 9 RAR, was packing up its claymores to leave its night position on a track when an unknown number of enemy fired three rocket-propelled grenades and AK-47s at it from the north. One grenade landed among a section of 2 Platoon gathered for orders, killing three Australians and wounding five. The platoon returned some fire and artillery and gunships were called in; the enemy withdrew with unknown losses. The lesson drawn was not to stand around in groups.

W Company, 4 RAR, had been led by the SAS into a major enemy infiltration area and set an ambush in a triangle on a main track; the enemy seem to have thought they were attacking an SAS patrol. The platoons detected movement and fired their claymore mines, and part of an enemy company replied with heavy automatic fire and at least ten rocket-propelled grenades, some of which burst in the trees. The company fired back at the muzzle flashes, supported by an AC-47 gunship and US and Australian artillery, and the enemy withdrew. Three New Zealanders were wounded by shrapnel, two lightly. The enemy removed their dead, but the next morning pools of blood, blood trails and drag marks showed heavy losses; one of the machine-guns had broken during the fight.

10 Platoon, D Company, 9 RAR, moving with two sections forward to clear higher ground, saw two enemy about 75 m on, and the left section fired on them. Two groups of enemy replied with automatic and rocket-propelled grenade fire from bunkers. Five Australians were wounded and evacuated; the record also lists five enemy wounded. The rest of the account is cut off.

While elements of A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, with A Company, 5 RAR, were escorting a convoy of US trucks up Route 15 in Bien Hoa province, two trucks hit mines 50 metres apart. Accounts differ: one records ten Australians and two Americans wounded, with ten more Australians wounded who stayed on duty; another records seven Australians and one American wounded and one troop-carrying vehicle damaged.

W Company, 4 RAR, was covering the approaches to Long Binh and standing to when a 1 Platoon machine-gun saw enemy movement and opened fire. Claymores were fired and the enemy made several attacks with infantry and rocket-propelled grenades, while closely coordinated artillery and mortars fired near the company and an AC-47 gunship attacked the withdrawal routes. At first light six enemy bodies were found, five in the arc of that first machine-gun, with nine drag marks, and rifles, seven rocket-propelled grenade launchers, 43 grenades and plastic explosive were captured. Five New Zealanders were lightly wounded by shrapnel.

11 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, ran into a platoon of enemy in a bunker system and, spread out along the objective, found every part of the platoon under fire at once, leaving the commander no reserve. It was hit by claymore mines, heavy small-arms fire and rocket-propelled grenades, which killed one man and wounded seven; two Australians were killed in all. 12 Platoon, helicopter gunships and air strikes joined in, and after four hours 11 Platoon disengaged and carried out its wounded. Artillery did not contribute effectively. A Company later found graves with four recently killed bodies, believed to be from this contact.

D Company, 9 RAR, reported rockets being fired from about 600 metres away over half an hour. Artillery and the mortar platoon replied, and afterwards yelling and people running about were heard. The next morning a party from the mortar platoon and 10 Platoon found seven enemy dead, six makeshift rocket launchers and nine rockets. On 5 March eight more bodies, some partly buried, and another rocket were found nearby, making 15 enemy killed.

4 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, set an ambush on a track with more than six claymore mines. When a party of 20 to 30 enemy, spaced eight to ten metres apart behind a scout 20 metres ahead, was in the killing zone, the claymores and machine-guns fired. The enemy took the full blast but fired back briefly; artillery was fired on their likely retreat route. At first light four bodies and many blood trails were found, and an AK-47, a map case, radios, batteries, rice, documents and medical supplies were captured.

2 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, following a track, heard that D Company was in a big contact 500 metres north and, guessing the track led there, formed an ambush. Seven North Vietnamese came down the track and were fired on by the machine-guns, killing two. The enemy fired back with AK-47s and a grenade launcher, wounding two Australians with shrapnel; the platoon attacked and wounded two more enemy, and they withdrew north. Two AK-47s were captured.

9 Platoon, C Company, 9 RAR, went by armoured personnel carrier to check an enemy camp spotted by a Possum aircraft, dismounted and advanced after the apparently deserted camp was shelled. Just past a creek the forward scout fired on the enemy and a firefight began; taking automatic fire from three sides, the platoon withdrew uphill under more shelling, and the enemy, who took casualties, stopped at the creek line. The platoon sergeant noted the enemy were well trained and gave no spoken orders, that panic was the platoon's greatest danger, and that withdrawals had not been practised enough. Artillery and an air strike hit the bunker system; the sweep next day found one enemy dead, six bunkers, mortar rounds, a rocket and an AK-47, though four enemy are recorded killed.

The leading section of 9 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, moving to high ground, saw five enemy grouped round a hammock and a bunker. The two other sections were deployed to the flanks and the platoon attacked through the bunker system, where 10 to 12 main-force enemy were seen; caught by surprise, the enemy were driven out and withdrew north-north-east. Three enemy were killed, possibly, and one or two wounded, and an AK-47 and two rocket-propelled grenade rounds were captured. There were no Australian casualties.

Three Australians of the 4 RAR Mobile Advisory Team and 22 Vietnamese of 1 Platoon, 612 Regional Force Company, laid an ambush in paddy fields 150 metres from the tree line of Dat Do. Within 15 minutes the enemy opened fire from the trees with machine-guns, automatic weapons and B40 rockets, killing the leader of the rear protection squad and pinning the patrol behind the paddy banks. As the platoon withdrew two more Vietnamese were killed, and an Australian corporal was killed by a machine-gun burst while the Australians sheltered behind a bank. The enemy advanced until mortar fire from 4 RAR at the Horseshoe stopped them, and they retreated leaving one dead. The platoon had ambushed regularly from this spot and the enemy had come to know its movements; the Australians thought the mortars would have driven the enemy off with fewer casualties had the Vietnamese not withdrawn.

12 Platoon, D Company, 9 RAR, found a latrine and was fired on by what proved to be an enemy platoon in a bunker system with a 200-metre front, well-cut fire lanes and snipers, using small arms, automatic weapons, a claymore mine and rocket-propelled grenades. With helicopter gunships in support, the platoon withdrew by fire and movement after 45 minutes, and artillery and mortars hit the bunkers. Seven Australians were wounded, three of whom were evacuated and one of whom died; one was slightly hit by spent shrapnel from Australian artillery. The rest of D Company joined the platoon and by evening had cleared 25 bunkers with grenades; one enemy sniper was shot and fell from a tree. It was noted that the enemy's fire seemed to follow the platoon's machine-guns, which should be moved during a long contact.

The Anti-Tank Platoon, Support Company, 4 RAR, in ambush, fired claymore mines and machine-guns at movement, using hand-held flares, artillery illumination and mortars. Moaning and movement were heard again later and the area was hit with grenades and machine-gun fire. A sweep at first light found seven bodies, two blood trails and a drag mark, and six AK-47s were captured.

2 Section, 2 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, in ambush, fired on two enemy groups totalling about 20 moving south to north, with 161 Field Battery in support. Six enemy were killed and five wounded, and the rest withdrew south-east.
