Enemy approaching 11 Platoon, D Company, 9 RAR, from the south-east were seen by a sentry, but they heard the platoon talking as it adjusted mortar fire and fired rocket-propelled grenades and machine-guns into platoon headquarters. Fire was returned, with an AC-47 gunship and helicopter gunships in support, and enemy movement continued near the night position for over two hours. One enemy was killed. Four Australians were evacuated, three with gunshot wounds and one in severe shock, and three more were wounded by grenade splinters but stayed on duty.

1 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR, counted eight enemy into its ambush and fired its claymore mines and machine-gun. The enemy replied with AK-47 fire and grenades from both sides until machine-guns and grenades silenced them. Two enemy were found dead and three blood trails, and an AK-47, a pistol, packs, a radio and many documents and photographs were captured. Three New Zealanders were slightly wounded by grenade fragments. Artillery fired on escape routes; one bank of seven claymores failed to fire.

12 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR, heard chopping and found an occupied enemy base. 12 Platoon formed a fire base while 10 Platoon swept into the camp, but it was pinned down by at least a squad of enemy in bunkers firing AK-47s and at least one light machine-gun. 10 Platoon withdrew and both platoons left to deal with its casualties, recorded as three or five wounded. Artillery fired and the enemy left overnight.

1 and 2 Platoons, A Company, 9 RAR, each fired on enemy who fled, and 2 Platoon, sweeping on, came under fire and found signs it was on the edge of a camp. A Company concentrated and searched for the camp in force, meeting AK-47 fire from bunkers; one Australian was lightly wounded and another seriously wounded with a gunshot to the head and urgently evacuated. With helicopter gunships and mortars in support, the company had cleared 20 bunkers by evening; the enemy was of platoon strength, and one was possibly killed and one wounded. After the company withdrew, field and medium artillery hit the area.

3 Platoon, W Company, 4 RAR, again made contact with the enemy in the same bunker system as that morning. One enemy was possibly killed and three New Zealanders were wounded, one of whom was evacuated. The bunkers were shelled and then bombed.
10 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, set off an enemy booby trap. Four Australians were wounded; two were evacuated by helicopter and two stayed on duty.

While operating with 9 RAR in swampy ground, an armoured personnel carrier of 1 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, hit an anti-tank mine made from a 155mm shell with added explosive, 40 to 50 pounds in all. The carrier was badly damaged and four Australians, two of them engineers, were wounded and evacuated, one with a compound fracture of the ankle and one with a severe back injury.

1 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, was ambushing a raised footpath from a patch of jungle when three enemy entered the killing zone. The machine-gunner sprang the ambush, killing the leading man, and the other two doubled back but were killed by the left flank. A claymore was fired in case anyone was lingering behind, and grenade-launcher rounds were fired at a suspected hide during the sweep. An AK-47, a pistol and two grenades were captured.
1 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, set off a mine. Three Australians were wounded and evacuated by helicopter.

8 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, was in ambush between a clearing and a track when an enemy soldier dressed in black came along the track and was killed by the rear protection party; his body, rifle, ammunition and documents were recovered. Between two and five enemy were involved. The platoon commander noted that the Viet Cong tended to move on tracks.

D Company headquarters, 5 RAR, had set up a base beside a clearing when it was hit by four rifle-launched anti-tank grenades. It returned fire with a machine-gun and rifles. One Australian was slightly wounded. The enemy were estimated at four, though another report gives 10 to 15; there were no known enemy casualties.

A standing patrol of the B Company headquarters support section, 9 RAR, fired on two enemy approaching along a track, killing one and capturing an AK-47 and binoculars. The other fired a burst and retreated.

3 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, moving in single file along an old, partly destroyed road through marshy ground, was fired on with AK-47s at the edge of a clearing. The machine-gun failed after one burst, but the platoon closed up, and when the enemy fired a rocket-propelled grenade that revealed their position, all weapons including grenade launchers and a light anti-tank weapon were turned on it. A fire started on the platoon's flank; artillery and three helicopter gunships hit the target accurately, and under this cover the platoon advanced 200 metres across the clearing, but the enemy had gone. One enemy is recorded wounded.

1 and 2 Platoons, V Company, 4 RAR, were in separate ambushes when enemy probing 1 Platoon threw a grenade, setting off the ambush. Of 8 to 10 enemy, three were killed in front of 1 Platoon; the enemy tried several times to recover the bodies, then fled towards 2 Platoon, whose claymores wounded and captured one man from headquarters, 274 Viet Cong Regiment. Three AK-47s, four packs and grenade-launcher rounds were captured, and artillery fired on the retreat routes.

Three enemy saw and heard a party of 8 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR, go out for a resupply, thought the area was clear, and walked into the ambush of one of the platoon's sections, which killed all three. An AK-47, a grenade launcher and a rocket-propelled grenade launcher were captured.

11 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR, was setting an ambush when four enemy approached and were hit by claymore mines and rifle fire. Those not caught in the ambush fired back with AK-47s as they withdrew west. Two enemy were killed, and an AK-47, a rocket-propelled grenade launcher and two rounds were captured.

Two enemy set off a trip flare in the perimeter of 7 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR, and were hit with claymore mines and rifle fire. Moaning was heard and the area was fired on again with rifles and a grenade launcher. One enemy was killed and there was a blood trail; a US-type rifle was captured.

Nine enemy advanced on a broad front into an ambush of 3 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR, but saw a sentry, and the firefight began before the claymores could be fired. One North Vietnamese soldier was killed, and an AK-47, a pack, webbing and documents including a paybook and a certificate with the unit number 2009 were captured.
An enemy soldier walked into an ambush of 2 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR, and was killed. A grenade and a transistor radio were captured.
An enemy soldier entered an ambush of 10 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR, as the sentries were changing, and was killed. A rifle was captured.

7 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR, supported by tanks of 2 Troop, B Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, fired on six enemy standing among houses, who returned fire; tank T22 fired on two enemy moving north-east. The result is not known. During the sweep two civilians were detained in a house where stores were found.

10 Platoon, D Company, 6 RAR, had been in ambush for two days in thick bamboo beside a plantation track in the Courtenay rubber when about 60 enemy, a porter party, a stretcher party and a protection party, walked into it. The claymores were fired when most were in the killing ground, followed by three machine-guns and rifles; the enemy fired a few wild shots and withdrew south and west. The sweep found 22 enemy dead and many blood trails, and captured six AK-47s, a rocket-propelled grenade launcher, 26 grenades, small arms, documents and medical supplies. Five of the 11 claymores failed because of faulty detonators, but the platoon's daily cleaning of its machine-gun ammunition paid off, as none of the three guns stopped. Mortars fired in support.

After spotting an enemy sentry sheltering under a plastic cape in heavy rain, 6 Platoon and half of 5 Platoon, B Company, 6 RAR, attacked what was thought to be a small camp, surprising and killing the sentry. The camp proved to be a large bunker system, and the enemy counter-attacked; the rest of the company was fed in, with artillery, helicopter gunships and an AC-47 gunship in support. After taking ten casualties, seven of them serious, the company was ordered to withdraw, made difficult by heavy rain and eight to ten enemy snipers in trees; two of 6 Platoon's machine-guns failed and it lost all its packs. Radio communications were poor, and the artillery forward observer was the only link to battalion. The enemy left overnight; a search of the camp found nine enemy dead.

A section of 2 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR, sent to ambush a trail, heard four enemy nearby, and the company commander attacked with 1 and 2 Platoons while 3 Platoon held a firm base. The leading platoons found they were in a bunker system and, though they fired first, were soon under fire from all sides by automatic weapons, rifles and rifle grenades. They took three bunkers before disengaging and withdrawing to base, firing a claymore to discourage pursuit; the system turned out to have 19 bunkers. The company sergeant was wounded in the knee and evacuated, and two others had minor phosphorus burns and stayed on duty. It was the company's first contact; six enemy are recorded killed.

About 15 to 20 enemy entered an ambush of D Company headquarters, 6 RAR, which fired two claymore mines. Two enemy were probably killed and an unknown number wounded, though six killed and two wounded are recorded in all.

1 Platoon, V Company, 6 RAR, in ambush on a track, saw about 200 enemy moving along the bush line carrying 20 to 25 stretcher cases; when a Possum aircraft flew over, the column split, some running forward and others back into the bush. The platoon opened fire at extreme range, and helicopter gunships, three teams over an hour, attacked the enemy under the platoon's direction; the enemy regrouped and fired on the platoon, but did not attack. A two-platoon sweep with 3 Platoon then killed three enemy and found many blood trails and much equipment, including mortar and heavy machine-gun sights, packs, ammunition and documents identifying heavy weapons companies of 33 North Vietnamese Regiment. Seven more enemy were recorded killed and 11 wounded by artillery. The platoon commander was annoyed that the Possum aircraft alerted the enemy, and the company commander argued that artillery would have been quicker than gunships.

Two enemy walked into the killing ground of a half-platoon ambush of 6 Platoon, B Company, 6 RAR, and a third looked at the bush hiding the machine-gun. The No 2 on the gun asked the gunner what to do; the enemy heard him and fired as the machine-gun opened up on the first two. The gunner was killed and his No 2 wounded. The enemy retreated as the rest of the killing group joined in; one lay dead in the killing ground, two were found dead 50 metres down the track, and the fourth left a blood trail. An AK-47 was captured and artillery fired in support.

2 Platoon, V Company, 6 RAR, was in ambush where a small track met a larger one when about ten enemy came along the small track; at ten metres claymores were fired and all weapons opened up, and the enemy fired back. The enemy then probed the platoon's flanks; artillery illumination revealed several groups, which were hit with claymores and rifles, and an AC-47 gunship fired once it found the platoon by a strobe light placed on the track, until bad weather forced it away. Artillery was brought within 80 metres, and the enemy crowded close to escape it; the platoon switched its machine-guns between prepared positions to confuse the enemy and suggest a larger force. The attacks stopped around midnight, and a sweep next day found four bodies; three AK-47s, a pistol and documents were captured. Several claymores failed because their detonators blew holes in them.

3 Platoon, W Company, 6 RAR, approaching the crest of a ridge, heard voices, and two Viet Cong who came down the track were shot. This set off a heavy volume of fire from an enemy force of platoon strength or more, with automatic weapons, rocket-propelled grenades, light machine-guns and a 12.7mm heavy machine-gun, and the enemy began to counter-attack from their bunkers around the platoon's flanks. Australian and US helicopter gunships, artillery and mortars supported the platoon, and after about two hours it disengaged successfully. One enemy was killed and one possibly wounded; during a sweep of the area one New Zealander was killed.

2 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, had settled and was preparing a patrol to check enemy tracks when 12 to 15 enemy came along a track; at 50 metres they were alerted by the patrol's movement, and the machine-gunner opened fire, joined by part of the patrol. Grenade launchers were used to lob rounds onto the enemy, which proved effective, and artillery fired a cut-off. A sweep found three bodies and two blood trails, and an M16 was recovered.

11 Platoon and headquarters of D Company, 5 RAR, were sweeping down a very steep, rocky slope when company headquarters killed an enemy soldier at the bottom. Continuing the sweep, they were fired on with a rocket-propelled grenade that wounded two Australians in the right leg. One section gave covering fire while another assaulted the enemy, who fired more grenades, a claymore and small arms; the attack killed the grenadier and the area was secured. Two enemy were killed, and a rocket-propelled grenade launcher, rounds, grenades, a pack and documents were captured.

1 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, came under fire from a well-covered hill about 150 metres away and attacked uphill to root out the enemy. About ten enemy in a well-prepared position among caves hit the platoon with claymore mines, rocket-propelled grenades, grenades and rifles, pinning it down in low scrub close to their position. 3 Platoon was sent in to extricate it and itself came under extreme pressure; eventually, with the help of a flamethrower, 1 Platoon was brought out after a seven-hour battle. One Australian was killed and one wounded.

The machine-gunner of 1 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, in ambush, saw movement on the track and fired, as an enemy soldier fired an AK-47 at the ambush, grazing a soldier's head; a claymore killed that enemy. The enemy then tried to lure soldiers into a trap by loud moaning, to use rocket-propelled grenades against them, but a sweep found and killed the man before he could fire. Two enemy were killed and one wounded, and an AK-47, a rocket-propelled grenade launcher, rounds and a compass were recovered.

1 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, had reset its ambush after the earlier contact when about ten more enemy came down the track, and the sentry came back to alert the platoon. The first enemy stopped to look at remains from the last ambush and was killed by claymores, and the second was shot; the machine-gun fired up the track at the enemy milling there. Artillery and helicopter gunships fired on the escape routes, and two sections followed a clear blood trail for 450 metres. Two enemy were killed, possibly three, and one wounded; two carbines were recovered.

1 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, heard enemy voices down the track at dawn; the enemy stopped to eat and later moved into the ambush. Claymores and machine-guns killed the first two, and the third, not yet in the ambush, fled back down the track. An AK-47, a grenade and food were captured. The company commander said the platoon had at last learnt to let the enemy into the killing ground before firing.

The Anti-Tank (Tracker) Platoon, Support Company, 5 RAR, moving from its night ambush to pick up enemy tracks, heard voices and found enemy moving parallel to it. The forward section took up a fire base and opened fire at 20 metres as four or five enemy heard them; they fired back and ran off up the track. Two graves found in the area five days later were attributed to the platoon.

2 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, in the same ambush position as two days earlier, saw three enemy approaching; at 40 metres something alerted them, possibly the smell of blood from the previous contact, and at 30 metres they broke from the track. A claymore failed to fire, but the machine-gun killed one and wounded another. A rocket-propelled grenade was fired into the position, and artillery fired in support. A submachine-gun was captured. A person in a loincloth with his hands tied behind his back was also found.

Fire Support Base Thrust, headquarters of 9 RAR, was hit by 25 to 30 enemy mortar rounds while its guns were firing in support of friendly forces repelling an attack on Ap Lo Gom. The enemy mortars fired while the base's 105mm guns were firing, making them very hard to locate; a patrol found the mortar position the next day. One Australian was killed and six or seven wounded, two of whom stayed on duty.

An engineer vehicle set off two of a cluster of four M16 mines in Dat Do, wounding seven soldiers of the Assault Pioneer Platoon, Support Company, 9 RAR; six were evacuated. The road had been swept with mine detectors the day before and by bulldozers that morning, but the mines were missed. 10 Platoon, 30 metres away, went to help.

6 Platoon, B Company, 9 RAR, had found an enemy camp and a seven-man engineer team from 1 Field Squadron was checking a track into it when about four enemy, who had followed a patrol into the camp, ambushed them from behind an anthill and from trees with rocket-propelled grenades and small arms. Two engineers and two members of the platoon were wounded; one engineer died of his wounds. The platoon and an armoured personnel carrier swept the area; one enemy was wounded and the enemy withdrew west.

After 1 Platoon's contact 800 metres away, 2 Platoon, A Company, 9 RAR, was on full alert when ten enemy walked into its killing ground. Claymores were fired at the first three, who had bunched up, and at the rest, and the killer group opened heavy fire; the enemy did not fire back, though 60mm mortars supported them. Mortars and artillery fired on escape routes and lit the area through the night, and grenades were thrown at any movement. Despite this the enemy removed their dead and wounded, leaving drag marks and blood trails; the platoon thought it had killed three and wounded seven.

A small reconnaissance party 300 metres behind 12 Platoon, D Company, 9 RAR, heard eight enemy approaching and warned the platoon, which stood to. The enemy had seen an earlier ambush position nearby and were cautious; about 15 minutes later one suddenly appeared in front of a soldier, who hit him in the chest with a grenade-launcher round. The enemy returned fire with rifles and a grenade, wounding four Australians with shrapnel, and withdrew south. A blood trail was found and a rifle captured.

A patrol including local South Vietnamese troops working with B Company, 9 RAR, ambushed three or more enemy approaching from the south-west with claymores, machine-guns and rifles. Two were killed at once and a third screamed; the enemy returned little fire. Artillery and mortars fired illumination and high explosive on retreat routes, and the next morning a third body was found. Tracks showed the three were part of a group of about 24, and screams suggested more were wounded. A submachine-gun and two carbines were recovered.

A district office vehicle set off a cluster of M16 mines on the south-east edge of Dat Do, wounding Australians of 10 Platoon, D Company, 9 RAR, and one local civilian. Accounts differ on the number of Australians wounded, from two to four; two were evacuated with shrapnel wounds. The vehicle was slightly damaged.

An armoured personnel carrier of 2 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, ran over a 60 to 80-pound anti-tank mine on a jungle track west of Long My. The carrier was destroyed and its two crew were killed. The record notes the tracks had been used too often.

From late morning to evening, B and D Companies, 5 RAR, with tanks of B Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, armoured personnel carriers of B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, Duc Thanh district Regional and Popular Force troops, helicopter gunships and 105 Field Battery, fought an estimated 90 enemy in the village of Binh Ba. B Company, with tanks, formed a blocking position while the village was swept. At least 27 enemy were killed and two captured, with 43 killed and six wounded recorded in all. One Australian was killed and eight or more wounded, and two Centurion tanks were moderately damaged.

A company of 1 Battalion, 33 North Vietnamese Regiment, attacked Duc Trung and overwhelmed the local defence platoon, and B Company, 5 RAR, was sent to restore the situation. Artillery was brought down to within 20 metres of the houses and helicopter gunships attacked the north and west of the village, then B Company attacked from the south with a troop of tanks and armoured personnel carriers. The enemy were routed, and the Popular Force took over clearing the rest of the village to avoid civilian casualties. Forty enemy are recorded killed.

An enemy company was seen moving towards Binh Ba from the south-west. B and D Companies, 5 RAR, with a troop of tanks and a troop of armoured personnel carriers about 500 metres south of the town, opened fire, killing one and wounding six, going by blood trails.

An estimated enemy platoon entered Binh Ba from the north, where D Company, 5 RAR, with tanks and armoured personnel carriers, was operating, and fighting continued on and off until last light. By then the cumulative results at Binh Ba were 51 enemy killed and 11 captured.

D Company and a platoon of B Company, 5 RAR, with tanks, armoured personnel carriers and two engineer teams, began a new sweep of Binh Ba from west to east, with B Company cordoning the south and carriers and infantry the east. Three wounded enemy were captured and evacuated.

During the night a small party of enemy trying to escape from Binh Ba ran into the defences of 4 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, camped about 500 metres south-west of the village. Two Viet Cong were killed by a claymore and machine-gun.
An enemy squad tried to fight its way between 6 Platoon and B Company headquarters, 5 RAR, firing rocket-propelled grenades and a light machine-gun at 6 Platoon. The result is not known.

On the south edge of Dat Do, a soldier of D Company, 5 RAR, stepped on an M16 mine that leapt two metres and exploded among 12 Platoon and company headquarters. Three Australians were killed, one of whom died of wounds, and 20 to 24 were wounded. Another M16 mine, laid in the previous two or three days, was found nearby. The district chief had been told three days earlier that D Company would be operating there.

C Company, 5 RAR, found a bunker system containing anti-vehicle mines, a claymore and a command-detonated 105mm mine on the south-east edge of the Long Hai hills. That night 7 Platoon hit an M16 mine, and another went off while the wounded were being moved; a third was found nearby. Three Australians were killed and 14 wounded, one of them an engineer.

After its ambush and evacuating its wounded, the combined force of ten Australians from 3 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, and 55 South Vietnamese soldiers was moving to a new ambush site when a platoon of main-force Viet Cong attacked it with heavy AK-47, grenade-launcher and rocket-propelled grenade fire from all directions. Poor communications delayed artillery until a Possum aircraft relayed the requests, and the enemy then closed in to avoid the shells, but two teams of helicopter gunships fired to within 25 metres of the force and the enemy withdrew. Seven South Vietnamese were wounded by rocket-propelled grenades. Two enemy were killed and possibly six more, going by many blood trails.

Five Australians of 3 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, an American and 53 South Vietnamese of 3 Company, 2/52 ARVN Battalion, moving south-east, killed two enemy in a fighting pit at the edge of a bunker system that a much larger enemy force was just entering with its wounded. The enemy at once counter-attacked, recovering the bodies and hitting the force with intense AK-47 and rocket-propelled grenade fire, and tried to slip round its left flank but were driven back into the artillery fire. The artillery then lifted for helicopter gunships, which attacked at close range, and the enemy broke up and retreated in small groups. Two enemy were killed and six possibly killed. One South Vietnamese soldier was killed and five wounded.

A patrol of 3 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, with South Vietnamese troops of 2/52 ARVN Battalion, made contact with an estimated enemy platoon, supported by Australian and US helicopter gunships. Seven Vietnamese were slightly wounded and not evacuated. Eight enemy were possibly killed.

9 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, with 11 men of company headquarters, set an ambush on a well-used track below a slight rise, with machine-guns covering the killing ground from each side, claymores in front and on the flanks, and weapon pits dug. Enemy came along the track using a torch, and when they entered the killing ground three claymores were fired, followed by the machine-guns and riflemen; artillery fired a cut-off and protected the flanks. The next morning five bodies were found, and a wounded man said before dying that his squad had numbered 14; drag marks showed at least two more wounded. Carbines, rifles, grenades, ammunition, 12 packs, a radio, documents and rice were recovered. The platoon commander noted that good flare illumination was essential, and that only two of five hand grenades and none of the grenade-launcher high-explosive rounds had gone off.

10 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, was attacked with small arms and rocket-propelled grenades by an estimated enemy squad. One Australian was killed and two wounded. Two to four enemy were killed, and rifles including an AK-47 and an M16 were captured. It seems the platoon had stayed in one place too long and the local force had spotted it.

A combined force of ten Australians from 3 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, and 55 South Vietnamese soldiers of 1 Company, 2/52 ARVN Battalion, ambushed a track. The South Vietnamese dropped the first two enemy coming from the east, but the enemy replied with AK-47s and rocket-propelled grenades, recovered the bodies and withdrew. Artillery was called in and a sweep found blood trails. One South Vietnamese soldier was killed and one wounded by a rocket-propelled grenade. The Australian advisers thought the South Vietnamese should have poured more fire into the area to keep the enemy off balance.

11 Platoon, D Company, 9 RAR, was clearing what it thought was an old, deserted enemy camp when a section leader and his forward scout moved 40 metres beyond the section and saw bunkers. The section leader called up the machine-gun but, without waiting for the rest of the section, threw a grenade into a bunker, drawing intense crossfire from an enemy force of at least 10, and possibly 20 to 30, strongly entrenched in hidden bunkers; he and the scout were both killed, and another man was wounded by rocket-propelled grenade and rifle fire. The section could not help because it was not properly deployed and did not know what its leader was doing, and the platoon withdrew. The camp, at least 75 by 175 metres and used for transit, was hit by RAAF helicopter gunships, mortars and artillery while the rest of D Company deployed to attack, but the enemy had withdrawn to the south-west. The platoon commander noted that the section leader had gone too far forward, out of sight of his machine-gun group, without deploying his section or telling his second-in-command.

As 10 Platoon, D Company, 9 RAR, withdrew from an ambush position, it was itself ambushed by six enemy with rocket-propelled grenades and machine-guns. It fired back with claymores and small arms, with artillery and mortars in support. One Australian was killed and one shot in the foot. The enemy withdrew into thick jungle and could not be followed. The company commander said the platoon had made too much noise, letting the enemy pinpoint it.

Two sentries of 6 Platoon, B Company, 9 RAR, saw three enemy approaching and went back to warn the platoon, which stood to. After 15 minutes with nothing happening, the platoon was preparing a clearing patrol when the enemy fired into the position, killing one Australian with an AK-47 shot to the chest, and withdrew at once. The platoon and company commanders said the enemy should never have got so close and the sentries should have fired on them, but the sentries had done what they were briefed to do.
2 Platoon, A Company, 9 RAR, in ambush, engaged one enemy approaching from the south and two from the north, killing one of the northern group. A later report also noted two blood trails.

An early-warning sentry of 4 Platoon, B Company, 9 RAR, in ambush, saw enemy moving down a track, and when their scout saw him he fired a claymore, wounding the scout. The other enemy fired back with AK-47s and a rocket-propelled grenade, grazing one Australian's arm with a bullet, and withdrew north; a sweep found a blood trail. The platoon commander complained that the killer group had not been lying ready when the enemy appeared.

2 Platoon, A Company, 9 RAR, was in ambush on a track when one or two enemy approached from the south and three from the north, and both groups were engaged. The southern group withdrew; the northern group lost one killed, and a weapon was captured. The record also notes another enemy killed and one wounded, shown by a blood trail.
A patrol of 5 Platoon, B Company, 9 RAR, saw five enemy and called down artillery on them.

1 Platoon, A Company, 9 RAR, in ambush, saw three enemy moving east who went behind a bamboo thicket. It fired a machine-gun and grenade launcher to try to drive them towards 3 Platoon, ambushing nearby, and artillery also fired. The result is not known.

3 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR, was clearing a harbour position about half a kilometre south-east of Hoi My when the platoon commander stepped out of the cleared area and set off an M16 mine. He was killed and 18 others were wounded, one of them a sapper. 750 pounds of rice in 15 drums were found.

B Company, 6 RAR, planned a three-platoon attack on a bunker system, but 5 Platoon was delayed by an earlier contact, so 6 Platoon ambushed the track out of the camp while 4 Platoon attacked. Twenty metres from the camp, 4 Platoon's right flank was hit by rocket-propelled grenades, a light machine-gun and about ten automatic rifles, and five men were wounded, one seriously. The support section sent to help swung too far right, but 4 Platoon's other sections moved up, killing two enemy, and 5 Platoon pushed through the south of the camp; by then the enemy had withdrawn, and two more enemy dead and a large amount of equipment, including rocket launchers, were found. The company concluded that a bunker system could be taken by fire and movement, provided a thorough reconnaissance had first found the enemy's size, positions and escape routes.

An M16 mine went off in 2 Platoon, W Company, 6 RAR, about 100 metres west of Lo Gom, killing one New Zealander and wounding five, two of whom later died of their wounds. The mine was on a track the platoon had used earlier while looking for an ambush position; the enemy had seen them and laid mines where they expected the New Zealanders to go.

While clearing up after the earlier mine explosion near Hoi My, the battalion's medical officer set off another M16 mine, killing one Australian and wounding five more, among them the medical officer and the battalion commander.
3 Platoon, V Company, 6 RAR, set off a booby trap made of an M26 grenade and a 60mm mortar shell, laid by South Vietnamese Regional Forces. One New Zealander was killed and five were wounded.

An M16 mine went off in 1 Platoon, W Company, 6 RAR's ambush position at the eastern edge of Phuoc Loi while the ambush claymore mines were being checked. One New Zealander was killed, another died of wounds and two were wounded, and a mine detector was damaged. The area had been swept for mines that afternoon, so the mine had been laid since.
Engineers with V Company, 6 RAR, prodding for mines in the northern Long Hai hills, set off an M16 mine. Two sappers were killed and one wounded.

2 Platoon, V Company, 6 RAR, ambushed six to ten enemy moving south, firing claymore mines and then section weapons. Two enemy died at once and the rest fired back; movement was fired on until dawn, and two more enemy were killed during the sweep at first light, making four killed and one wounded. Weapons, packs, documents and a large quantity of food were captured.

12 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, was in two half-platoon groups 70 metres apart when an enemy force moved north along the track through the southern group towards the northern one. The northern group opened fire when the leading enemy were in its killing ground, and the southern group fired on those still passing; 45 enemy had been counted and more were still coming. The enemy withdrew hastily east and south-east without firing back, dragging away bodies and helping wounded, and were fired on whenever they were heard; helicopter gunships, artillery and mortars covered the area, and at first light a sweep found seven enemy dead, possibly five more, and signs of nine wounded. One Australian was wounded in the head by a grenade fragment but stayed on duty, and weapons, ammunition, food and documents were captured.

After a briefing by a prisoner, 3 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR's anti-tank platoon, called in artillery and attacked a bunker system held by an estimated enemy company, on a broad front with two sections forward to stop being outflanked. The attack pinned the forward enemy in their bunkers, but machine-guns on the flanks and snipers in trees pinned the platoon down, and the undergrowth was too thick for grenades; a helicopter gunship could not fire closer than 50 metres because the vegetation hid the battlefield. The platoon broke contact and the area was hit by artillery, gunships and air strikes with napalm, rockets and 250-pound bombs. Seven enemy were killed by the platoon and four blood trails found; two Australians were wounded, one of them evacuated.

After 9 Platoon's contact, C Company, 5 RAR, concentrated to reconnoitre the bunker system and called artillery onto the camp, but one shell fell short and wounded three Australians of 7 and 8 Platoons; this is recorded as friendly fire. Helicopter gunships covered their medical evacuation, and when enemy following a reconnaissance party tried to interfere with it, three were seen to fall; a strong blood trail led away, and a grave was found next day. Early next morning, after more shelling and gunship fire, C Company swept through three new bunker systems of 8, 24 and 7 bunkers, occupied by a regular enemy unit, and took the camp without casualties.

Two hours after its first contact at the edge of a bunker system, 7 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, tried to attack a flank of the system, covered by helicopter gunships, but met 20 to 30 enemy who at once opened intense fire with rocket-propelled grenades, machine-guns and automatic rifles. One Australian was killed and two wounded, one of whom was evacuated while the other stayed on duty, and the platoon withdrew to its company base. Three enemy graves were later reported found, and a body was found by a 5 RAR platoon nearly two weeks later.

4 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, followed a telephone cable to a bunker system and reached the first bunkers unseen, but when the first occupied bunker was grenaded the enemy opened fire with rocket-propelled grenades and automatic rifles. The leading section was pinned down and took casualties, and the platoon medic was also wounded; the record shows five Australians wounded, all by rocket-propelled grenades. Anti-armour rockets were fired into other bunkers, and a helicopter gunship covered the platoon's withdrawal, with 105 Field Battery in support.

At dawn the enemy returned against 5 Platoon and B Company headquarters, 5 RAR, from the same direction as the night before, firing rifles, rocket-propelled grenades and a machine-gun into the position. The company fired back, and cries and dragging noises were heard before the enemy withdrew after about five minutes towards their suspected bunker system. Three enemy were killed and three possibly killed, and two Australians were wounded; a sweep recovered weapons, grenades, rockets, ammunition and medical supplies. 105 Field Battery supported the contact.

The anti-tank (tracker) platoon of Support Company, 5 RAR, was leading a search along a track, followed by 3 Platoon, and had stopped to rest its tracker dog when one section moved 20 metres forward to check a branch of the track. It met six enemy moving along the track, and an enemy light machine-gun opened fire on the section; the record's account ends there. One Australian was recorded wounded and two enemy killed and two wounded.

5 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, trying to enter a bunker system after an air strike, met at least two enemy. The record shows four Australians wounded, one carried out on a stretcher with shrapnel wounds to the back and stomach, and others possibly wounded but staying on duty. The result is not known, and more gunship and air strikes were ordered; a gunship in the same area was thought to have killed two enemy.

A Company, 9 RAR, ambushed a large enemy group of 50 to 60 at night. 1 Platoon let five leading enemy pass, and they were followed by a group of 20 and then another of 30; 2 Platoon, 200 metres away, let the vanguard through and ambushed the group of 20. Artillery was then called down on the larger group and a Spooky gunship aircraft fired on the enemy. Reports vary on the result, from three possibly killed and six wounded, shown by blood trails, up to six killed and six wounded; 100 pounds of rice were recovered.

A patrol of 2 Platoon, A Company, 9 RAR, came under fire at five metres from an estimated 60 enemy in a bunker complex more than 200 metres deep; the forward scout was killed and a man trying to reach him was wounded. 1 and 3 Platoons came up in support, backed by artillery, including 161 Field Battery, and helicopter gunships, but the enemy replied with intense fire: five aircraft were fired on, a helicopter was shot down, and a gunship and a medical evacuation helicopter were hit. The record shows one Australian killed and three wounded, the wounded being helicopter crew; enemy casualties were thought minimal, and they withdrew overnight.

The rear protection group of 8 Platoon, C Company, 9 RAR, in ambush, engaged five enemy in blue shirts and shorts who were following small groups of civilians returning to Thai Thien. Two enemy were killed, and a sweep found three blood trails. The record shows one Australian wounded.

8 Platoon, C Company, 9 RAR, with a section of armoured personnel carriers, let several groups of civilians returning to Thai Thien pass along an ox track, then ambushed with claymore mines a party of four enemy trying to slip by with the last group. A second group of six enemy, 40 metres behind, opened fire on the platoon, and the enemy withdrew by fire and movement. One enemy was killed and three blood trails found; one Australian was shot in the upper body and evacuated by helicopter.

3 Platoon, A Company, 9 RAR, on the fringe of a large enemy camp complex, ambushed the forward scout of an enemy party and killed him. The rest of the party counter-attacked the ambush's flank with rifles and rocket-propelled grenades, and one Australian was killed by a gunshot to the head. An AK47, a rocket launcher and two rockets were captured.

5 Platoon, B Company, 9 RAR, was moving section by section from the scrub line onto the open Firestone Trail to set an ambush when the last section saw five enemy on the track. The rest of the platoon, taking them for the last section, waved them in and the wave was returned; then the last section opened fire at 70 metres and the platoon joined in. The enemy, thought to be part of a force of 30 or more, fired back; two were killed and one wounded, but failing light and strong enemy fire prevented a sweep. 161 Field Battery fired in support.
6 Platoon, B Company, 9 RAR, fired a bank of claymore mines on three enemy moving north, killing all three. Three automatic rifles and several grenades were captured.

A sentry of 10 Platoon, D Company, 9 RAR, near two rice caches, fired two claymore mines at one Viet Cong and a third, which misfired, at a second. Two were killed, and the body of a third was found the next day; AK47s, magazines and webbing were captured. The caches held 350 and 650 pounds of rice, and four more bags were found later; 161 Field Battery fired in support.

6 Platoon, B Company, 6 RAR, made contact with three Viet Cong moving south-east and killed all three. Automatic rifles and a compass were captured, and two Australians were wounded and evacuated; 101 Field Battery fired in support.

2 Platoon, V Company, 6 RAR, in ambush, made contact with 12 or more main-force enemy carrying cooking pots and rice. Four were killed, and two AK47s, 350 rounds, four packs, 100 pounds of rice and North Vietnamese webbing were captured; 101 Field Battery fired in support.

The scout of 10 Platoon, D Company, 6 RAR, smelt smoke on a track just as the enemy opened fire from a bunker system with rifles, automatic weapons and rocket-propelled grenades. Before artillery could be used, a rocket-propelled grenade fired down the track wounded four men of the leading section, which was pulled back through the rest of the platoon; the platoon broke contact and rejoined the company. The bunkers were hit by an air strike and artillery, including 101 Field Battery, and the company then cleared the area, finding 38 bunkers.
3 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR, made contact with an unknown number of enemy. One Australian was killed and two wounded and evacuated; enemy casualties are not known.

2 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR, was preparing to attack a bunker system when an enemy soldier stepped out of a bunker and was shot dead. The platoon attacked and drew fire from three or four enemy, who quickly fled, leaving one trapped in a bunker; he was wounded and captured. Two Australians were slightly wounded by grenades the enemy threw back, and 101 Field Battery shelled the area to the south to cut off the fleeing enemy; an AK47 and an Australian compass were recovered.

The forward scout of 1 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR, leading along a well-used track, saw four or more enemy crossing a crest 40 metres ahead and opened fire, quickly joined by the machine-gun. The enemy went to ground and disappeared over the crest, and when the platoon attacked, they had gone, leaving traces of blood. Two graves found some days later were attributed to this contact, and 101 Field Battery fired in support.

A sentry of a 6 RAR patrol, recorded as 6 Platoon, B Company, saw six Viet Cong and opened fire, killing two. Two AK47s, rocket-propelled grenade rounds, claymore mines and grenades were captured, and 161 Field Battery fired in support.

11 Platoon, D Company, 6 RAR, following an active track, found an extensive, occupied bunker system; it withdrew, leaving a section in ambush on the track. Two hours later two enemy came along and were killed by claymore mine and machine-gun fire, and an AK47, a rocket launcher and ammunition were recovered. The company then moved into the bunkers, found no sign of the enemy, and recovered much other equipment.

12 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, found enemy in a bunker system and was eventually seen, then opened fire at 40 to 50 metres and drove the enemy out. An air strike, helicopter gunships, and medium and field artillery were brought down with great accuracy on their withdrawal routes. Two enemy were killed, and two heavy blood trails were found.

7 Section of 6 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, moving along a track, made contact with six to eight enemy, and the platoon followed up quickly to stop them removing bodies. Two enemy were killed and two wounded, shown by blood trails and drag marks, and an AK47 and magazines were captured. The company commander noted the machine-gun fire had been good and low, while the enemy fired high.

9 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, in ambush, made contact with five enemy moving from the north, including a woman carrying a radio. Two were killed and possibly a third, and two AK47s and a quantity of stores and equipment were captured; 105 Field Battery fired in support.

12 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, reached a creek, smelt smoke, and saw five Viet Cong in a camp across it. The enemy spotted the forward section as it deployed, and the section opened fire; the enemy fired back for about 15 minutes, then withdrew under artillery, helicopter gunship and air attack. The platoon swept and secured the camp; two enemy were recorded killed and one wounded.

A section of 9 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, was in ambush when the left-flank sentry heard voices, saw enemy, gave the warning and took his position. As the leading enemy reached the right-hand man he turned and saw the machine-gun; the gunner opened fire, two claymore mines killed the leader, and rifle fire killed the second man and wounded the third. A fourth man, out of sight, fired three rounds well overhead and withdrew with the wounded man, probably helped by a woman, as a female voice and small footprints were noted; the machine-gun stopped after 75 rounds. Three enemy were killed in all, the third found nearby having died of wounds, and two AK47s were captured.

7 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, moving into the area of an enemy camp, found a track and saw what looked like a red flag, and began moving a section round the left flank; the record's account breaks off there. One enemy was recorded killed and one Australian wounded.

The anti-tank (tracker) platoon, Support Company, 5 RAR, dropped off by armoured personnel carriers half an hour earlier, sent a reconnaissance patrol along a very fresh track; 50 metres on it saw five enemy 20 metres ahead and opened fire, possibly killing two, but came under fire from the left flank. As the patrol withdrew to the platoon, the enemy fired from the north, hitting a sentry as he came into the perimeter; he was evacuated by helicopter under gunship cover. Carriers brought up mortars, which shelled the area, and a Viet Cong staging camp was found 150 metres west.
A trip flare went off at 10 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR's position and shots were exchanged. Two Australians were wounded.

Men of 6 RAR's mortar platoon and D Company, with the South Vietnamese 3/52 Battalion, set off an M16 mine near houses north of Lo Gom. Two Australians were killed, an engineer and a D Company soldier, and six wounded, two of whom stayed on duty.

An armoured personnel carrier of 1 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, sweeping past a bunker complex with D Company, 6 RAR, was ambushed by about three enemy, and two rocket-propelled grenades both hit it, causing serious damage and casualties. One Australian was killed and three wounded, one of whom died three weeks later.

1 Platoon, V Company, 6 RAR, bypassed a Viet Cong sentry to make an immediate assault on a camp of seven or more enemy, the medical group of D445 Battalion, with a large central hut, a sandbagged bunker and sleeping places for 12. One enemy was killed, and drag marks and blood trails led north to the river; medical documents, supplies, a carbine, a pistol, food and clothing were captured. One New Zealander was wounded in the leg by shrapnel and evacuated by helicopter; 101 Field Battery fired in support.

1 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR, had secured a third of a local Viet Cong base camp beside a fast-flowing creek when three or four enemy approached and were fired on at 25 metres. A two-section sweep found and killed a wounded enemy and a heavy drag mark. The camp stretched 150 metres along the creek, with 19 huts and 19 bunkers, and held weapons, 1100 pounds of rice, food, ammunition, detonators, documents, clothing for 20 people, bedding, medical supplies, tools and other equipment.

A patrol of 1 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR, following fresh footprints to a creek, was getting water when it heard splashing and saw two local-force enemy, one in swimming trunks, wading up the creek. The machine-gun fired when the first was 20 metres away; the second, further back, was knocked over backwards and crawled away up a gully. The patrol was too small to check the enemy casualties and returned to the platoon base; one enemy was recorded killed and one wounded, and artillery fired in support.

A reconnaissance patrol of 6 Platoon, B Company, 6 RAR, sighted four Viet Cong with AK47s in a camp and called the platoon forward. The enemy saw the patrol, but it pushed forward, killing one; the rest fled.
A sentry of 6 Platoon, B Company, 6 RAR, saw two local-force enemy crossing a clearing outside the harbour position and fired; they ran, and a sweep found one dead. Two rifle grenades were captured.
1 Platoon, V Company, 6 RAR, made contact with a female Viet Cong and killed her.

C Company, 5 RAR, was being carried by armoured personnel carriers of 2 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, when soldiers riding on top of a carrier saw three enemy and opened fire. The full firepower of two carrier sections and two platoons was brought to bear on about ten enemy hiding in a grassy swamp, who returned inaccurate fire; the platoons swept round the flanks and rear while the carriers held the front, and artillery cut off escape routes. Six enemy were killed, two wounded and one captured, and weapons, documents, ammunition and packs were taken; an enemy soldier who surrendered next day said he had seen eight bodies, and 9 Platoon found four more. The company commander said all carrier sections needed to be on the company radio net, and praised the usefulness of high-explosive and white phosphorus rifle grenades.

4 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, on a fighting patrol, heard noises and found a bunker system 35 metres away, then waited on a footpad leading into it for about two hours. When 12 enemy came down the track, two machine-guns and rifles opened fire; the enemy replied with about 12 rocket-propelled grenades, automatic rifles and possibly 60mm mortars, and the platoon fired a large number of rifle grenades that punched through the bamboo into bunker openings, killing five enemy within 20 metres. Artillery cut off the south, helicopter gunships hit the whole complex and an air strike followed; one enemy was captured wounded, and two Australians had minor shrapnel wounds. The platoon commander commented that it was better to ambush the likely exits of a bunker system than attack it, and that the quick follow-up threw the enemy into complete confusion.

The forward scout of 5 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, saw a bunker and two enemy and opened fire, and heavy fire came back. The platoon fanned out to find the flank of the bunker system but was itself outflanked, and its weapons could not suppress the enemy fire, so it called for artillery and held on until tanks of B Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, and armoured personnel carriers of 3 Cavalry Regiment arrived. As they did, the enemy who could get away did so, at least 24 of them, and the rest were destroyed by tank and carrier fire or crushed in their bunkers. In the two-hour battle six enemy were killed, two by the infantry and four by the armour, and one Australian was killed; the record notes the artillery had little effect but the tanks destroyed the enemy.

3 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, was in ambush when three or more enemy in camouflage clothing, carrying rocket launchers, were heard pushing through the scrub into its rear. The rear machine-gun had a double-feed stoppage after one round, and a claymore mine failed to fire because of a faulty firing device; the enemy fired three rocket-propelled grenades and withdrew east. Eight Australians were wounded, four of them evacuated by helicopter and the rest staying on duty, and a pack of clothing, food and documents was recovered.

6 Platoon, B Company, 5 RAR, was ambushing inside an enemy bunker system when two enemy, followed by a larger group, came to get water from the well. The sentry fired a claymore mine, blowing down the first two, and the machine-gun fired on the rest; a sweep was then fired on with rocket-propelled grenades and automatic rifles, and two Australians were wounded by rocket fragments. The enemy also fired on a helicopter gunship and on the platoon with a light machine-gun, which was silenced by machine-gun and rifle-grenade fire. Intelligence concluded four enemy were killed, one wounded and one killed from the air; a grave with three bodies was found the next day.

South Vietnamese Regional Forces with B Company, 5 RAR, and tanks of 1 Armoured Regiment attacked six bunkers held by 15 main-force enemy and were pinned down by fire from east and west, suffering four casualties. Armoured personnel carriers, tanks and helicopter gunships came to help, and when the enemy tried to withdraw they were caught in the open and the Regional Forces killed four.

9 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, searching for bunkers, was fired on by well-concealed enemy and advanced 25 to 30 metres by fire and movement to the edge of a system of 20 bunkers; one soldier had a minor shrapnel wound but kept going. A section leader moving to grenade a sentry bunker was shot twice and killed, and sniper fire pinned down the leading sections; the platoon sergeant was shot in the leg trying to recover his body. Artillery and helicopter gunships were used to get the platoon out, and a tank troop was sent, delayed when the troop commander's tank bogged, but the enemy slipped away; one blood trail was found. The platoon commander said rifle grenades worked well despite the thick vegetation, though trees easily deflected them.

2 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, was ambushing a junction of two fire trails, with its main body and a cut-off group, each with two machine-guns, 75 metres apart. A machine-gunner's number two in the cut-off group turned to see enemy three metres away following the group's tracks; they had not noticed it, but heard the gun being moved and ran back. No one could fire for fear of hitting the main group, until a section second-in-command grabbed his machine-gun, chased them 30 metres and hit the last two, while the platoon commander swung the main group round to fire as well. A sweep found two bodies and a closer search next day found two more; an AK47, an M1 rifle and a pistol were captured, and 105 Field Battery fired to cut off escape.

An armoured personnel carrier of 2 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, moving from fire support base Picton to Discovery just north of Thua Tich, hit an anti-tank mine of 30 to 60 pounds of explosive, which set off two more. The carrier was heavily damaged; a crewman and a passenger, a sapper, were killed, and a crewman and another passenger, also a sapper, were injured. During the medical evacuation the helicopter landed on another mine, which damaged it and injured another soldier.

3 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR, following up its earlier contact with an enemy sentry post, saw and fired on movement; the forward section deployed and was hit by claymore mines, rocket-propelled grenades and light machine-gun fire. The forward scout and the platoon commander were killed and the section commander wounded, and the rest of the platoon, under the platoon sergeant, used fire and movement to recover them, supported by artillery, mortars and air strikes, including napalm on an adjacent camp. The medical evacuation helicopter drew ground fire; the enemy camp was not entered, and at last light signal shots suggested the enemy had broken contact and withdrawn. An enemy body, killed by mortar fire, was found four days later.

The forward scout of 12 Platoon, D Company, 6 RAR, saw what looked like bunkers and called up his section leader, who was engaged by rifle and rocket-propelled grenade fire from two or three Viet Cong as he came forward. One Australian was shot dead and another wounded by rocket fragments; the platoon came up to support and the lead section withdrew. Two hours later another platoon attacked with rifle grenades and cleared the position, where the enemy had set a claymore mine behind them covering the track in. Steep slopes and gullies meant the artillery observer could not bring in supporting fire for 90 minutes.

1 Platoon, W Company, 6 RAR, ambushing the junction of two rivers, saw two local-force enemy; the sentry waited until they were midstream and opened fire, hitting both. The machine-gun swept the bank of the Suoi Luc, and artillery and grenade launchers fired; two AK47s were captured. Two enemy were killed, and a third body found later by the anti-tank platoon was credited to this contact.

11 Platoon, D Company, 6 RAR, had halted on a well-used track when the forward scout saw a Viet Cong approaching and shot him dead; papers showed he was a corporal, and his AK47, webbing and first aid kit were captured. A grenade launcher round fired during the contact hit heavy foliage nearby and exploded, wounding two of the platoon's own men.

The forward scout of 11 Platoon, D Company, 6 RAR, signalled bunkers ahead, and the enemy opened fire with AK47s and rolled grenades down the slope, wounding two Australians. The platoon fired back at two Viet Cong in a bunker, the sentry group of a large base complex, and called artillery and air strikes onto the bunker and several caves; the complex was captured the next day after an air strike. Rifle grenades again proved very useful in the difficult ground, and the air strikes landed 100 metres off target from the platoon's smoke marker.

3 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR, searching a gully, got between enemy sentries and their camp; a Viet Cong sentry set off a claymore mine early from within the camp, wounding the section leader. The forward section deployed and killed one of the sentries as they tried to withdraw, capturing an SKS rifle, and the rest of the enemy withdrew, followed up by the platoon. US artillery at fire support base Picton fired in support.

The scout and a section leader of 5 Platoon, B Company, 6 RAR, leaving a firm base, saw two of three Viet Cong and opened fire; the enemy fired back with AK47s. A sweep found two wounded North Vietnamese, and a medical evacuation helicopter was called, but they were so badly wounded that they died before it arrived. Two packs of clothing were captured, and an old camp of 16 weapon pits was found nearby.

D Company, 8 RAR, found 30 to 40 well-trained enemy occupying six bunkers; 10 Platoon was first fired on by two enemy in a well-built trench, and an engineer was wounded. Supported by 11 Platoon, 10 Platoon assaulted the bunkers for 2 hours 40 minutes, putting one out of action and beating off a counter-attack; one soldier was shot dead in the chest while trying to recover the wounded man and another was grazed on the head. Helicopter gunships and artillery supported, and at dusk the company withdrew with its dead soldier and his weapon; it returned next day with tanks, but the enemy had gone, leaving one dead and an AK47. At least one enemy was killed and one wounded, though losses were probably higher.

1 Platoon, A Company, 8 RAR, was in a harbour and ambush position on a track, still arming its claymore mines, when two enemy appeared. The machine-gun sentry opened fire, and the second enemy fired a rocket-propelled grenade at the belt-feeder kneeling beside the gun, seriously wounding him; others were also wounded. The record gives four or six Australians wounded, four of them evacuated; one enemy was thought wounded by the machine-gun. 161 Field Battery fired in support.

A section of 4 Platoon, B Company, 8 RAR, set an ambush at a T-junction on the edge of jungle and rubber, with trip flares on the roads covered by claymore mines. About ten enemy came along the road at night, one hit a trip flare, and the sentry fired the claymores at once; the enemy fled 100 metres down the track and tended their wounded. Three were killed, one wounded and one possibly wounded, and four AK47s were captured. The platoon commander concluded claymores were very effective and should be aimed low.

11 Platoon, D Company, 8 RAR, was in a harbour and ambush position on an old overgrown track when an enemy with a torch was seen coming towards the gun group. The section second-in-command let the first man pass and the gun group engaged the six who followed, killing three; two AK47s and an M1 carbine were recovered, and there were no Australian casualties.

Four enemy approached a 9 Platoon, C Company, 8 RAR, ambush from the west; when two were close enough, the section leader opened fire with his rifle and the sentry with the machine-gun, at 30 and 10 metres. The others opened fire with a light machine-gun and a firefight followed before they withdrew south-west; a sweep found two enemy dead. An AK47, magazines, ammunition, packs of documents, rice, cooking gear, hammocks, clothing and medical supplies were recovered. The record also shows one Australian wounded; 161 Field Battery fired in support.

The tracker platoon of 8 RAR, in ambush, fired claymore mines and a machine-gun on about seven enemy who walked into the ambush area at night. For hours afterwards the enemy came back with torches, apparently looking for something; the ambush was reinforced by two sections of the assault pioneer platoon and a section of armoured personnel carriers, and when enemy approached from three sides they were met with heavy machine-gun, rocket and rifle fire. Movement round the position was engaged periodically until the early hours, and mortars, 161 Field Battery and US artillery fired on the escape routes. A sweep next morning found three blood trails; one enemy was recorded killed and two wounded.

12 Platoon, D Company, 8 RAR, had been ambushing for 24 hours and was about to cross a creek, covered by one section, when three enemy were heard coming down the creek; the section set an immediate ambush. All three Viet Cong, two men and a woman, were killed, and an AK47, an M2 carbine, a pistol, a map, documents, medals, food and a large picture of Ho Chi Minh were captured. 161 Field Battery fired in support.

Three North Vietnamese in blue shirts and green trousers walked into the rear protection group of 5 Platoon, B Company, 8 RAR's ambush and were engaged with a machine-gun and grenade launcher. Two were killed and one wounded, shown by a blood trail; three AK47s and a pack with magazines, food, an identity card, a diary and a birth certificate were captured.

2 Platoon and the headquarters of A Company, 5 RAR, in ambush, saw about 20 enemy approaching and waited until they were five metres from the machine-gun before firing claymore mines and the machine-gun. The Viet Cong returned heavy fire for about 20 minutes, with helicopter gunships and artillery supporting the Australians. A sweep found two enemy dead, drag marks from two more probably killed and four blood trails; one Australian was wounded and evacuated by helicopter. Two AK47s, a pistol, packs and documents were captured.

7 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, in ambush on a north-south track with ten claymore mines and machine-guns, hit seven or more enemy spread along 100 metres of the track. Six enemy were killed and one wounded; three AK47s, five packs and medical equipment were captured. One Australian was wounded by the backblast of a friendly grenade launcher. The enemy were thought to be part of the force from 8 Platoon's bunker contact that afternoon; mortars and 161 Field Battery fired in support.

The sentry of 7 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, ambushing a track, heard eight enemy approaching from the west, and a section engaged them; the enemy fired back with AK47s and a rocket launcher to get their wounded out. When the firing died down, a sweep went out and was fired on by wounded enemy, and three Australians were wounded and evacuated by helicopter before the sweep resumed. Two enemy were killed, one possibly killed and one wounded, and two AK47s were captured; artillery and helicopter gunships supported. The platoon commander said the Australian casualties should have been left until the sweep was finished, and noted that the three M16s used all had continual stoppages.

A standing patrol of 11 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, watching a north-south track engaged three to five enemy with its machine-gun. A sweep found two enemy dead, with an AK47, a rocket-propelled grenade launcher, rounds and grenades. One enemy had placed a grenade under his body as he died, which exploded when he was moved, wounding four Australians, who all stayed on duty.

8 Platoon, C Company, 5 RAR, stumbled on a bunker system held by about a platoon of enemy and fired on them as they ran for their bunkers. In a three-hour firefight the platoon was pinned down and called in artillery and mortars; helicopter gunships helped its sections pull back, and tanks of A Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, then attacked the bunkers, and the enemy withdrew in two groups. Five Australians were wounded by rifle and rocket-grenade fire, three of them evacuated; one enemy was wounded or possibly killed, and a machine-gun, pack, documents and equipment were captured. Some of the enemy were later ambushed by 7 Platoon.

A standing patrol of 12 Platoon, D Company, 5 RAR, watching a track, fired claymore mines and an M60 at six enemy, four in blue and two in khaki. The enemy did not fire back. A sweep found two bodies and two blood trails; two AK47s, rice, munitions and documents were captured, and a US artillery battery fired in support.

1 Platoon, A Company, 5 RAR, was ambushing a track intersection with only eight men and two machine-guns in place, the rest being 200 metres away collecting a resupply, when the machine-gun sentry saw three enemy with AK47s approaching and fired the claymore mines and opened fire. The first and third were killed; the second took much of a claymore blast but ran into the bush wounded. Two AK47s were captured, and 105 Field Battery fired in support.

8 Platoon and the headquarters of C Company, 5 RAR, were ambushing a main track when the rear machine-gunner saw enemy coming along a footpad behind the position and opened fire with others. The enemy fired back; one was killed and the others, up to two more, got away. One Australian was wounded by fragments when claymore mines shorted out and exploded. A carbine, packs, documents, food and equipment were captured.

6 Platoon, B Company, 6 RAR/NZ, ambushing a track junction, fired claymore mines at three enemy, who were knocked off their feet but escaped into the bush; later the machine-gun engaged two more enemy who appeared one after the other. Enemy then fired rocket-propelled grenades and rifles at the eastern flank, and the platoon fired back until the enemy withdrew when illumination was fired. Five Australians were wounded by rocket-grenade fragments and evacuated. An AK47, two RPG-7 launchers and three blood trails were found next day; the commanders agreed not enough fire had been used against the rocket-grenade teams.

Following blood trails from its earlier contact, 2 Platoon, W Company, 6 RAR, broke into a large clearing and saw six enemy dressed in black running down a track, and engaged them. An enemy soldier hidden in long grass opened fire from two metres, wounding one soldier, and the machine-gunner was wounded while changing a belt; another soldier loaded the gun and opened fire, killing that enemy. Two enemy were killed, two wounded and two AK47s captured; two New Zealand soldiers were wounded.

The forward scout of 3 Platoon, V Company, 6 RAR, moving east along a track, saw four enemy and opened fire, killing two, and the machine-gun killed two more and wounded one, out of a group of 11 or 12. Eleven packs and an M1 carbine were captured, and a complex bunker system was found nearby; 101 Field Battery fired in support.

1 Platoon, W Company, 6 RAR, made contact with three enemy, one of whom was wounded. A prisoner later said he and seven others had been trying to get into Ngai Giao village for food when they were hit; four were killed and he was wounded.

Half of 1 Platoon, W Company, 6 RAR, was in ambush when trip flares went off at each end of the position in turn, and both were engaged with claymore mines and machine-gun fire. Grenades were also thrown, and one thrown by the ambush commander appears to have struck something in the dark and bounced back, wounding four New Zealand soldiers. Two enemy were contacted with no result, and artillery fired in support.

3 Platoon, W Company, 6 RAR/NZ, moving in single file through thick bamboo, had found a freshly used track when four to six enemy crossed behind it and were seen by the rear section, which opened fire and killed one. Two more were killed in the sweep that followed. The rear section's machine-gun jammed when the gunner's sweat rag was caught in the belt and fed into the gun. An AK47, packs and documents were captured, and 101 Field Battery fired in support.

V Company, 6 RAR, had found six packs and halted while looking for their owners when a group of Viet Cong came along a track at the edge of the bamboo. Men of company headquarters engaged five to eight enemy at 15 to 20 metres, killing two and wounding one or two; a pistol, packs and ammunition were captured.
Continuing its morning contact, the assault pioneer platoon, Support Company, 6 RAR, killed two more North Vietnamese and wounded and captured another.

Near the Long Hai hills, the headquarters of C Company, 8 RAR, met three Viet Cong and captured one, who said about 40 enemy were in a nearby bunker system surrounded by anti-personnel mines. The company attacked with armoured personnel carriers of B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, and tanks of A Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment; a carrier was destroyed by two rocket-propelled grenades, and two Australians were killed and several wounded. After artillery and air strikes a second assault led by tanks fought through the bunkers, but was stopped by a deep creek and an anti-tank minefield and ordered to withdraw, coming under heavy fire again from enemy who had reoccupied the bunkers and suffering more wounded; in all 13 Australians were wounded. That evening tanks recovered the lost carrier's casualties, and 12 enemy were killed, mostly by tank canister and high-explosive rounds, with many blood trails found; the system, held by 30 to 40 enemy or perhaps a battalion, was struck by B52 bombers before 8 RAR returned two days later.

1 Platoon, A Company, 8 RAR, moving carefully through a known minefield south-east of the Long Hai hills with engineers clearing the way, had reached its ambush site when a member of the engineer team set off an M16 jumping mine while the platoon was gathered around its headquarters. Seven Australians were killed and 13 wounded (one account gives eight killed, probably including a man killed by a second mine soon after).

9 Platoon, C Company, 8 RAR, set a carefully planned ambush on a track north of the Long Hais, inserted by tanks that then made a diversion, with 15 claymore mines and close artillery and mortar support. An enemy force of about a company, some 100 or more in four groups, came through; the platoon let the first group pass and blew the claymores on the second and third, and the first and fourth groups counter-attacked. With the platoon running short of ammunition, tanks of 2 Troop, 1 Armoured Regiment, came out from Fire Support Base Isa within 40 minutes, cleared the killing ground and stayed all night, while mortars, several artillery batteries and helicopter gunships fired in support. Three Australians were wounded and evacuated; ten enemy were killed, including two in small contacts during the next morning's sweep, and 22 drag marks suggested many more killed or wounded. Weapons, grenades and documents were captured.

Following C Company's heavy contact, B Company, 8 RAR, was being rushed into blocking positions by armoured personnel carrier. 4 Platoon had just dismounted and was moving forward with the carriers when it came under heavy fire from a bunker position, and rocket-propelled grenades hit a carrier, wounding its two crew, and a tank. A sweep was stopped ten metres into the jungle when claymore-type wires were seen, and the platoon was pulled back. Eight Australians were wounded by the rocket-grenades; six enemy were recorded killed, and three bodies were later found.

11 Platoon, D Company, 8 RAR, was hit by rocket-propelled grenades from an unknown number of enemy. Seven Australians were wounded; two were evacuated by helicopter and five stayed on duty. Enemy casualties are unknown.

Armoured personnel carriers of 2 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, taking B Company, 8 RAR, to an ambush position, were ambushed on a jungle trail by a rocket-grenade team; two rockets pierced the leading carrier, wounding its two crew. The carriers drove off the enemy, who also fired AK47s, and 5 Platoon, nearby, swept the area without finding anything and secured a landing zone for the evacuation. The enemy had come from a bunker system not then known. A cache holding three bodies about a week old was later found by 10 Platoon, D Company, and credited to this contact.

6 Platoon, B Company, 8 RAR, and a section of armoured personnel carriers from 1 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, were in ambush on a fire trail when enemy ran through it. A carrier fired one machine-gun round and the claymore mines were fired at once, killing four enemy. Noises heard later were enemy carrying off three of the dead, whose bodies were afterwards found buried nearby. An AK47, webbing and letters were captured.
A mine, probably an M16, exploded among the headquarters of a platoon of A Company, 8 RAR, south-east of the Long Hai hills, killing one Australian and wounding two.

3 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR/NZ, searching for the D445 Battalion camp, found a well-used track and a poncho when both forward sections came under intense rocket-grenade, machine-gun, heavy machine-gun and rifle fire. The rest of the platoon helped them pull back, and nine Australians were wounded. The platoon withdrew 100 metres and artillery, mortars and helicopter gunships engaged the area, where C1 and C4 Companies and the headquarters of D445 Battalion were present; 2 Platoon then joined them. The commanders noted that dense undergrowth limited the use of rockets and grenade launchers, and that navigation errors made supporting fire less effective. Four enemy were recorded wounded.

D Company, 6 RAR/NZ, under command of 8 RAR, was moving in column with 10 Platoon leading when it found bunkers, and 10 Platoon was sent to check them. Five to ten enemy in the bunkers opened fire with AK47s and rocket-propelled grenades, and the company took heavy losses; artillery was called in and most of 12 Platoon came forward, and the combined fire of the two platoons suppressed the enemy, while company headquarters covered the rear and evacuated the wounded. 10 Platoon's right flank machine-gun had been malfunctioning. After two and a half hours the enemy withdrew along well-prepared routes; three Australians were killed and six wounded, one of them accidentally. The nine bunkers guarded the northern approach to a more important system 200 metres away, which 11 Platoon occupied with tanks; artillery support for that attack was delayed because the guns were busy with another mission.

2 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR/NZ, blocking south of the suspected D445 Battalion base, followed a recently used track until it heard coughing, talking and a radio, and pulled back undetected. When 3 Platoon ran into the enemy across the river, 2 Platoon moved to help, met four or five enemy leaving the river area, and came under rocket-grenade, heavy machine-gun and rifle fire from unseen bunkers. Artillery and helicopter gunships attacked the position, and the platoon was then ordered across the river to join 3 Platoon; the first attempt was driven back by fire and one soldier was wounded by rocket-grenade fragments, but the platoons joined up that evening. Six enemy were recorded wounded; 101 Field Battery fired in support.

In the first contact of an attack on the new base of D445 Battalion, 3 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR/NZ, moving to an ambush position, was fired on by a three-man sentry group with AK47s and rocket-propelled grenades, badly wounding the forward scout and wounding another man. Two sections swept round the left flank and found only rocket boosters; as the platoon reorganised, one enemy in a shell crater fired on the forward section, which killed him with rifle fire and a grenade. An AK47 was captured. The company commander said the platoon had been advancing too fast for the country.

4 Platoon, B Company, 6 RAR/NZ, moving along old armoured personnel carrier tracks in overgrown rubber, saw four or five enemy moving towards its left flank, and the platoon commander opened fire with the patrol. Two Viet Cong were killed and two wounded; the blood trails were followed with no further result. A large quantity of food, medical supplies and four packs were captured.

1 Platoon, W Company, 6 RAR/NZ, in ambush, engaged six Viet Cong at ten metres, two scouts preceding the main body by 20 metres. Two enemy were killed with no Australian casualties. An AK47 and six packs holding 200 pounds of rice, tobacco, sugar, tea and freshly laundered clothing were captured.

A section of Support Company, 6 RAR/NZ, was sweeping an area where an informant had said a political meeting would be held. A man and a woman were called on to halt, ran away, and were fired on; the woman was killed and the man wounded but escaped. The patrol also detained 26 people, one of them wounded and all but two without identity cards; all were released after questioning. The record lists this as a contact with civilians and notes the growing difficulty of telling Viet Cong from civilians working in the scrub.

Half of 3 Platoon, W Company, 6 RAR/NZ, was guarding a landing zone for a backload of stores when the sentry saw a Viet Cong soldier and fired, then noticed two more enemy closer than the first. An immediate follow-up killed one enemy, and a pack and documents were recovered.

A combined Australian and South Vietnamese platoon of 7 RAR from the Horseshoe made contact with six Viet Cong moving west. The record gives one Viet Cong killed in its detail, though three enemy were recorded killed. An M16 rifle, a pack with 20 kilos of rice and documents were captured, and three young boys acting as guides for the Viet Cong were detained; their questioning pointed to a possible camp for 27 Viet Cong, and a recently used resting area was found the next day.

3 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, harboured beside a landing zone it had cleared at the edge of a rubber plantation, covering a track with three claymore mines, a trip flare and an M60. At stand-to at dawn the trip flare went off, the claymores were fired and the machine-gun fired a burst. At first light two bodies were found, one near the claymores and one three metres from the M60; a carbine, two packs, rice and documents were captured.

2 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, had its leading troops across a track when 4 Section's leader saw an enemy running up it and opened fire, joined by his section; the machine-gunner fired at a second enemy running along the track.
