The section cleared the area by fire and movement, and the enemy did not fire back. The first body was found 30 metres along the track and the second 150 metres away at the end of a heavy blood trail; documents were captured.

7 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, in ambush, heard voices about 50 metres away, and a sentry who heard movement to his front found a claymore mine turned face down. Half an hour later the platoon fired a claymore and everything went quiet. One enemy was recorded killed.

An enemy soldier crawled towards the ambush position of 9 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR. A sentry went to investigate, thought it was a pig and knelt up, and was shot in the lower leg. The section's machine-gun returned fire.

A patrol from 7 RAR battalion headquarters fired two claymore mines and rifles at two or three enemy approaching its night position from the east at 25 to 50 metres. The enemy fired back and withdrew. One Australian was wounded by a fragment in the back.

The headquarters of A Company, 7 RAR, found signs of heavy enemy movement and followed them into a dry creek bed, where it began setting an ambush with a sentry covering a 60-metre approach. An enemy soldier came round the bend, sensed activity ahead and began to pull back, and the sentry opened fire, seriously wounding him. A sweep captured him, though not his four companions, along with a Chinese-made pistol, a transistor radio and documents including maps.

4 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, in ambush, saw a torch about 200 metres away, picked up one enemy in its night-vision scope and engaged him at 150 metres. Torches were seen again afterwards, and 106 Field Battery fired on the area while 101 Field Battery fired illumination. The result is not known.

The Anti-Tank Platoon of 6 RAR/NZ, 24 strong, sprang an ambush on the advance guard of a larger enemy party of 10 to 15, killing one. The enemy fell back and were attacked by D Company and 3 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, placed across their main escape route, and four more were killed. An AK50 rifle, eight packs, eating utensils and documents were captured.

1 Platoon, A Company, 6 RAR/NZ, made contact with 13 people, ten adults and three children, who were foraging for food; they withdrew north-west. Three were killed, recorded as Viet Cong, and there were no Australian casualties, though one Australian is shown as wounded in the casualty figures. Equipment and digging tools were recovered. The record lists this as a contact with civilians.

6 Platoon, B Company, 6 RAR/NZ, in ambush, engaged 10 to 20 main force enemy dressed in green and carrying weapons and packs. Three enemy were killed and two wounded; about 20 Viet Cong withdrew north and were attacked by helicopter gunships. An AK47, a pistol, a submachine-gun, two US compasses, a map, a radio and documents were captured, and 101 Field Battery fired in support.

Sentries of 9 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, let two enemy come close along a creek line before firing, but at least three more following behind fired back. After several magazines, one sentry left cover and knelt to get a better shot, and was hit in the chest; he died before he could be evacuated. Three blood trails were followed for 250 metres until the light failed; an AK47, ammunition, three packs holding 150 pounds of rice and documents were captured.

Elements of V Company headquarters and 3 Platoon, V Company, 6 RAR/NZ, made contact with three or more Viet Cong moving south-east at a bunker system. One Viet Cong and one New Zealand soldier were killed, and an SKS rifle was captured.

3 Platoon, W Company, 6 RAR/NZ, made contact with 12 Viet Cong moving south, killing one. A New Zealand soldier was wounded in the lip by a fragment but stayed on duty. A Garand rifle, two SKS rifles, a carbine and 12 packs were captured.

10 Platoon, D Company, 6 RAR/NZ, moving to a landing zone, saw four to six local force Viet Cong standing on a bunker 30 metres away, and the scout fired aimed shots through the scrub. The enemy withdrew into the bunker system; a Bushranger helicopter gunship gave close support as near as 50 metres ahead, and the platoon moved through the system. Two prisoners, a nurse and a cabinet maker, were taken from a bunker, along with two weapons and a large quantity of medical supplies; the two bunkers, huts and cookhouse were destroyed, and a grave about a day old was found. 101 Field Battery fired in support.
1 Platoon, W Company, 6 RAR/NZ, in ambush, opened fire on two enemy, killing one and wounding the other, who left a blood trail. An M14 rifle was captured, and 101 Field Battery fired in support.

1 Platoon, A Company, and the Reconnaissance Platoon, 7 RAR, were directed by an aircraft to an occupied bunker system 800 metres away and went in on armoured personnel carriers of 2 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, led by tanks of 3 Troop, A Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment. In the middle of the bunkers the two platoons attacked on either flank with the tanks in the centre, and met intense rifle and rocket-grenade fire; some bunkers were taken, but 1 Platoon took casualties and pulled back 75 metres, a rocket-grenade having killed a machine-gunner and wounded his number two and the forward scout. The Reconnaissance Platoon did not get the withdrawal order and fought on, losing four wounded, and a carrier hit by rockets was towed clear by another before the action was suspended. One Australian was killed and 12 wounded, four of whom stayed on duty; five Viet Cong were killed and three captured, and weapons and ammunition were taken.

To let 5 Platoon get clear and evacuate its wounded, a patrol from B Company headquarters, 7 RAR, went into a bunker system of 18 bunkers along the Song Rai and came under intense rifle and rocket-grenade fire for an hour, taking three casualties. A section of 4 Platoon and platoon headquarters then attacked the line of bunkers so the wounded could be evacuated, and also met intense fire; helicopter gunships fired to within 10 to 15 metres ahead of the troops. All troops were withdrawn and an air strike hit the bunkers; tanks could not get through the jungle before dark, and next morning the enemy had gone. One Australian later died of a head wound and five were wounded; four enemy bodies were later found and credited to this contact, and the company commander rated the grenade spigot a good answer to the RPG-2.

An armoured personnel carrier of 3 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, carrying troops of 5 Platoon, B Company, 8 RAR, on a track off Route 23, hit an anti-tank mine of about 40 pounds of Chinese-made explosive. The carrier was heavily damaged; one crewman was killed and ten others riding in it were wounded, one of them an engineer.

An ambush patrol of 9 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, saw 12 enemy, and through its night-vision scope the patrol leader counted more than 50 still coming. The ambush was sprung, and 12 to 15 enemy were seen to fall, but others carried them away as fast as they went down; the enemy fired back with many rocket-propelled grenades, machine-guns and rifles. Helicopter gunships, a Shadow gunship aircraft firing 28,000 rounds and flares, tanks and artillery supported the patrol. Eight enemy bodies were positively identified, including one found later, and one Australian was wounded by a rocket-grenade; an M16 rifle and a rocket round were captured.

7 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, after a 1,000-metre night move, was setting claymore mines for an ambush when a section leader's cover man moved towards a paddy bund and found seven enemy crouched behind it watching the platoon. He shot the first from one metre, and the gun groups and a recoilless rifle firing splintex rounds supported him as he and his section leader got back. The enemy returned rocket-grenade and AK47 fire, and an AK47 round hit a grenade mounted on a weapon, which exploded, killing one Australian and wounding four. Later an enemy seen trying to drag away a body was fired on; next morning no bodies remained, though two enemy were recorded killed and documents found showed elements of D445 Battalion. 101 and 161 Field Batteries fired in support.

A section of 1 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, had dropped 9 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, at an ambush position near Phuoc Hai and was returning through an established gap in the minefield when an armoured personnel carrier hit an anti-tank mine of 60 to 70 pounds of explosive in the swamp north of Lo Gom. The carrier was wrecked and an infantry officer killed; the two crew and four other members of the squadron thrown from the vehicle were wounded. A local Viet Cong had been watching the carriers deliver the platoon.

Following up the blood trail from its ambush the night before, in the sandhills south-west of Phuoc Hai, a patrol of 9 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, set off an M16 mine. Two Australians were killed, one died of wounds and one was wounded. The enemy had come back and laid the mine where he could be fairly sure an Australian follow-up would go.

Engineers of 1 Field Squadron and A Company, 6 RAR/NZ, in the jungle 7 kilometres south of Xuyen Moc, set off an M16 mine on a bullock track leading into a clearing, killing one Australian and wounding four. At least four men had walked over the mine before it went off, and a Viet Cong marker, a broken branch, pointed towards it; it had apparently been laid after 8 RAR left the area. The company commander believed the enemy had mined every track into the clearing, expecting it to be used as a landing zone, and warned that other obvious landing zones could be mined too.

3 Platoon, A Company, 8 RAR, moving to an ambush position, made contact when its leading section saw and fired on 40 to 50 Viet Cong armed with AK47s, rocket-propelled grenades, machine-guns and grenade launchers. The platoon formed a fire base; enemy parties attacked from both flanks and, using fire and movement, came within ten metres to recover their wounded and some dead. After an hour's fighting armoured personnel carriers of 3 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, arrived, and the enemy broke contact soon after. Six Australians were wounded by rocket-grenades and grenades; two Viet Cong were recorded killed and five wounded, with blood trails and drag marks leading south, and intelligence later claimed over 50 enemy killed. Artillery, aircraft, mortars and 161 Field Battery supported the platoon.

3 Platoon, A Company, 8 RAR, set its ambush in groups of four in a rectangle, and a party of about 15 Viet Cong moving in single file about seven metres apart walked into the south-west group. Machine-guns and M72 rockets opened fire, killing six in the first burst and a seventh as he tried to run. A rocket launcher, a grenade launcher, two SKS rifles and two M16s were captured; 106 Field Battery fired illumination.

After the Regional Force post at Ap Lo Voi was attacked by D445 Battalion, the retreating enemy walked into the ambush of the Assault Pioneer Platoon, Support Company, 8 RAR. They came in three groups; the first stopped and bunched in the killing ground to wait for the others, and when the second joined it, some 45 men in all, the ambush was sprung. The third group at once counter-attacked twice with rifles, rocket-propelled grenades and machine-guns and was held on both flanks, and the groups in the killing ground pulled out by fire and movement with accurate, heavy fire. Armoured personnel carriers of 3 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, came to spend the night with the platoon; two enemy were killed, and a sweep next morning found eight heavy blood trails and 14 drag marks. Two rifles, 100 phials of penicillin and clothing were captured, and US artillery probably fired cut-off fire.

3 Platoon, A Company, 8 RAR, was setting up an ambush in paddy fields when a sentry saw 15 enemy and shot one dead. The enemy, 30 to 40 in all, armed with AK47s, rocket-propelled grenades, machine-guns and grenade launchers, returned fire and tried to recover the body by fire and movement, then counter-attacked; armoured personnel carriers of 3 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, were sent to help, and a trooper was wounded by a fragment. The enemy withdrew in three parties towards Dat Do and the Long Hais, leaving the body and an AK47; next morning four blood trails and several drag marks were found, and intelligence later said seven enemy had been killed. The platoon fired all the ammunition it carried; 161 Field Battery fired in support.

3 Platoon, A Company, 8 RAR, had just occupied an ambush position when its sentries saw six enemy and opened fire, killing one. The rest took cover behind paddy bunds, fired back with rifles, a light machine-gun, grenade launcher and rocket-propelled grenades, and worked around to attack from three sides; one Australian was wounded by a grenade-launcher round. The enemy stayed until they had collected their casualties, then withdrew into the village; sweeps found one dead Viet Cong that night and drag marks next morning, and three Viet Cong were finally recorded killed and an AK47 captured. The platoon commander noted that the enemy moved during the period when ambushes were being occupied, and that the grenade was the most effective weapon in paddy fields; 107 Field Battery fired in support.

A half-platoon patrol of 1 Platoon, A Company, 8 RAR, in a triangular ambush in paddy fields, sprang its ambush after dark; the enemy fired back with AK47s, two rocket-propelled grenades and a rifle. Heavy rifle fire, M72 rockets and grenade launchers forced them to withdraw, the M72 proving most effective. An hour later an enemy automatic weapon opened up and was answered the same way; a sweep nearby killed one enemy, and a wider sweep by armoured personnel carriers later killed two more. Artillery fired in support.

9 Platoon, C Company, 8 RAR, ambushing a river crossing and water point, saw a group of about 20 Viet Cong with torches and lanterns approach along the far bank. When they seemed to be turning away, the two forward machine-gun groups and the command group opened fire; the enemy returned AK47 fire, killing one Australian and wounding another, and moved to outflank the ambush but did not cross the river and broke contact. Heavy drag marks showed where bodies had been removed; 161 Field Battery fired in support. Later a lone enemy carrying a lantern came within 50 metres and was fired on; he dropped the lantern and escaped.

5 Platoon, B Company, 8 RAR, ambushing from a dry rice paddy 300 metres south of Xa An Nhut, watched through a night-vision scope as 11 Viet Cong, spread over 200 metres, crossed its front at 150 metres. Claymore mines, two machine-guns and a 90mm recoilless rifle fired together; two enemy were seen to fall, and the rest fell back, firing for about three minutes, then stayed 20 minutes under heavy fire clearing their casualties. Armoured personnel carriers swept the area 30 minutes later with artillery and flareship illumination and a gunship overhead. Three enemy were recorded killed and two wounded; a sweep next morning found two blood trails.
8 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR/NZ, set off a claymore-type mine with a pressure or electric switch, possibly an M16 mine according to intelligence. Two Australians were killed and three wounded.

The forward scout of a patrol of 3 Platoon, W Company, 2 RAR/NZ, leading along a narrow path round a rocky bluff, set off a booby trap of two grenades tied to trees and joined by a trip wire. One New Zealand soldier was killed and one wounded. Bushranger helicopter gunships fired rockets and machine-guns into the area to the north.

A patrol of 3 Platoon, W Company, 2 RAR/NZ, smelled smoke and heard talking, and swept forward in line towards an enemy camp at the bottom of a steep, boulder-strewn re-entrant. One enemy came out, saw the patrol, and it opened fire and swept through the camp by fire and movement, killing one of about seven Viet Cong and wounding another. The enemy fired back with a rocket-propelled grenade, wounding one New Zealand soldier. An SKS rifle, a carbine, a pistol, seven packs, 140 pounds of rice, medical supplies and documents were captured; mortars, artillery and helicopter gunships fired in support.

9 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR/NZ, in ambush astride a track, saw two lights coming towards the machine-gun sentry, who waited until they were covered by the claymore mines and challenged them. They immediately tried to take cover, so he fired the claymores and opened fire. Two bodies were recovered, with an AK47, a carbine, two torches and documents. Mortars fired illumination and artillery fired cut-off fire in case a larger group was following.

A patrol from V Company headquarters, 2 RAR/NZ, saw and fired on one enemy, with possibly two others present, and the enemy fired back. One Viet Cong was possibly killed; drag marks led north-east, and another enemy was seen withdrawing west. 107 Field Battery probably fired in support.

5 Platoon, B Company, 2 RAR/NZ, harboured astride an old track, heard movement north of the perimeter. The claymore mines covering that side did not go off, and the M60 and rifles fired instead, with artillery north of the position. A sweep next morning found only footprints, showing that about ten enemy had been there.
3 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR/NZ, heard the noise of seven to ten people, and artillery fired on the area. The result is not known.

A base patrol from 104 Signal Squadron, under command of 2 RAR/NZ, saw two enemy and heard noises, and artillery fired on the area and again on what were possibly the same two further south. During its sweep the patrol was fired on and followed by the enemy, perhaps 7 to 20 of them, as it withdrew. 106 and 161 Field Batteries and a US battery fired in support.

Two sections and headquarters of 2 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR/NZ, investigating smoke, saw three enemy sitting around a fire near a bunker system, and the forward scout opened fire, wounding two. As the leading section pressed forward, the enemy set off a command-detonated 105mm shell, causing heavy casualties, and machine-gun and AK47 fire from the bunkers down prepared fire lanes hit more. Helicopter gunships suppressed the bunkers so the platoon could pull back, and artillery and mortars hit the camp; the platoon withdrew because of the danger of more mines, and the enemy, a force of nearly a platoon, withdrew north-east. One New Zealand soldier was killed, one died of wounds and five were wounded; three blood trails and two drag marks were found.

8 Platoon, C Company, 8 RAR, following a new track, saw two enemy near a bunker and killed one; heavy fire from two bunkers then pinned the forward section, wounding two men, who were taken back for evacuation. The enemy began to pull out but then reoccupied the bunkers and fired again, hitting two more, who were evacuated under cover of helicopter gunships while ammunition was flown in; the casualties were caused by a grenade, a rocket-grenade and AK47 fire. After holding the enemy for an hour, the platoon withdrew 800 metres for an artillery bombardment and joined a tank troop and an armoured personnel carrier troop, and the assault later that day met no resistance. One Australian was killed and three wounded; documents were captured, and 161 Field Battery and two US batteries fired in support.

An armoured personnel carrier of 2 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, carrying troops of 7 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, south-west of Long Phuoc Hai, hit an anti-tank mine of 80 to 100 pounds of explosive. The carrier was badly damaged; a soldier of an engineer team riding on it was killed, and others were wounded, with broken legs, a broken nose and burns.

8 Platoon, C Company, 8 RAR, moved into its ambush at dusk to keep it secret, and the gunner later saw four enemy moving into the killing ground. A bank of four claymore mines was fired but only two went off; both machine-guns raked the area, illumination was fired, and two groups moved forward to secure the killing ground while grenade launchers covered escape routes. Four enemy bodies were recovered, with a pistol and two grenades; the enemy were possibly from a group in contact with Regional Forces earlier that evening. A US battery fired illumination.
The Anti-Tank Platoon, Support Company, 7 RAR, 6 kilometres south of Xuyen Moc, set off an M16 mine, wounding four Australians. Another mine was found four feet from the first.

Nine men of 1 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, built a small bunker position at night on an enemy route from the Long Hai hills to Long Phuoc Hai, in an area under close Viet Cong watch. When about 15 enemy came down in single file and got within 15 metres, the M60 and a 90mm recoilless rifle opened fire, but the M60 jammed after ten rounds because of sand. A party sent forward to secure bodies was driven back by heavy fire from a flank, and eight claymore mines and two Bangalore torpedoes were blown to silence it; the enemy replied with rocket-propelled grenades, and the rest of the platoon swept in under illumination. The enemy broke contact leaving two bodies, a heavy blood trail and drag marks; an AK47 was captured. The company commander thought the machine-gun failure prevented complete success, and that belts should be carried in tins to keep sand out.

D and E Platoon, 1st Australian Task Force, in ambush on a trail fringed by thick jungle, heard movement and Vietnamese voices and, warned they might be civilians, lay low until the group was seen at 15 metres carrying packs and all armed. The enemy, a food party of about 20 from Hoa Long supplying Viet Cong cadres, stopped to rest in front of the ambush; when two moved into the jungle and saw the soldiers, fire was opened at once. The enemy fled in all directions under covering fire and the ambush pursued them for 150 metres, while artillery and Bushranger gunships hit likely escape routes; a tracker dog team found the area deserted. Two enemy were killed and three heavy blood trails found; 21 packs holding 400 pounds of rice, 100 pounds of other food, clothing and cigarettes, and two carbines and a submachine-gun were captured. The platoon commander was disturbed that his men had shot high, but his superior, noting how new the unit was, thought it the best result that could have been expected.

A section leader of 4 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, had just returned from placing claymore mines when he turned and saw eight to ten enemy following in his footsteps, unaware of the platoon. He fired his rifle, and the enemy fired back with two AK47s and a rocket-propelled grenade, wounding three Australians in the ankle, knee and leg, who were evacuated. The enemy withdrew into dead ground; 106 Field Battery fired illumination and high explosive. The platoon commander thought the section leader should have fired the claymores, which would have killed the leading enemy, instead of his rifle.

8 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, saw an enemy at the edge of the scrub gazing across the paddy towards Dat Do and set an ambush at once; six local force enemy then crossed the paddy 30 metres apart. The platoon fired for three minutes at 150 metres and then advanced by fire and movement; the enemy in the paddy went to ground and fired back, and about nine others who had stayed in the scrub hooked round the platoon's left rear, wounding one Australian in the leg. The platoon saturated the area with fire and grenades and pulled back to the wounded man. The enemy left four dead and dragged away two wounded; one body had an M16 mine attached, and an M16 mine and an M16 rifle were captured.

The Reconnaissance Platoon, Support Company, 7 RAR, in a night harbour, saw a Viet Cong approaching, and the sentry waited until he was a metre away and shot him dead. A second, unseen Viet Cong opened fire with an AK47, and the dead man's pack of explosive blew up, wounding two Australians in the shoulder and eye; the platoon killed the second enemy with machine-gun fire and a grenade. Following a track, the patrol found an M16 mine, another that had been triggered but failed to go off, and bunkers used a day or two earlier, with ammunition, documents, an M16 mine and a training mine.

A half-platoon ambush of 3 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, on the reverse slope of a sand dune west of Long Phuoc Hai, sprang its ambush as five enemy crossed the crest, killing two at once. A third took refuge behind a gravestone and was silenced by the fire and movement that followed, and a drag mark seen under mortar illumination was followed 250 metres. On return the enemy by the gravestone had gone, but the two bodies remained; a pistol and a grenade were captured.
2 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, set off an M16 mine 1.5 kilometres south-east of Hoi My, and three Australians were wounded.

A patrol from the support section of C Company headquarters, 7 RAR, in ambush facing a paddy field, saw by flashes of lightning five enemy walking towards it 150 metres away, and sprang the ambush at 15 metres; ten more were then seen behind. The enemy scattered and fired back with AK47s and M16s, and many were seen to be hit, but a sweep found only one body 150 metres away, the rest having been dragged off, with three heavy drag marks. A rocket launcher was captured. Both M60s stopped when mud splashed onto their belts, and the company commander thought the sweep had also been made too late; 106 Field Battery and a US battery fired in support.

A patrol from C Company headquarters, 7 RAR, in ambush, opened machine-gun fire on two Viet Cong at 30 metres. A sweep by fire and movement 20 seconds later caught one trying to drag the other, wounded, into the bush, and both were killed. Two packs, an AK47 and documents were captured.

2 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, 100 metres north of Phuoc Hai, set off an M16 anti-personnel mine. Two Australians were wounded, one seriously with fragments to the head, and were evacuated by helicopter.
9 Platoon, C Company, 7 RAR, set off a booby trap, possibly a grenade attached to a trip wire, and two Australians were wounded.

2 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, was relieving 1 Platoon in the bunker system taken the day before, and the commanding officer was showing his counterpart around with a protection party, when a booby-trapped 155mm shell went off. One soldier was killed and four wounded, one of whom died soon after; both commanding officers were among the casualties and lost legs.

3 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR/NZ, following Viet Cong tracks for several days, came on caves with old enemy signs, and its reconnaissance element saw signs of mines and heard voices before being attacked with grenades. The platoon moved up, came under grenade and AK47 fire, and replied with grenade launchers as the rocky ground allowed nothing else; while helicopter gunships engaged the enemy, the platoon was hit by rockets, possibly B40s, from the valley, bringing its casualties to six, five New Zealanders and one Australian. Checking the caves later, it was hit by two command-detonated mines, wounding more men. 107 Field Battery and a US battery fired in support.

1 Platoon, W Company, 2 RAR/NZ, fired on at least four Viet Cong, who fired back a rocket-propelled grenade that wounded three New Zealand soldiers, and withdrew. Mortars and artillery, including 161 Field Battery and two US batteries, fired on the withdrawal route. A sweep found one dead enemy, an AK47 and a pack; another enemy was also wounded.
3 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR/NZ, examining caves after its morning contact, set off a 2-pound pressure mine marked by a red cloth on a tree. Two or three men were wounded.

A half-platoon patrol of 4 Platoon, B Company, 2 RAR/NZ, moving down a track, bumped a well-concealed bunker system; a rifleman heard voices, and as he signalled, an AK47 opened fire and the enemy set off three claymore mines, lightly wounding three Australians. The patrol formed all-round defence and brought maximum fire on the four enemy, and 6 Platoon came from 150 metres away and swept through, firing heavily, but the enemy had withdrawn. Four packs holding personal items, 375 AK47 rounds, rice and documents from D65 were captured. The company commander thought the company had had too little training in stealthy reconnaissance in small groups.

A section of 3 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, which had been ambushing a fire trail with a Regional Force company for three days, was disconnecting its claymore mines when three North Vietnamese were seen moving along the trail. The picket carrier fired when they were five metres away, killing the first at once; the second ran 30 metres and was shot dead, and the third appears to have been wounded when the claymores were blown, leaving a drag mark and his pack. An AK47 and two packs were captured, and one of the dead was identified as a squad leader of D65 Battalion.
A command-detonated mine exploded while 3 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR/NZ, was examining caves after its earlier contacts, wounding two more New Zealand soldiers.

1 Platoon, W Company, 2 RAR/NZ, set an immediate ambush when three suspected enemy approached. They were ordered to halt and surrender; the two men ran and were both wounded, and one was captured but died, while the woman surrendered. A party of children followed 30 metres behind, and 15 children were detained in all; enemy documents were captured. The record lists the dead man as a civilian and this as a contact with civilians, and notes that civilians had been warned repeatedly that the area was forbidden to them.

8 Platoon, C Company, 8 RAR, ambushing Route 2 as a supply route into Hoa Long, watched 50 to 60 Viet Cong move carefully into the village, well spaced and crouching, but not through the killing ground, so it let them pass and shifted the ambush to catch them on their return, with armoured personnel carriers of 1 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, on standby. At about 3 am they came back in two groups of about 25, closely spaced, carrying packs and much less alert, and headed straight for one group, so the ambush was sprung early; claymore mines and a crossfire from all four machine-guns, rifles and M72 rockets killed or wounded the whole first group. The second group counter-attacked briefly, then withdrew south-east with the first group's wounded as the carriers arrived; the carriers pursued, killing more and capturing five who had hidden in scrub 800 metres away. Nineteen Viet Cong were killed and six captured, and one surrendered; one Australian was wounded. Weapons, ammunition, documents and large quantities of food, including 550 pounds of rice, were captured; three batteries fired blocking fire west of Hoa Long.

The Anti-Tank Platoon, Support Company, 2 RAR/NZ, examining an enemy camp, set off a Chinese-made mine, recorded as 2 or 20 pounds of explosive. Seven Australians and one South Vietnamese soldier were wounded (another report adds a New Zealander).

The Anti-Tank Platoon, Support Company, 7 RAR, looking for a harbour, saw an enemy and the platoon commander opened fire, but eight enemy then hit the platoon from several directions, wounding the scout and the forward section leader. The other two sections swept through and found a camp of eight shelters, where the enemy were beginning to build bunkers, and drew more bursts of fire; an incoming burst set off a grenade about to be fired, lightly wounding three more Australians. One Australian was killed and four wounded in all; a small quantity of arms, food and clothing was captured, and 106 Field Battery fired in support.

A party of 12 Australians of 2 Platoon, A Company, 7 RAR, and seven Regional Force soldiers had been in ambush at a track junction for 30 minutes when seven enemy in black with light webbing came along. Fire was opened at 15 metres, and the enemy did not fire back; an immediate sweep by fire and movement followed. Four Viet Cong, two men and two women, were killed and an AK47 captured; 106 Field Battery fired in support.

3 Platoon, W Company, 2 RAR/NZ, moving along a track, got a signal from its rear element that Viet Cong were crossing a swamp to the north, and two minutes later the lead section opened fire on movement to its front. Of about six enemy, two were killed and two wounded; an AK47, grenades, ammunition and documents from D65 Battalion were captured. 107 Field Battery fired in support.

The forward section of 3 Platoon, A Company, 8 RAR, heard enemy around a bend in the track and set an immediate ambush, killing three Viet Cong from a food-gathering party with rifle fire. The enemy did not fire back. A pistol was captured, and a US battery probably fired in support.

6 Platoon, B Company, 2 RAR/NZ, following an enemy track, had its forward section at a junction when four or five enemy came round the corner; the section leader and an enemy fired at the same moment and the enemy was killed, a North Vietnamese. The rest deployed on a broad front with a well-rehearsed fire and movement drill and another was seen to fall; the section advanced by fire and movement and the enemy withdrew. One Australian was lightly wounded when a grenade-launcher round hit a twig and exploded 15 metres in front of the firer. An AK47, magazines and a pack were captured; the commanders thought the enemy's aggressiveness had made the section waste ammunition and wanted better fire control, and 107 Field Battery fired in support.

4 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, had just set an ambush on a track through high grass when the sentry saw an unarmed woman and challenged her. The left flank section commander stood up to look over the grass, saw an armed enemy and opened fire to cover the sentry's return; the enemy fired back, wounding him in the shoulder. The M60 and claymore mines were fired; a sweep found one dead enemy and an SKS rifle, and the other two escaped. The platoon commander thought the sentry was right to challenge, as the woman might have been an innocent civilian, though the area was closed to civilians.

About 45 Viet Cong walked into an ambush laid by 6 Platoon and B Company Headquarters, 7 RAR, with a section of B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment; the ambush held fire until the killing ground was full, then fired all its claymores and weapons. The enemy fought back with rifles, rocket-propelled grenades and machine-guns and made many attempts to recover their dead. There were no friendly casualties; 21 Viet Cong were killed and nine wounded, and a large haul of weapons, ammunition, mines, a radio and very significant documents, at least one of strategic value, was captured. The dead included the second-in-command and political officer of D445 Local Force Battalion and several of its platoon and section leaders.

6 Platoon, B Company, 2 RAR/NZ, in ambush in a rubber plantation covering the house of a known Viet Cong food supplier, first saw 10 unarmed people, who ran and were not fired on. Later, after signals with torches and a lantern, enemy crept towards the position and the ambush was sprung when whispering was heard in front of the machine-gun; the enemy threw a grenade and fought back with AK47s and a rocket-propelled grenade until armoured personnel carriers were heard approaching. Two Australians were wounded and 10 enemy were killed, dressed in black; two AK47s and two packs were captured. A prisoner later said 14 were killed and five or six wounded.

6 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, in ambush, let a party of 15 pass because the ambush was badly aligned, then re-sited it on the track; shortly after, about 20 enemy, a Viet Cong food party of the Long Dat district force, came the other way and the platoon opened fire on the first seven at five metres. The enemy fought back with grenades and rifles, and a dying enemy soldier threw a grenade into the machine-gun pit, killing one Australian and wounding another; the official history says a machine-gun also jammed. Five enemy were killed and seven blood trails found, and an M16, packs and a large quantity of food were captured. Artillery fired in support.

A lying-up ambush patrol of 5 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, ambushed about 20 enemy approaching from the Long Hai hills, who fired back with rifles, a rocket-propelled grenade and two grenades. One Australian was killed and three wounded; the medical evacuation helicopter was briefly fired on and left with the most badly wounded man, and armoured personnel carriers withdrew the rest. The carriers' arrival revealed two enemy dead and six blood trails. US and Australian artillery fired in support.

6 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, searching for a suspected bunker system, followed a track showing about 20 enemy nearby, found an old bunker and was fired on by hidden enemy with machine-guns and rocket-propelled grenades, wounding three soldiers; as the sections moved to contact another was hit, and he later died. When the enemy began to work around the flanks, helicopter gunships attacked with miniguns and rockets, and armoured personnel carriers of 2 Troop, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, came in, engaged the enemy and evacuated the wounded. The platoon then cleared the bunker area, but the enemy had gone, leaving two blood trails. The company commander said casualties would have been heavier had the battalion commander not controlled the air support from a helicopter overhead, and the gunships arrived quickly because the battalion command post had ordered them up in advance.

A half-platoon ambush of 4 Platoon, B Company, 7 RAR, three days in position near a new D445 Battalion bunker area, was mortared and then attacked by 25 to 30 enemy with machine-guns, AK47s, rocket-propelled grenades and grenades. The enemy's first assault went the wrong way, missing the position by 50 metres, and the patrol's fire brought down four of them; helicopter gunships broke up the attack, one being shot down and another hit, though the downed helicopter was recovered. Two Australians were wounded; one enemy body and heavy blood trails, suggesting at least seven wounded, were found, and later patrols found a 55-bunker complex. The company commander credited good fire control, and the platoon commander thought the enemy gave themselves away by talking.

8 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR, with a tracking team following a fresh enemy track, saw an enemy in a grassy clearing, challenged him and fired when he ran. The main enemy body of 20 to 30, digging in in thick bamboo beside the platoon's flank, opened fire with AK47s, automatic rifles and rocket-propelled grenades, catching the platoon in open ground; one Australian was killed and two or three wounded. Artillery, including 107 Field Battery and a US battery, and helicopter gunships supported the platoon, and aircraft engaged the enemy's escape routes as they withdrew south. Fifteen shelters, hammocks, tools, clothing, webbing, a B40 round and a grenade were recovered.

A patrol from 3 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR/NZ, ambushed six or more enemy, the M60 sweeping the killing ground, and the enemy withdrew north-east. A sweep was driven back to the ambush position by automatic fire, and mortars and Bushranger helicopter gunships then attacked, the gunships also firing on movement 300 metres away; a second sweep met no resistance, and artillery fired in support. Five Viet Cong were killed and one wounded and captured, and two more were possibly killed by the gunships; weapons, webbing, food and documents were captured.

D Company, 3 RAR, in a circular harbour beside a strip of rice paddy during its in-country training, fired claymores and machine-guns at enemy 20 to 30 metres away, then at about 10 enemy trying to recover bodies, while more enemy attacked 10 Platoon's perimeter with heavy AK47 fire. A satchel charge thrown inside the perimeter killed the platoon commander and wounded a soldier, who stayed on duty, and rifle fire killed another soldier and wounded one more. C Company nearby was also probed; the enemy signalled with tin whistles and fired rifles and rocket-propelled grenades. Helicopter gunships, artillery illumination and fire on withdrawal routes, and a tank of C Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, supported, and casualties were evacuated by helicopter. Two Australians were killed and two wounded; three enemy were recorded wounded.

While the Anti-Tank Platoon, Support Company, 7 RAR, was in an ambush position in jungle south of Xuyen Moc, a machine-gunner rolled over onto an M16 mine, which exploded. Five Australians were wounded, two of whom later died.

A half-platoon ambush of 9 Platoon, C Company, 8 RAR, on the main route into Hoa Long, fired its flank claymore mines at an estimated 20 to 30 enemy. The enemy fired back with rifles, rocket-propelled grenades and a grenade launcher and made three probing attacks from different directions at once over 40 minutes, driven off by claymores and rifle fire; one machine-gun failed with a broken firing pin and the other kept stopping. Seven armoured personnel carriers of 1 and 3 Troops, B Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, arrived and the enemy broke contact; three Australians were wounded by rocket-grenades. Three wounded enemy were captured by the carriers, and heavy drag marks, bloodstains and a blood trail were found next morning; 161 Field Battery fired in support.

A sentry of 1 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR/NZ, ambushing a track, killed an enemy soldier with two rifle shots and captured his AK47, and the machine-gun and grenade launcher fired into the area. During the sweep, a grass fire started by the machine-gun's tracer set off a claymore mine, wounding two New Zealand soldiers, one of whom, the platoon commander, died. The sweep was abandoned.

After its earlier contact, 8 Platoon, C Company, 2 RAR/NZ, called in helicopter gunships and began clearing the bunker system, but the 8 to 10 enemy there, armed with AK47s, rocket-propelled grenades, grenades and claymore mines, were too strong and well dug in, and three Australians were wounded. Gunships and artillery then fired on the bunkers. The recently renovated system held 11 bunkers in a line 150 metres long; US claymores, a radio aerial and cooking gear were captured.

The forward section of 5 Platoon, B Company, 2 RAR, heard enemy talking 30 metres ahead, crept forward, and opened fire with a machine-gun when three enemy saw them. A sweep found one body and heard moaning from a bunker already grenaded, which was grenaded again, killing the man inside; the rest of the four to six enemy had withdrawn. Two enemy were killed and two wounded, and an AK47 and documents were captured. The platoon had not known a bunker system was there. Artillery fired in support.

Four or five enemy who had camped overnight 50 metres from an ambush of 2 Platoon, V Company, 2 RAR/NZ, walked into it the next morning; the platoon fired claymores and a machine-gun, killing three and wounding one. Only two of the six claymores went off; the platoon commander blamed weak leads, which he said needed changing every fortnight. Weapons, 100 pounds of cooked rice, other food, documents and medical supplies were captured.

A patrol of 2 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, was hit by two mines, one a US claymore; one Australian was killed and one wounded, apparently an engineer. The record says one was command-detonated, though the battalion commander and his staff thought both had been set off by pressure switches.

1 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR/NZ, under command of 3 RAR, following a freshly used track, fired on a group of five enemy 10 metres ahead, who seemed to be hit, and ran into the headquarters of D445 Battalion and its C2 Company. Heavy fire came from three sides with machine-guns, mortars, rocket-propelled grenades, grenades and satchel charges; gunships struggled to identify friendly positions, and several helicopters, including a Possum and a medical evacuation helicopter, were hit and forced to land. After two hours, low on ammunition, the platoon broke contact with its own fire and withdrew, abandoning packs and the weapons of the wounded, and was relieved by the Assault Pioneer Platoon of 3 RAR; a helicopter evacuation attempt was hit and a crewman mortally wounded. The contact report lists nine Australians wounded, two of whom died, one of them an RAAF crewman; enemy losses were two killed, including a body found later in a grave, and six wounded, and the enemy recovered a machine-gun, rifles, claymores and explosives left behind.

A half-platoon of 8 Platoon, C Company, 3 RAR, patrolling a track, heard chopping, digging and a dog barking, fired grenades at the sound and swept forward into a bunker system; two explosions, possibly grenades, wounded the platoon commander, who later died, and the machine-gunner, and heavy fire pinned the patrol down. It withdrew, leaving the two wounded at first, and another soldier was hit. Gunships could not pick out the friendly troops because the smoke grenades had run out, and one gunship was hit by ground fire, its co-pilot later dying; the Assault Pioneer Platoon in armoured personnel carriers, the rest of the company and a troop of tanks converged, and the enemy, thought to be a stay-behind group, withdrew. The camp was new and possibly a headquarters. The dead platoon commander was criticised for attacking without a reconnaissance, and most ammunition and smoke had been in packs dropped at the start of the contact; artillery could not fire because the platoon's location was uncertain.

The Assault Pioneer Platoon, Support Company, 3 RAR, sent to help 1 Platoon, A Company, 2 RAR, joined it and helped evacuate the wounded, then covered its withdrawal. As it withdrew downhill it was followed by four to six enemy with heavy weapons and rifles and drove them off with fire and movement. One Australian was wounded; one enemy was recorded killed and four wounded.

9 Platoon, C Company, 3 RAR, moving in single file along an armoured personnel carrier track, saw four enemy approaching from the side 20 metres away; two riflemen of the lead section crouched and waited until they were five metres away, then killed the first and critically wounded the second, who was captured but died after evacuation. A third left a light blood trail. An AK47, a carbine, grenades, detonators and documents were captured and two ox-carts destroyed. Artillery fired in support.

9 Platoon, C Company, 3 RAR, 15 minutes after a resupply by aircraft, saw four or five enemy approaching; the enemy opened fire, then split up and withdrew north-east and north-west. Following the tracks, the platoon found one enemy dead with an AK47 and documents, and an M16 and a bloodstained, bullet-holed pack, showing another was wounded. The dead man was identified as a member of D445 Battalion.

An armoured personnel carrier of A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, carrying B Company Headquarters, hit an anti-tank mine on Route 328 north of Thua Tich. The accounts disagree: one says a 20-pound mine badly damaged the carrier and wounded two crew, the other a small mine, possibly fitted with a rocket-grenade warhead, causing light damage and no casualties. The record lists two wounded.

An armoured personnel carrier of 1 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, set off a 40-pound mine buried 18 inches deep on Route 328 just north of Route 23. One account says the carrier was heavily damaged and its two crew lightly wounded, another that damage was moderate with no casualties; the record lists two wounded. A patrol of the Assault Pioneer Platoon, 3 RAR, detained two young women and an old man without identity papers, who refused to answer questions.

An armoured personnel carrier of A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, set off an anti-tank mine of 20 to 40 pounds on Route 328 just south of Thua Tich, apparently recently laid with a pressure switch. The carrier was badly damaged and two crew were wounded.

After a night of artillery and mortar fire on the bunker system it had found the day before, 5 Platoon, B Company, 3 RAR, advanced up a spur and ran into heavy fire at 15 metres from bunkers held by part of 3 Battalion, 33 Regiment, with machine-guns, heavy machine-guns and rocket-propelled grenades; the rest of B Company came up in support. The fight went on for most of the day: helicopter gunships and later US Cobras attacked with miniguns and rockets within 30 metres of the platoon, the company's artillery forward observer was killed, and a helicopter dropping ammunition was shot down, two of its RAAF crew dying. Tanks of C Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, attacked the bunkers from the rear and, with D Company and cavalry, secured the system by late afternoon; packs, documents, food and a radio were found. Three Australians were killed, including the two RAAF crew, and about 12 wounded, four of whom stayed on duty; five enemy were recorded killed. The company commander noted that smoke grenades dissipated under the 150-foot canopy while a marker balloon worked well, rifle grenades were effective, and machine-guns failed badly, three having to be replaced during the fight.

Three armoured personnel carriers of A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, carrying D and E Platoons, were patrolling a track when the lead driver saw an artillery illumination canister he suspected was part of a mine and stopped; the enemy, of 274 Regiment, then opened fire with rifles and rocket-propelled grenades. A grenade hit a pile of claymore mines on the back of the last carrier, which exploded, killing its crew and five soldiers of D and E Platoons and wounding three others, one of whom later died. Eight Australians died in all. Australian and US artillery fired in support.

Tanks of 5 and 3 Troops, C Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, with armoured personnel carriers of 2 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, moved to support 5 Platoon, B Company, 3 RAR, and attacked the bunker complex; the lead tank was fired on by rocket-propelled grenades and rifles, and two tanks were hit, one slightly damaged and the other by a round that failed to explode. The tanks destroyed at least five bunkers with their guns, canister and machine-guns and, after waiting for D Company, swept on to find more bunkers, by then deserted. Three Australians were slightly wounded by grenade fragments and stayed on duty. Three enemy were counted killed, though the record suggests at least six is a conservative estimate.

After the morning ambush, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, and B Company, 4 RAR, flown in, surrounded the enemy in the jungle along a nearby creek. 1 Section, 3 Troop, patrolling 400 metres from the first ambush site, was itself ambushed by the enemy, of 274 Regiment, with rifles and rocket-propelled grenades; three carriers were hit and two Australians wounded. The enemy withdrew south-west.

Two sentries of 9 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR/NZ, harboured beside a fresh track, shot dead an enemy soldier armed with an AK47, then withdrew into the perimeter while two machine-guns swept the area. An AK47, ammunition, a compass and documents were captured; he belonged to a convalescent company of 274 Regiment.

A sentry of C Company Headquarters, 4 RAR/NZ, fired at an enemy soldier in front of him and was shot in the leg by another he had not seen. The enemy withdrew and artillery and mortars fired on the area; moaning was heard during the night, but a sweep the next morning found nothing. The platoon commander thought the sentry had let the first enemy slip past and had expected them only from the creek, and that sentries must expect the enemy from any direction.

An armoured personnel carrier of A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, set off a 50-pound shaped-charge anti-tank mine at the northern edge of the Cam My rubber, which penetrated and badly damaged it, wounding one crewman. The carrier was recovered.
Elements of C Company, 4 RAR/NZ, heard movement and fired on the area. One enemy was possibly wounded and was seen being dragged away.

1 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, set a series of ambushes along the southern edge of the Courtenay rubber plantation on a dark night of heavy rain; four armoured personnel carriers of 11 Section ambushed an enemy force at 10 metres with claymores and machine-guns, and when they swept the area the enemy counter-attacked with grenades. The other sections left their ambushes and swept the area with spotlights, and light contacts went on until about 3 am, with further prisoners taken the next morning. Twelve enemy were killed and three Viet Cong captured, one of them wounded; weapons, 22 packs, a large quantity of documents, food and a field surgical kit were captured. Another body was found in July. Artillery fired illumination.

Following up 2 Platoon's contact, 1 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR/NZ, under command of C Squadron, 1 Armoured Regiment, advanced with tanks and armoured personnel carriers on a large bunker system held by 1 Battalion, 274 Regiment. A rocket-propelled grenade hit the forward tank; when a second was fired, the platoon engaged and was met by heavy fire from enemy who had moved out onto its left flank, and for 15 minutes the infantry, tanks and carriers fought back with canister and machine-guns. The enemy used heavy and light machine-guns, rocket-propelled grenades and claymores, and CS gas was noticed; Cobra gunships and artillery supported, and the carriers and tanks came under fire again during the evening, including during a medical evacuation. The record lists seven Australians and New Zealanders wounded, including two cavalrymen hit by a rocket grenade or claymore; three bodies were later found, and the armoured report estimated five and possibly 12 enemy casualties. The area was not swept, so the true enemy losses are unclear.

2 Platoon, V Company, 4 RAR/NZ, found signs of a bunker system and probed forward on a broad front with three sections; at the edge of the area an enemy soldier walked towards the platoon and was shot at 15 metres. The machine-guns fired on enemy voices and were answered with rocket-propelled grenades, machine-guns, rifles and claymores along a 50-metre front, and the platoon withdrew under helicopter gunship cover with two wounded; the enemy followed, wounding a third. The platoon commander complained the artillery was unacceptably late because of repeated check-fires, and that he had to keep insisting the gunships fire closer. Lessons drawn were that advancing on a broad front revealed the enemy's main killing area, machine-guns must support each other because the enemy concentrated on them, and a plan for withdrawal was needed when attacking bunkers.

7 Platoon, C Company, 4 RAR/NZ, ambushed three alert but fast-moving enemy on a track with claymores, killing all three, and a machine-gun then fired into the area. Three AK47s, packs, torches, documents and batteries were captured. Company and battalion commanders were impressed by how little ammunition was used. Artillery fired in support.

The support section of V Company Headquarters, 4 RAR/NZ, on reconnaissance, found several Viet Cong tracks, one blocked with logs and tied-down trees; while investigating it the section leader saw movement 30 metres away and opened fire, and two other enemy fired on two scouts exploring the other tracks, hitting one. The enemy fired a rocket-propelled grenade that missed widely and withdrew south. The wounded New Zealand soldier was evacuated by helicopter but later died. A body in black found nearby a few days later, with an AK47, was probably from this contact.

The rearmost soldier of 6 Platoon, B Company, 4 RAR/NZ, following a track north, saw three enemy approaching from behind and fired two aimed shots and a burst. A sweep found one dead and two blood trails; documents, medals and a belt were captured, and what looked like a cache was seen hanging in a tree. A second body found nearby some days later by 10 Platoon was almost certainly from this contact.

11 Section, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, moving to an ambush position, saw two people in rubber 600 metres away and went to investigate, finding about 10 armed enemy, apparently a porter party, running away. They ignored a warning burst and scattered, and the carriers opened fire, killing one and wounding two, one of whom died; the other was captured, with two AK47s and a pistol. During the sweep that followed, two shots hit two carriers and the area was fired on.

11 Section and Troop Headquarters, 1 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, moving through long grass towards an ambush position, met 10 armed enemy and opened fire with machine-guns; the enemy split into two groups and disappeared into the grass. Two wounded enemy were later captured and a body was found in the area.

12 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR/NZ, deploying from its night position, was fired on from a well-established bunker system of 3 Battalion, 33 North Vietnamese Regiment, and one Australian was killed and two wounded; artillery and a wide range of aircraft attacked the position to within 40 metres, and 11 Platoon fought off an enemy probe. In the afternoon D Company assaulted, but 15 metres short of the bunkers it came under intense fire from the flanks, and the leading section lost three killed and one who died of wounds; the company withdrew, leaving its dead, while napalm was dropped. The enemy followed up and D Company, having bumped into a second bunker system, fought a heavy contact until dark, with artillery brought to within 100 metres. Two days later, with V Company, it recovered the dead and all lost equipment. Five Australians were killed and nine wounded; the enemy lost 18 dead, nine of them to air attack. The commander noted how hard it was to find and indicate targets in close country.

6 Platoon, B Company, 4 RAR/NZ, still following the telephone wire, fired on a man rolling it up and followed his tracks; later a reconnaissance party looking for a night position fired on enemy on three sides and fell back, and the main body came under rifle and 60 mm mortar fire and took many casualties. 4 Platoon, sent to help, killed one of three enemy on the way and joined 6 Platoon at a helicopter winch point; B Company Headquarters was also mortared. Artillery, three US Pink Teams and airstrikes with napalm and bombs hit the area. Fifteen Australians were wounded, three of whom stayed on duty; the enemy were thought to be headquarters and support elements of 33 North Vietnamese Regiment, and seven enemy were recorded killed. Two bunker complexes were later found around the contact area.

11 Platoon, D Company, 4 RAR/NZ, checking a track, met about 20 North Vietnamese soldiers coming round a corner 20 metres ahead and opened fire, killing the leading man; the enemy quickly deployed and returned automatic fire, then were ordered by their commander to withdraw. Artillery and a US Pink Team helicopter team followed them up, though the artillery was interrupted while the helicopters got organised. A body and an AK47 were found, and a second partly buried body the next day. The enemy were believed to be from 3 Battalion, 33 North Vietnamese Regiment.

11 Section, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, escorting a vehicle along Route 2, ran into an ambush about 100 metres long by around 20 enemy, who fired rifles and rocket-propelled grenades; the rockets all missed, but the second carrier was hit by rifle fire. The enemy dispersed under continuous machine-gun fire, and a sweep found one enemy dead and an AK47. One Australian was slightly wounded above the eye. The ambush was well designed and would have been very effective had the first carrier been hit and blocked the road; the enemy were probably of 33 North Vietnamese Regiment.

1 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, driving back through the Cam My rubber, had an armoured personnel carrier hit a pressure-switched Chinese block-charge mine, and a second carrier on its way to help set off another. One account says belly armour prevented serious harm and two crew were wounded; the other says both vehicles were badly damaged and four Australians wounded.

1 Troop, A Squadron, 3 Cavalry Regiment, driving back through the Cam My rubber, had an armoured personnel carrier hit a 60-pound pressure-switched mine, wounding two crew; another carrier going to help hit a second mine, wounding a crewman and an engineer. Belly armour prevented more serious damage and injuries, though one account says both vehicles were badly damaged. Four Australians were wounded in all.

6 Platoon, B Company, 4 RAR/NZ, following a telephone wire it had found, stopped briefly; two enemy approached, apparently checking the wire, and the sentry killed one. An AK47 was captured. Later the platoon fired on a man coiling up the wire, believed to be the second.
